The Council should be replaced with a democratic executive
The cancellation of Third World debt
Freedom and justice for the Palestinian people as the essential foundation for lasting peace in the Middle East
Israel must implement UN Resolution 242, ending its occupation of all the Palestinian territories and allowing a real peace process to begin
No carte-blanche facilitation of NATO forces at Irish airports

The ending of sanctions against the people of Iraq which are responsible for the deaths of thousands of children through deprivation of medicines, and no extension of war to that country by the US, Britain and their allies
An end to the United States' embargo of Cuba
That the "Tobin Tax" - a proposed tax on international financial speculation with revenue - to be used to promote development in the poorer regions of the world
The Irish Government promote human rights and disarmament worldwide
An increase in Irish Government aid to the Third World
An international alliance for the closure of Sellafield
MEDIA
Sinn Féin believes that the operation of the media should be as much in the public domain and under as much public scrutiny as the media itself demands of other bodies and institutions
Public access to information is a fundamental right
Public Service Broadcasting
Sinn Féin supports public service broadcasting and views publicly owned and democratically accountable media, free from state or government control, as a mainstay of democracy

In particular the legal obligation on RTÉ to provide a varied programme output, to promote the Irish language and to present news and current affairs in an objective, impartial and fair manner is a positive factor in Irish society
Despite our criticism of the effect of state censorship directed against Sinn Féin and its lingering effects on some RTÉ personnel, Sinn Féin is committed to support for public service broadcasting
We are for more public accountability and freedom and less state control over broadcasters

It is clear that the amount of home produced programmes, employment levels and the development of a broadcasting skills base in this state is primarily a consequence of the existence of a publicly owned RTÉ
Highly successful innovations represented by Radio na Gaeltachta and TG4 would not have had any hope of existing in a market driven broadcasting environment
The institution of Radio na Gaeltachta helped to give confidence to Gaeltacht communities as a rich and viable linguistic community
In addition music and culture in the Irish language was revitalised by Radio na Gaeltachta
This would not have happened, had the task been left to the market
The advent of Telifis na Gaeilge, now TG4, has reinvigorated programme quality and brought new talent to Irish television, as well as bringing the language to a new generation
The democratic rights of an important linguistic community are safeguarded by this recognition of their informational and cultural rights and is supported by the vast majority of Irish people
New technology

It is clear that there are new technological developments in broadcasting which will have little indigenous involvement if the market is allowed to dictate who will and will not be involved in the digital revolution in television
The winners will be multinational communications companies with their headquarters outside Ireland
The vast majority of programming will be sourced outside this country, with consequent knock on effects on employment and downstream broadcasting activity
There have been massive private sector failures in Britain and Germany recently, to the advantage of already dominant players such as News International

Sinn Féin considers it essential that the origination of news & current affairs and the depiction and encouragement of elements of Irish culture in all their diversity, including the Irish language, are safeguarded by the continuation of public provision for broadcasting
If this provision is not forthcoming RTE will lose significant parts of its audience to broadcasters with greater programming and marketing budgets
This vicious circle could in turn undermine public support for RTE
Sinn Féin will vigorously oppose such moves and will support new innovations within the public service model and state provision for such innovations
The Challenge of Change: Independent Productions
RTE must change; there is no doubt about that
It must be responsive to its statutory responsibilities, but it must also be flexible in its approach to innovation in programme making:
For example, Sinn Féin proposes that RTE's commissioning process for independent productions be financially and organisationally independent of the station itself
This will aid diversity is programming and will aid transparency in the commissioning of programmes
License Fee
In the past ministers have used the license fee as a means of punishing RTE for being too "independent"

We believe that RTE has made an adequate case for the level of financing required for preparation for digital television services and we believe that the Minister is withholding that increase for political reasons
Sinn Féin supports an adequate level of financing for RTE and believes that the decision on license fee levels should be taken out of the political domain
The level of the license fee should be set on an objective basis
Sinn Féin proposes:
That License fee renewal be agreed on a five yearly basis by an independent panel comprised of representatives of the social partners, the Film Board, the Arts Council and Conradh na Gaeilge
That such a group also be empanelled to evaluate the future of television and to propose a level of capital funding required to prepare RTE for the digital age
The Minister's current forum on broadcasting is a delaying mechanism instituted by a Minister who is hostile to RTE

Public Service Independent Broadcasters Sinn Féin proposes that such broadcasters make a biennial public report to the Broadcasting Commission at public hearings on their adherence to public service requirements in their licence and that the Commission make two yearly legally binding proposals to such broadcasters on the carrying out of their public service remit
This proposal is in line with our view that those who run the media should run it in public, and not behind closed doors

No more Privatisation of Culture Satellite broadcasting has bought access to major national and other sporting events, which were previously, free to terrestrial television viewers of public service television
This has distorted the market in sport, has raised the price for the consumer, and has enriched a few individuals
Despite an early commitment from the previous minister on this issue, nothing has been done to ensure universality of access to these events
Sinn Féin proposes the immediate designation of certain sporting events as having a statutory entitlement to universal audience access
Print Media
There is increasing concern about the dominance of a small number of individuals and companies in the print media
Sinn Féin proposes:
A statutory 'right to reply' law for persons subject to serious allegations in print media
Severe curtailment of the current libel laws

That all privately owned media with an average yearly circulation above 20,000 audited sales per issue be governed by legally binding trusts that safeguards media professionals from pressure or interference from media owners
Editorial staff at senior level and representatives elected by journalists would have representation on the board of such trusts
A review of monopoly legislation to prevent any one media company having a monopoly position in any given media sector
Sinn Féin believes that such a regulation will lead to a more independent, robust and vigorous press
Under-regulated market driven print media leads to monopoly control and the stifling of real diversity
FINE GAEL MANIFESTO 1997
Securing and sharing our prosperity.
This publication is our first of a series of statements of Fine Gael's policy priorities to be released throughout the campaign.
These statements are Fine Gael's core elements of a programme to secure out nation's prosperity and share it fairly for the benefit of all our citizens.
The tasks and the challenges which confront the Millennium Government are outlined.
We then address the requirements for continued prosperity in terms of key public and private-sector policies to cope with and overcome the future challenges.
There is a focus on elements necessary for a continuation of sound management of the public finances including the key ingredients of radical tax reform.
Finally, we outline specific targeted measures to aggressively tackle unemployment, especially long-term unemployment.
Tasks for the millennium Government Objectives for the millennium government. The economy is working well but we clearly have a further road to travel.
Fine Gael's objectives for Irish society, as we look to the dawn of the new Millennium, are:

To consolidate our high growth and low inflation performance of recent years through promoting competitive public and private enterprise, sound public finances and continued tax reform and reductions.
To continue the fight against crime; especially drug-related crime, and attacks on the elderly and on women.
To support families in their care of their children, their elderly and their incapacitated members, in a way that takes account of the pressures on family structures.
To substantially reduce long-term unemployment, especially its persistence over time and from one generation to the next in some families.
To promote greater access to education and to deepen the quality of its delivery at all levels.
To stop environmental degradation, and start the process of renewing the environment.
To work for a lasting reconciliation and peace in Northern Ireland, and for an end to sectarianism, intimidation and triumphalism emanating from either side of the traditional divide.
Our ability as a nation to make progress towards achieving most of these objectives depends on our success in consolidating and enhancing the economic prosperity we've enjoyed in the last few years.
Measures to secure this prosperity and thus to permit a fair sharing of the gains arising are set out in this statement.
Our targets to secure prosperity for the next 5 years are to see our economy grow by at least 5% each year.
If that happens, within 15 years the total value of the goods and services Ireland produces will have doubled.
Keep inflation below 2% per annum.
Achieve mortgage and other interest rates of no more than 5% - 6% from 1999 onwards.
Increase the total number at work in Ireland by at least 35,000 - 40,000 each year.
Substantially reduce the overall rate of unemployment and the rate of long-term unemployment consistent with the government's ten-year targets.
The challenges ahead:
But we cannot take the continuation of this prosperity for granted.
It will have to be achieved in the face of several possible challenges.
Entry to European Monetary Union.
A possible reduction in Structural Funds after 1999.
Enlargement of the European Union to the East to include up to ten additional countries.
A new World Trade Organisation agreement, further trade liberalisation and globalisation of the economy.

The emergence of blockages to prosperity, such as congestion in the employment market as some skills become scarcer, the need for further improvements in our infrastructure and to ensure the availability of quality housing at affordable prices.
Partnership 2000, Social Inclusion and Equality:
Partnership 2000 gives us the confidence to plan for the future.
An unprecedented wide group of people were involved in its negotiation.
This agreement sets out the foundation for future progress across a range of policies for the next two years and many of our strategies for the future are informed by this agreement.
As a member of the Government that agreed Partnership 2000, we are in the best position to deliver it.

We reiterate in particular our commitment to see practical effect given to the pledges in Partnership 2000 to accelerate the process of social inclusion through the vehicle of the recently inaugurated National Anti-Poverty Strategy.
The promotion of equality of treatment for all individuals and groups which have not previously been accorded the rights due to citizens of this.
State is also a key theme of this agreement and one which Fine Gael fully supports as being consistent with its steadfast endeavours to promote a "Just Society".
Challenges Ahead:
The government which distinguished itself during the recent EU Presidency can validly claim to have the best credentials to overcome the following possible challenges in the next five years.
The establishment of European Monetary Union.
Structural Funds after 1999.
The enlargement and deepening of the Union.
European Monetary Union.
We believe the time for debating whether to join the single currency without the UK's participation has now past.

The debate must now shift to how best we can extract maximum advantage for this country from involvement in the single currency and in particular how to chart the correct policy course in the event of the UK not joining in the early years of the single currency.
A recent study by the ESRI has shown that Ireland will benefit from joining the single currency, even without the UK, on any reasonable appraisal of the risks involved.
The main benefits will be in terms of relative price and exchange rate stability and of course low interest rates.

These benefits will ensure that we continue to remain highly attractive to internationally mobile investment, which has been one of the foundation stones for the huge advances we've made in employment creation in recent years.
But there is no room for complacency.
By joining the single currency, we will be giving up for good the freedom to adjust our exchange rate as we see fit.
We thus face the potential risk of Sterling volatility.
Action across a number of fronts can insure employment in Ireland against this risk.
A continued emphasis on sound, public finances, and, in particular, on reductions in tax burdens for workers and enterprise.
This will provide our trading sectors with greater room to respond to competitiveness' shocks if they arise.
Further emphasis on developing an educated and trained workforce, with globally tradable skills.
We therefore place an especial emphasis on investing in human capital, especially through the acquisition of foreign language and computer skills.
Active encouragement of market diversification.
Forbairt, the IDA and An Bord Trachtala (ABT) will be required to propose schemes to encourage the necessary marketing and re-training investment to facilitate such diversification.

Building on Fine Gael-inspired initiatives to promote more flexible systems of wage and salary compensation, we want these issues to be placed at the centre of negotiations on a successor to Partnership 2000.
In this respect, measures to improve partnership between workers and employers at firm level, as stressed in Partnership 2000, are of crucial importance.
Structural Funds:
Ireland has been the success story of the EU Structural Funds.

The claims of other poorer member states and the prospect of new member states requires that Government will have to construct a robust case to retain the Structural Funds after 1999 at the highest possible level.
Fine Gael's position is simple.
Ireland should not be penalised because of our recent success.
Fine Gael in Government be seeking substantial funding for the whole country.
We believe that there are several arguments which justify this position.
First, Ireland continues to have an exceptional long-term unemployment problem despite significant recent improvement.
Second, we have further investment requirements for public infrastructure in relation to roads, water and waste management, our ports and telecommunications.
Third, the Structural Funds eligibility criterion is based on GDP which in Ireland's case considerably exceeds GNP because of our high level of profit repatriations.
Fourth, while the flawed GDP per capita measure pushes us into the vulnerable zone as far as maximising our entitlement to Structural Funds, our "catch up" has been fairly recent.
Finally, any sizeable and precipitous reduction in the level of Structural Funds after 1999 could undo the real convergence gains which the current funding has achieved.
EU Enlargement and deepening of the Union.
The possibility of a Union of up to 25 members brings both opportunities and threats.
The prospect of a single market with an additional 100 million people promises opportunities for all existing members and provides further assurance for continuing peace and stability in Europe.
Following our successful Presidency of the EU, Ireland's role at the centre of Europe is now assured.
Fine Gael will protect Ireland's vital national interests where representation on the Commission and voting rights are concerned.
The biggest threat to our economic interests, however, will emerge in relation to agricultural policies.

CAP reform will be driven by the continuation of the MacSharry reforms, the implementation of commitments given by the EU in the last international trade agreement and any new ones which may emerge from the Round which will commence in 1999.

Fine Gael reiterates the commitments given in Partnership 2000 to ensure "that any change to EU policy is achieved in a manner which protects the legitimate interests of Ireland's farming and rural communities and the food industry".
Fine Gael will oppose any attempt to re-nationalise the CAP.

In the light of the European Commission's Agenda 2000 proposals, we call for the development and implementation of a ten-year plan for Irish food and farming which will enable Ireland to become a competitive world-class food producer.
Securing Prosperity Through Promoting Competitive Public And Private Enterprise.
Maintaining competitive advantage.
Our recent prosperity, in terms of high growth, low inflation and record employment creation, has been based on the achievement and maintenance of international competitiveness.
In the short to medium term, domestic wage rates, exchange and interest rates are crucial to keeping our competitive edge.
Constant improvements in the productivity of all our resources are, however, critical in the medium to long term as they are the foundation for enduring gains in our productive capacity.
Fine Gael wants to see Ireland attain a permanent place in the "top 10" league of international competitiveness.
That will require action on several fronts.

Prudent management of the public finances, and especially the ultimate elimination of the Exchequer deficit over the economic cycle is a necessary condition for ensuring competitiveness along with successful adherence to the disciplines of Monetary Union after 1999.
But it is not sufficient.
Sustained competitiveness requires every sector of our economy, both public and private, to be constantly engaged in the process of innovation.
Fine Gael believes innovation needs.
Investment in "human capital", that is, education and training of people and in "knowledge capital", that is, R&D.

Investment in public and private infrastructure, e.g., transport, telecommunications, water and sewerage services and Institutional flexibility and adaptability in the private and public sectors to embrace change.

Fine Gael believes that the establishment of a top-level National Competitiveness Council reporting to An Taoiseach, to develop, monitor and propose actions for a pro-competitiveness agenda embracing the role of R&D, training, information technology should be an important national initiative to achieve our competitiveness agenda and attain our place in the top-ten league of international competitiveness.
Ireland's recent growth and employment performance can to a substantial degree be attributed to our investment in "human capital" which is now really beginning to bear fruit.
"Human capital" investment repays dividends through higher earnings for more educated and trained persons than for those with poorer levels.
It also permits complementary investment in physical capital and R&D.
The most obvious example of this process is the increase in the level of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
There is thus a double prosperity dividend from investment in "human capital".
An enhanced commitment to education and training will be one of our principal obsessions over the next five years.
Investment by the State complemented by EU Structural and Cohesion funds has resulted in tremendous improvement in the infrastructure for enterprise in recent years.
But also of importance has been the unleashing of competitive forces in many State utilities which provide vitally important services to the enterprise sector.
Fine Gael will continue to promote both of these areas as a means to improving our competitiveness ranking over the next five years.
The Information Society (Back to top).
Bringing the information society to our schools.
Due to the quality of our young educated labour force we are uniquely placed to harness the great potential of the so-called "information society".
We envisage opportunities for commercial exploitation in several fields including software, education, retail, financial and consulting services.
An awareness of the potential of this technology must be quickly instilled in industry, especially small industry.
Fine Gael believes we should assign a priority to upgrading knowledge of the "information society" in our schools.
Establish a joint venture between RTE and other interests to develop digital broadcasting.

Digital broadcasting technology will not only enhance picture and sound quality, but will increase the number of channels available for television and other information and data transmission services.
The public interest requires the protection and enhancement of Ireland's national public service broadcasting network in these changed circumstances.

Fine Gael will support a joint venture between RTE and other interests to invest in, and develop, digital broadcasting which will greatly improve the range of our potential television services, including educational, cultural and commercial opportunities.
The additional channels made available by digital technology will also be a major input into Ireland's programme of developments to exploit the Information Society in the new Millennium.
Introduce regulation of decoders.

Fine Gael supports the introduction of a system of regulation of decoders for digital broadcast reception which will ensure universal and primary access to the national broadcasters, safeguarding Irish national interests.
Protecting national sporting events.
The televising, free of charge, of key sporting and cultural events should be safeguarded, in the national interest, by law.
Prioritising Infrastructural Investment (Back to top).
Establish an Institute for Transport and Logistics.
Investment should be prioritised in the basic infrastructure such as roads, sea ports, rail and airports, transport services, and particularly in the area of "system logistics".

Fine Gael supports the establishment of an Institute for Transport and Logistics at a suitable third-level institution to provide degree and diploma awards and to act as a research resource for what has been an underdeveloped aspect of our transport infrastructure.
Environmental issues will assume a central role during the life of the next government.
The interests of the environment and enterprise are very much in harmony.
The pursuit of sustainable development ensures that enterprise is conscious that its activities today will not undermine its capacity to reap profits in the future.
Opportunities for developing new markets for goods and services must also be created.
We are well positioned to exploit these in Ireland.
At the same time Fine Gael is concerned that the additional compliance requirement on industry be minimised.

We favour the advance designation, following extensive local consultation, of suitable sites for industrial development and the prior clearance of these sites for development on environmental grounds.
Innovation and Change in our Public and Private Institutions (Back to top).
The responses of our public and private institutions to the demands of change also affect our competitiveness.
Our educational and training institutions must be responsive to the changing requirements of enterprise.
Our industrial development agencies should be alert to the exploitation of "early mover" opportunities in all sectors and in the provision of relevant information for and assistance to enterprise.
Our competition and regulatory agencies must maintain a constant vigilance against anti-competitive practices in both the State and private sectors.
All our State services must strive to provide the best-quality service at the lowest price, where relevant, to its customers.
At the same time the burdens imposed by compliance have to be minimised.
In short, Fine Gael seeks to impose the same disciplines on public bodies as the marketplace places on the private sector.
Competition and Regulation.
Effective competition means better and cheaper goods and services for households and businesses.

We believe that the full powers and resources of the Competition Authority should be used to promote competition in the economy and to uncover and eradicate imperfectly competitive trading activity, including within the State and semi-State sector.

As the commercial semi-State sector is undergoing unprecedented change and the traditional monopolistic market structures are beginning to be replaced, there is clearly a need to put in place effective independent regulation of these sectors.
Without effective regulation of imperfect competition, the consumer won't fully benefit from the introduction of much-needed outside capital into public enterprises.
In Government Fine Gael started this process with the appointment of an independent regulator for the telecommunications' sector.
Fine Gael wants to see this process continued with the other public utilities.
In time we would like to see trading companies and sectors operate in close to competitive conditions subject to rigorous independent regulation where appropriate.
Innovation in Local Government and Community Development (Back to top).

With the assistance of Structural Funds from Europe and backed up by national investment, Fine Gael have championed the renewal of communities through promoting "bottom up" local economic development.

We developed innovative programmes, which are being emulated in other countries, through schemes, such as Urban Renewal, Area Development Management, County Enterprise Boards and LEADER which deliver investment into communities over which local people have control as to how its spent.

We championed the development of the West of Ireland through the appointment of the first ever Minister of State for Western Development and creation of the Western Development Commission with a funding facility of £25 million.
We took specific steps to improve the quality of life of island life through additional spending in the improvement of island infrastructure of piers, airstrips, dredging works, roads etc.
The Rainbow Government actively promoted rural Resettlement as an option for urban-based families who want their children to experience the quality of life which rural living offers.

Our commitment to distributing the benefits of a buoyant economy on a widespread geographical basis was underlined by the Rainbow Government's decision to pay higher rates of industrial development grants for major commercial investment outside of the main centres of population.

In addition Fine Gael supports the continued provision of industrial financial incentives biased in favour of smaller regional locations, with higher grant levels as appropriate to each individual case.

This also includes the involvement of private sector investors to stimulate and support a major programme of modern advance factory construction at key locations and working in partnership with local authorities to have available quality-serviced sites at priority locations for new industrial investment.
Fine Gael is committed to developing thriving town, village and rural communities.
Fine Gael believes that pro-active rural/local community-led initiatives, fully supported by Government, must be developed to maintain and enhance their quality and economic life.
Fine Gael is committed to enabling communities in disadvantaged areas to share in the nation's prosperity.

The vigorous implementation of better standards of service to the public and value for money will be assured by our commitment to implementing "Better Local Government" as announced by the Rainbow Government in December 1996.
The changes outlined will bring benefits in the form of giving local people a greater say in decisions made by Local Authorities (LAs) which intimately affect their lives.
To achieve these benefits the following initiatives should be implemented.
Enhance the accountability of Local Authorities to the public which they serve, especially through providing user-friendly and easily accessible information on key activities, such as planning.
Local representatives should be given policy formulation and over-seeing roles in a Cabinet-style local administration.
Local development organisations should be given a greater role in decision-making by LAs.
In the longer term Fine Gael is committed to transferring functions and ultimately powers, which are at present administered centrally, to the LAs.
Delivering better public administration (Back to top).
We support the implementation of the Public Service Management Act which should be a pivotal vehicle for achieving real change in the delivery of public services.
The implementation of this Act will result in real and tangible benefits for all.
First, it will result in more being achieved for less resources, and the consequent release of savings to be used to improve services in priority areas such as health, education and fighting crime.
Second, the implementation of the Public Service Management Bill will ensure that better quality services which are more responsive to the needs of the public are put in place.
For example, we believe public offices should be open for longer hours and during lunch times.
We want to see public offices to be more responsive in dealing with the public.
Third, and most importantly, public servants will have more responsibility and accountability for the services they deliver.
Public Hospital Boards.
We will establish Boards for all our public hospitals with membership drawn from all relevant partners involved in the health sector.
Private Institutions.
Private institutions also play a central role in underpinning our competitive economy, especially those institutions which assist in the funding of investment.
Good, "safe" ideas will never be short of funding but there exist difficulties for innovative projects.
The Developing Companies Market on the Stock Exchange should be actively encouraged.

As Fine Gael has done in the recent past, we will continue to support State involvement in low-cost long-term loan schemes which are targeted towards small scale high-growth potential investments, where management advice and support are part of the overall support package.
The £60 million provision for Venture Capital for small start-up companies has been very successful and Fine Gael would like to see it being expanded.
We believe that active ways of involving the private sector in greater equity provision for small companies should also be explored.
Pension Funds are a potential source of funding for long-term investment projects in both the public and private sectors which Fine Gael will aim to exploit in a new government.
Social Partnership has been an undoubted contributory factor to our recent prosperity.
The various National Agreements have delivered moderate wage settlements and overall peaceful industrial relations.
The most recent agreement broadened the scope of the Partnership considerably and provides a better basis for a fair sharing of the gains from material progress.
This framework must be called on to play a prominent role in the reform of our public institutions which is underway at present.
It will also be of pivotal importance in ensuring that our trading sectors adapt successfully to the challenges of Monetary Union.

In this context the extension of the partnership model which has clearly worked at the national level to the level of the "shop floor" will determine to a large extent whether we can rise to that challenge.
Fine Gael supports every effort to deepen Social Partnership in this way.
Competitiveness in Our Key Economic Sectors (Back to top).
Taxation on PAYE workers and enterprise affects the level of profits which are available for re-investment in enterprises.

Fine Gael is determined to see a significant reduction in the taxation burdens consistent with fairness, enhancement of public services and achieving a deficit close to balance over the economic cycle.
This is a key strategy to deliver competitive advantage.
Our policies are developed in full in a later section and here we outline specific sectoral priorities.
Agriculture, Food and Rural Development (Back to top).
Fine Gael in government will negotiate the future development of Ireland's agriculture and food policy on the following guiding principles.
We are committed to ensuring that any change to EU policy is achieved in a manner which protects the legitimate interests of Ireland's farming and rural communities and the food industry.
Recognising the importance of agriculture and food to the national economy, we are adamant that.
Any reductions in agriculture prices will be compensated through direct income support payment;
The principle of common financing of the CAP be fully respected;
The EU financial resources necessary for the continued implementation of Union policies in the existing Member States, as well as in the new Member States, must continue to be provided;

Quotas and similar production rights must be protected, subject to Ireland maintaining our strategic advantage in grass-based production, so as to ensure that national production capacity is not reduced;
An adequate level of Community preference must be preserved.
Partnership 2000 contains a number of key pledges to protect the legitimate interests of Ireland's priorities in farming, food and rural development.
We are committed to seeing that these undertakings are fully delivered.
There are, however, a number of additional policy initiatives which we will introduce to underpin the competitive basis of rural society.
Establish a Food Safety Authority.
Since March of 1996, the world's beef markets have been convulsed by the fallout from the human health scares evoked by BSE.
We have to restore confidence in beef products among consumers at home and abroad.
We need a bold measure to do this, not just for beef but all foods.

We therefore propose to build on the establishment of a Food Safety Board and work towards the institution of a new and independent statutory regulatory authority - The Food Safety Authority - with a brief to regulate all food and related products which may indirectly or directly impact on human health.
This Authority would execute licensing, labelling, monitoring and control functions.
For the Office to function effectively it will thus require all inspectorate and technical staff to be brought under its direct control and hence redeployed to it from all relevant Departments.
This initiative requires extensive consultation in order to be implemented successfully.
The Authority would operate under the aegis of the Department of Health.
Establish an Office of Minister for Rural Development.

Fine Gael recognises that rural development policy is a function of the Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry and to this end we are committed to establishing an Office of Minister for Rural Development, consolidating and co-ordinating all policy formulation for the future in this regard.
Publish a White Paper on Rural Development.
Fine Gael will publish a White Paper on Rural Development which will address the integration of all aspects of rural development.
Particular emphasis will be placed on the findings of the recent `Cork Declaration' of November 1996.
Farmers would benefit, like other taxpayers, from our proposed tax-reform programme.
As a result of a Fine Gael-inspired initiative, Corporation Tax was reduced to only 28% for small companies - a decline of 12% in three Budgets.
This regime encourages re-investment in the business which is the lifeline to a competitive future.
We believe, given this reduced tax rate and our initiative to see the rate fall to 12,5%, farmers will consider the potential gains from incorporating their businesses.
Fine Gael will actively explore all the complex issues involved in facilitating this option.
The Forestry Sector (Back to top).
The Strategic Plan for Forestry, published by Fine Gael in Government, aims to double the level of afforestation leading to 11,000 additional jobs.
Fine Gael believes that this increase in afforestation must take place in harmony with the environment and with conventional farming.
We will also, through urgent negotiations with the EU, ensure that the current disparity which exists between supports for conventional farming and forestry is removed.
Tourism (Back to top).
Tourism is one of our biggest industries and it is important for us to continue setting new aims and objectives.
We pledge to:
Increase foreign tourism revenue, keeping performance ahead of targets set in the six-year Operational Programme.
Continue to support nationwide capital investment in our tourism infrastructure.

Sound Management of the Public Finances in the Era of Monetary Union (Back to top) Budgetary Framework 1997-2002 The prosperity which is possible over the next few years - up to 5% annual growth in real GNP - holds out the prospect for delivering substantial tax reform and reductions, improvements in services, an assault on unemployment and a tackling of the problems of disadvantage and exclusion
Fine Gael thus believes the Government should set itself rigorous but balanced budgetary targets for tax reform, public expenditure and reductions in borrowing
But it must also be quite explicit about the process required to achieve the targets set, especially as regards public expenditure
Prudent management of public expenditure means that the Government must recognise that there severe limits to the scope for new spending programmes

The Budgetary Framework must be designed in order: To fulfil the requirements of EMU and especially the necessity to target for the elimination of the Government deficit over the economic cycle (""Stability Pact"")
To implement the tax reform and expenditure commitments under Partnership 2000
To continue to deliver serious tax reform and reduction for PAYE workers to ensure fairness and to promote employment and enterprise
To continue to invest in public capital infrastructure to underpin our prosperity

To recognise that the level of EU Structural Funds must be renegotiated after 1999 in the light of the accession of new members and the fact that Ireland already has increased its income per head above many other EU States
To ensure adequate funding for the enhancement of public services, especially in the areas of health, education, social welfare and in combating crime
To make adequate contingency provisions for unexpected expenditure requirements and for a possible growth out-turn below our expected level of 5%

Recognising these factors, Fine Gael believes that in sharing the gains which are possible for all our citizens from a continuation of prosperity, an appropriate balance should be struck between tax reform and improvements in services such as policing and crime, health, education, welfare and other public services
This balance is a matter of political choice

To achieve this balance Fine Gael believes the new Government should adopt the following five-point Budgetary Framework over the next five years: Whilst recognising that borrowing in individual years is affected by cyclical ecnomic factors, Fine Gael asserts that the Government should aspire to eliminate all Government borrowing for capital or current purposes
This factor would condition the entire Budgetary Framework
Within this constraint the following guidelines should be adhered to: 1
A continued reduction in the percentage of total Government expenditure (current and capital) relative to GNP
The maintenance of the Public Capital Programme at a level sufficient to underpin our national competitive advantage and prosperity
A tax-reform and reduction package for PAYE workers which builds on Partnership 2000 and extends those commitments to reward work and enterprise to 2002

The implementation of a number of new public service programmmes, over and above commitments in Partnership 2000 and the improvement in existing services, will be entirely conditional on achieving our objectives in relation to the Government deficit and the Maastricht criteria
Achieving expenditure control (Back to top) The adherence to this Budgetary Framework is to a large extent conditional on successfully controlling the growth in public expenditure

Government has a responsibility to ensure that waste and fraud are eliminated and Value for Money (VFM) in the supply of all services is continuously striven for, and that spending programmes which have gone past their ""sell by date"" are wound up
The imposition of a spending target helps expenditure control

We also need to tackle the process of decision-making on public spending using the best management practices borrowed from the private sector and from successful approaches implemented in other countries

A Fiscal Transparency Act In government we will bring forward a Fiscal Transparency Act with the objective of making the implications of government decisions transparent to the public in terms of the full future taxation and expenditure consequences of all current decisions

This legislation will set out a set of basic principles and control measures which will govern the conduct of decision-making on fiscal policy, such as: Setting targets for public debt and deficit levels consistent with Monetary Union objectives
Committing Government to guarantee a reasonable degree of stability and predictability of future tax levels
Requiring Government to publish medium-term projections with appropriate sensitivity analysis (5-10 years) at each Budget of the evolution of the public finances consistent with the Budget decisions
Committing Government to publishing information on the public finances on the basis of committed expenditure rather than on a cash basis

Requiring all Government departments and agencies to produce balance sheets of all their assets and liabilities so that by establishing the net worth of the State more informed decisions on the efficient use of State assets can be made
Pledging Government to pursue a strict financial ""envelope"" approach to maintaining overall spending control as opposed to the traditional ""brick by brick"" system
Establishing rigorous procedures for Value for Money (VFM) evaluations of expenditure in all Government departments along the lines currently employed for the Structural Funds and other EU spending

These evaluations would cover not just the ends and means of Government programmes but would also include important tasks of Government administration which have consequences for the level of expenditure such as payments by the State, the management of public procurement and claims on Government and large public infrastructure investments
In regard to the latter Fine Gael believes that more cost effective public investment programmes can be delivered if a greater role is invited from the private sector
Fine Gael wants to see the development and publication of guidelines to encourage private sector involvement in public investment programmes
All evaluations would be published and subject to VFM audit
Establishing productivity targets equal to best practice, on the basis of unchanged policies, by programme/departmental expenditure category

Departments should be incentivised to achieve productivity savings by permitting up to 70% of productivity savings to be retained for new services or improvements in existing services in those departments which have achieved productivity savings, provided these new expenditures are justified on rigorous VFM grounds
Requiring all new spending proposals sponsored by individual departments to specify how the additional expenditure could be financed
Fine Gael believes that, as has been shown in other countries, by enshrining the measures outlined above in law there will be a requirement for visible application of the various measures

Delivering Sustainable Tax Reforms and Reductions (Back to top) Aims Fine Gael seeks a tax system that ""makes it pay to make a job and to take a job""
We want a system which is fairer and simpler
We want real tax reform and reductions for all workers
We firmly believe that the commitments given in Partnership 2000, which covers the period up to 1999, should be delivered on and to continue the thrust of the agreed tax reductions up to 2002
Real tax reform and reductions is one of our principal obsessions
We have two key objectives which we want our tax system to achieve
First, we want to see the progress made in recent years in reducing, in a fair way, the amount of money all taxpayers pay out of their pay packets,to be continued
Second, we want our tax system to encourage work and enterprise
Our income tax system is complex
Take-home pay depends on tax rates, tax bands, allowances, levies and PRSI contributions
Tackling any one of these factors in isolation is not of itself sufficient to deliver real and fair tax reductions
Our view is that the vast majority of PAYE taxpayers are primarily concerned about the amount of income tax and PRSI paid out of their total pay packets
We thus believe that in a tax- reduction programme priority should be given to reducing the Real Tax Rate, that is, the amount of total income tax and PRSI deducted from gross income
This would require action in particular on tax-free allowances and bands

Our general aim is to see a reduction in the Real Tax Rate for an average earner to at least 22p in the £ for a single person and 14p for a married person, (before taking account of any discretionary allowances)

Reducing the burden of taxes on Workers Our package would reduce the Real Tax Rate - the income tax and PRSI take expressed as a fraction of income - on the average income to about 22% for a single person and about 14% for a married person
This is the rate which really matters to taxpayers

The achievement of these objectives would involve five key commitments: ¥ Increase tax free allowances To raise the level of allowances towards the present exemption limits, that is, to increase tax free allowances from £2,900 (single)/£5,800 (married) to £4,400 (single)/£8,800 (married) by 2002
This objective will benefit all earner s but particularly middle and lower income workers
It will promote employment creation
It will remove the poverty traps inherent in the present Marginal Relief System

¥ Widen standard rate tax bands To widen the tax bands so that, in conjunction with the increased tax allowances, no taxpayer will pay tax at the top rate on a single penny if their total gross income is less than the average industrial wage in 2002 which we expect by then to be around £17,000
This target confronts the real problem with our tax system which is that too many taxpayers begin paying tax at the top rate on modest incomes
¥ Reduce Employee PRSI To reduce the full-rate of employee PRSI
¥ Cut the top rate of Income Tax To cut the top rate of income tax from 48% to 45% over the period of Government
this and our commitment on PRSI are part of a reforming package which would address marginal rates of taxation to encourage people to take on extra responsibilities at work

¥ Dismantle Health and Employment Levies To begin the process of dismantling the Health and Employment levies, which add 2.25% to the marginal tax rate, should be initiated through substantially raising the liability threshold from £10,250 at present towards the average industrial wage by 2002
These measures are fair and balanced
They would principally benefit people on middle to low incomes
They would give single persons, in particular, who are taking up employment for the first time a very real break
They would also help create jobs because we know low-income employment is more responsive to changes in wage costs and wage incomes than high-income employment
And these measures underline our basic commitment to sharing prosperity
Between 1994 and 1997, the tax burden, for a single person on average earnings, has been cut by five percentage points and by four points for a married person on the same income
The actual overall tax burden on workers fell by only three points for a single person and by only two points for a married person between 1989 and 1992

Because of targeted reductions in tax burdens, which proportionately benefit middle and low-income taxpayers more, a single worker on average earnings in 1997 had to work the best part of a month less to discharge his or her tax and PRSI obligations compared with the period 1989-1992

This decisive measure would underscore our attractiveness as a location for mobile international capital, support our indigenous industry, allow us to continue our job creation record of almost 1,000 jobs per week since 1994 and to halve the total unemployment rate to below 6% and the long-term rate to 3.5% within the next ten years

A New Social Contract With The Unemployed (Back to top)
Aims We want to see substantial reductions in the level of unemployment and especially long-term unemployment which lies at the root of poverty and social exclusion over the next five years
Fine Gael believes that the successful achievement of this objective would come about through the continuation of our economic prosperity underpinned by the policies adopted by this government
A carefully constructed strategy is required based on several planks - taxation, education, welfare and direct employment creation
We want to see our employment support and welfare policies transformed so that no person who becomes unemployed is condemned to a permanent existence on welfare
Permanent welfare is destructive of the individuals concerned, and creates alienation from society, and attendant ills such as crime and illicit drug taking
It wastes the single most important resource we have as an economy which is people who are willing and able to work

Our new social contract with the unemployed is, as set out in Partnership 2000, based on the reciprocal obligations of society to provide decent incomes and worthwhile supports in job seeking for the unemployed, and of the unemployed to seek and accept reasonable employment, development and training opportunities
The State's Obligations To The Unemployed (Back to top)
Fine Gael commits itself to seeking improvements in the scale and quality of State-sponsored services to the unemployed

The resources to fund this pledge are accounted for in our Budgetary Framework in so far as they are consistent with Partnership 2000 and would be supplemented by savings arising from the continued fall in unemployment levels and from the successful progression of anti-fraud measures
Ensure minimum social welfare payments Fine Gael wants to see the minimum rates of social welfare payments, as recommended by the Commission on Social Welfare, implemented by the end of 1999
Thereafter payments should be improved consistent with the avoidance of any labour market distortions

¥ Make work attractive Taxation burdens on workers should be reduced in such a way as to maximise the attractiveness of working and gains should be biased towards reducing the burden on middle to low-income earners
¥ Improve the Family Income Supplement Fine Gael believes the Family Income Supplement (FIS) is an excellent means of improving the returns from low-income employment
It encourages people with families to choose work over welfare
There are problems with the operation of FIS which render it much less effective in this regard that what it might be
First, because FIS is withdrawn as gross income increases means that the take-home pay of a worker on FIS doesn't increase much over a large range of modest income levels
In other words, poverty traps are created
The incentive for people on FIS to earn more income by taking up a better paid job or working overtime is reduced
This may also discourage some married people, who are unemployed from taking up employment
Fine Gael calls for the tackling of this particular deficiency in FIS by relating payments to net income
The second concern, is that only a third of people who would appear to be entitled to FIS are actually taking up the payment
The reasons for this low take up may be inadequate awareness or a perceived stigma associated with the measure
Steps need to be taken to ensure that everyone who qualifies gets the FIS
Unless these steps are taken, this scheme will be less effective in incentivising work than it might be
Therefore, we propose that the feasibility of having the supplement paid as a tax credit should be examined, direct to the employee through his employer on an automatic basis
This would get rid of the problems associated with low take up
It would significantly increase the incentive to work
If feasible, FIS could be replaced by a Refundable Work Tax Credit
The scheme would operate by crediting what the person gets under FIS against their tax bill
Where there is no tax liability the person in question would simply get a refund from Revenue
The take-up rate under the administration of FIS in this way should be increased because payment would be automatic
¥ Establish the National Employment Service A revamped National Employment Service should provide a nationwide integrated service for the unemployed
The service is based on the successful operation of the Local Employment Service

It will offer unemployed people a pro-active, high quality, highly intensive, and individual-based job counselling and advisory service, initially, for the most disadvantaged groups as set out in Partnership 2000
The Service will refer people to other agencies for training, and job placement as appropriate

We already have a wide range of direct job-support programmes in place which are achieving success, e.g., Community Employment (CE) and the Conference of Religious of Ireland's (CORI) schemes which provide direct employment to over 40,000 persons the Back to Work Allowance which permits an unemployed person who takes up a job or becomes self employed to retain unemployment payments for a period of time at a reducing level plus other non-cash benefits which he would have had when unemployed such as the Medical Card obstart which provides a subsidy of £80 per week for an employer to take on a person who has been unemployed for three years or more, etc
These measures will be subject to on-going examination and review
We see two worthwhile specific modifications to these programmes

First, the Service should work with FAS to offer special short courses (1-2 weeks) in job application/search and interview/presentation targeted to people who have been unemployed for at least 12 months
Second, for the State to credibly expect the unemployed to accept reasonable employment opportunities it must provide a job guarantee
Community Employment, CORI and other measures should play a critical role in this regard
The evidence from other countries suggests that the existence of a guarantee like what we propose would be successful

The cost of introducing an open-ended guarantee for all long- term unemployed people would be prohibitive in the initial years but we believe it is worth introducing this guarantee for persons under 25 who have been unemployed for at least a year
This would serve as a pilot before considering any extension of the guarantee to all long-term unemployed people
