We spent £8 million in 1995, £12m in 1996 and another £8m in the first half of 1997, resulting in a reduction of over 10,000 people on waiting lists
By early 1997 we had cut that number to under 26,000opened up the private health insurance marketopened up the private health insurance market
Choice and competition are now a reality in the private health insurance market for the first time with the emergence of BUPA onto the market
While enabling this to come about, we also ensured that the fundamental principle of Community Rating is guaranteed
launched a plan for the development of our health services for women

The Women's Health Plan, put together after an extensive consultation process, addressse the particular health issues of concern to women and aims to ensure that these are dealt with throughout the Irish Health Service

Key components in creating a quality, women-friendly health service included the establishment of a Women's Health Council with similarly structured bodies in each Health Board, the development of a national screening programme for Breast Cancer and a national screening programme for Cervical Cancer
published a plan on Physical and Sensory Disability

People who are affected by various physical and sensory disabilities such as those who are wheelchair bound, or those who suffer from blindness or deafness, have long awaited the publication of a plan for the development of these services
The report of the Review Group on Persons with Physical and Sensory Disability,published by the Rainbow Government in December 1996, provided such a plan
The development of these services has been enhanced by an extra £3. 6m in 1997
Regional co-ordinating committees were being put in place while the process of compiling a definitive database of people in need of these services was begun
established a National Intellectual Disability Database
In each of its 3 budgets, the Rainbow Coalition provided significant extra monies to fund improved services for those who are mentally handicapped
For the first time we now have a National Intellectual Disability Database which provides a list of named persons who require either new or improved services

The Database highlighted, in particular, the urgent additional requirements for residential care as mentally disabled people are surviving longer and their parents, as they grow older, require extra support
Respite care opportunities for carers and adequate educational and transport resources need to be enhanced as a matter of urgency
Each year since coming to Office the Rainbow Government devoted significant additional resources to develop services for mentally handicapped persons and their families
In 1997 an extra £12 million was allocated to provide additional residential, daycare and respite places
The Drugs Problem

Heroin addiction, particularly in the greater Dublin area, and the rapidly increasing prevalence throughout the country of so-called soft drugs such as ecstasy are problems which required and got an immediate and co-ordinated response from Fine Gael in Government
The need to reduce the demand for these drugs is being targeted in many ways: waiting lists for methadone maintenance were dramatically reduced
extra detoxification and rehabilitation facilities were provided
additional investment was put into drug awareness programmes aimed at young people
a special committee of Ministers of State was set up to concentrate on Demand Reduction Measures
£14m has been allocated in 1997 for a series of measures recommended by their first report
These measures recognised that reducing demand for drugs requires a complex, integrated approach at community level combined with a need to tackle the social factors which give rise to drug addiction
launched the first National Plan for Cancer Services
In the past, Irish Cancer Services have developed in a largely ad-hoc fashion with many areas of the country having little or no service
This will change following the adoption and launch, in November 1996, of the first nationwide Action Plan for Cancer
A budget allocation of £6m enabled the first phase to be implemented
A key feature in ensuring that all regions have an appropriate level of service was the appointment, at consultant level, of a Director of Cancer Services in each Health Board area
In addition, significant extra resources were provided for Hospice Care
""So what would we do in Goverment?"" (Back to top) The Fine Gael Millennium Pledge - supporting families and improving healthcare The government must support the family
The family is the institution which best provides care, nurture and love for children, for the elderly and for the incapacitated
Changes in society such as the growth of individualism and secularisaton, urbanisation, technological change, changing work practices and changed gender roles are placing some families under pressure
In some instances impairing their capacity to provide adequate care for family members in need
The Government must start by ensuring that none of the State's policies make it financially attractive for family units to break up
The State should endeavour to support families by targeted interventions which address stress points in the family lifecycle

It should support initiatives for pre-school child carefor care of mentally and physically incapacitated family members and for assisting the elderly and their families to provide for long-term care needs
HELPING FAMILIES (Back to top) appoint A Minister of State for Family Affairs In the modern world, families are placed under increasing stress
The issues which give rise to these stresses, cross over several aspects of Government including taxation, social welfare, health, education, justice and law reform
Because of the breadth of issues which arise and because of our commitment to the family, Fine Gael will appoint a Minister of State for Family Affairs

Re-examinethe Unemployment Assistance Parental Means Test Fine Gael is concerned that the operation of the Unemployment Assistance parental means test and the availability of rent allowances can sometimes act to encourage young people to leave the family home prematurely, thereby fracturing the family unit

The treatment of the young person as an individual in his or her own right is an important principle, but our aim will be to ensure that there is no artificial incentive encouraging young people to leave home
SUPPORTING THE CARE OF OUR CHILDREN (Back to top) Increasingly both parents are working full-time
This trend is set to continue and will have profound consequences for the way society organises itself, particularly in caring for children
Men and women are responding to the challenges presented by combining paid work and family responsibilities, and the State should help them
That means giving practical support to job sharing and encouraging parental leave
A New Parents' Childcare Supplement Fine Gael is fully committed to State financial supports for child- care
This is done primarily through universal Child Benefit payments, which the Rainbow Government increased by up to 60%

The costs of child-rearing are also explicitly recognised in our social welfare code, through additional payments for children in the rates of Unemployment Benefits/Assistance and Family Income Supplement
What characterises these payments is that they are paid to families regardless of whether child-care is paid for or is freely provided from within the family's own time and resources
State support is child centred and thus neutrality exists between families which buy in childcare, and those who provide it from their own resources
The principle of neutrality and fairness is one which Fine Gael fully supports
We believe a further initiative is required to provide real additional child-care support to families

Fine Gael proposes that a Parents' Childcare Supplement of £300 per child per annum, for children up to the age of five inclusive, be introduced on a phased basis and paid through the existing Child Benefit Scheme
In 1998, the supplement should be paid in respect of 1 and 2 year olds and in 1999 it should be paid for all children up to 5 years of age, inclusive
Establish an Ombudsman for children
We call for the establishment of an independent Office of Ombudsman for Children with statutory powers to promote aand protect the rights of children
Implement Childcare sections of Partnership 2000 Fine Gael is determined to see a speedy implementation of the commitments given in Partnership 2000 in relation to childcare
Specifically we want: the relevant section of the 1991 Child Care Act which covers the regulation of safety and health standards in pre-school services implemented
a national registration system for childcarers established
a nationally recognised system of certification and accreditation for childcare workers providing for an appropriate minimum qualification

While we support the vigorous pursuit of high standards, at the same time we don't want to see well-run creches having to close or rates to be raised substantially because of overly bureaucratic standards

Exempt Childcare from VAT Fine Gael believes that all childcare services are inherently educational in character and that it is not possible to construct a meaningful distinction between caring and educational services
Thus we believe that childcare services should be completely exempt from Value Added Tax
Increase the supply of Quality Childcare Services A real problem which many families, but especially those in rural areas, face is an insufficient supply of quality childcare services

To address this problem we want to see the various local development agencies being actively encouraged to support community and private provision of childcare services in co- operation with Fás and the Health Boards
An EU funded pilot project undertaken by Limerick County Enterprise Board and which involves a joint community-based facility for children and the elderly, could serve as a model

A BETTER DEAL FOR OUR ELDERLY CITIZENS (Back to top) Increase income tax exemption limits for the elderly Over the term of the new government the incom-tax Exemption limits and allowances for pensioners will be increased in line with our commitments to improve the generalexemption and allowances levels
For persons aged between 65 and 75 we will seek to increase the Exemption limits from £4,600 (single)/£9,200 (married to £5,200 (single)/£10,400 (married)

For persons over 75, the limits will be raised from £5,200 (single)/£10,400 (married to £5,200 (single)/£11,800 (married) Increase tax free-allowances for the elderly The age tax free allowance for persons over will be increased from£400 (single)/£800 (married) to £1000 (single)/ £2000 (married
We l also call for the introduction of a new higher age allowance for the over 75s
Thus in the next budget, we will bring forward a proposal for an enhanced age allowance of £500 (single)/£1000 (married) for persons aged over 75
This allowance will be progressively raised to £1,100 (single)/ £2,200 (married) over the new term of government

These improvements in the age allowances when combined with our commitments in relation to general allowances will mean that the tax-free allowance for persons aged between 65 and 75 will rise from £3,300 (single)/£6,600 (married) by 2002

For persons over 75 years of age, their tax free allowance will be increased from £3,300 (single)/£6,600 (married) to £5,500 (single)/£11,000 (married) by 2002 Enhance tax treatment of surviving spouses Fine Gael believes that all persons with dependent children who become widowed should retain the full married person's tax-free allowance and bands
For a person without dependants they should retain entitlement to these deductions for a two-year period following the year of bereavement
Health Care Provision for Eldery People All elderly people over the age of 65 should be entitled to a free medical checkup by their GP every year
We would also extend eligibility for Medical Cards to all persons over 75
We would examine ways of ensuring that spectacles and dentures are more readily available to the over 65s
Day-care and Residential Centres for the Elderly We would put in place an enhanced capital programme to develop day care and residential centres for older people

Special House Repair Grants for the Elderly We would review the present scheme of special housing repair grants for the elderly which is funded by the Department of the Environment with a view to make the scheme more responsive to the needs of the elderly
FURTHER IMPROVEMENTS IN OUR HEALTH SERVICE (Back to top)
Health care is a major preoccupation for all families
We are fortunate that, in Ireland, we have a public health-care service which provides not only top-quality care but also compares favourably with anywhere else in the world
There is of course always room for improvement
Waiting Lists We believe that the reduction of waiting lists should continue to be prioritised

On a phased basis we favour the introduction of a programme to ensure that the waiting period for operations for hip replacements, cataracts, cardiac, and gynaecological procedures varicose veins and ear, nose and throat (ENT) procedures for children would be dramatically cut
Fine Gael feels that there should be a maximum waiting period of no more than six months, from the time of GP referral to the time when the patient is operated on
We want to see the maximum waiting period for cardiac and varicose vein treatment be no more than 12 months
Services for the Physically Disabled

The ""Report of the Review Group on Services for People with Physical and Sensory Disabilities"" has been considered by an Inter-Departmental Taskforce set up to look at implementation of the wider report published by the Commission on the Status of People with Disabilities
We support the implementation of this blueprint as the basis for a radical improvement in services such as day care, respite, sheltered workshop, residential, personal assistance and other services
Nursing Commission
A Commission, chaired by Judge Mella Carroll has undertaken a root and branch review of nursing in Ireland
We believe that its recommendations should be implemented while a similar review of the paramedical professions should also be undertaken
Hepatitis C The infection from the blood supply of many Irish women and men with Hepatitis C is one of the greatest disasters in the history of the Irish health system
Monitoring and re-assessment,on an ongoing basis, of the health care requirements and other needs of those who have been diagnosed as positive for Hepatitis C virus/antibodies should be continued
This should be with a view to ensuring that the necessary support services are provided to meet their needs
Investment in research should also be continued
Strategic Partner for the VHI
Over 1.4 million people are members of the VHI
The continued strength of this organisation, in the face of competitive pressures, must be ensured
Accordingly Fine Gael urges that the company forge a strategic alliance with an appropriate partner
Community Rating should also remain as a core principle in the Health Insurance Market
Minister of State for Public Health

We believe that a Minister of State at the Department of Health who will have responsibility for Public Health issues including Drug and Alcohol Addiction, Health Promotion, and the Irish Medicine Boards, should be appointed
The Minister should also have responsibility for implementing the recommendations of the Taskforce on Suicide
Mental Health Bill Legislation governing Mental Health and Mental Health institutions is significantly out of date
This legislation should be updated through the publication of a Mental Health Bill
Structural Reform
The Department of Health and Children should be renamed as the ""Department of Health and Personal Social Services"" to reflect the growing significance of these services
An Eastern Health Authority with responsibility for all services in the Dublin, Wicklow and Kildare should replace the present Eastern Health Board

The question of representation of Voluntary Bodies on the Health Boards must be dealt with while a pilot scheme to introduce Boards of Management in a number of Health Board hospitals should be set up
High Quality Blood Supply A secure, high quality blood supply is vital for the Irish hospital service
A radical reform of the Irish Blood Transfusion Service should be initiated by, among other measures, implementing the recommendations of the Finlay Tribunal
Resources should also be provided for the development of a new state of the art headquarters for the BTSB
As many Irish people travel to Europe either to work, for business or on holidays, work at European Union level should be undertaken to achieve this objective
Mental Handicap Plan
We are committed to a plan for the development of services of the Mentally handicapped based on the National Intellectual Disabilities Database
This would comprehensively address the needs of carers and handicapped people over a five year period
Action Plan for Cancer Services
Cancer is among the three major causes of death in the Under 65 Age Group in Ireland
We are committed to seeing the full implementation of the remaining phases of the National Cancer Strategy
This would reorganise treatment services on a regional basis with three supra-regional services in Dublin, Cork and Galway for the more highly specialised treatments

The shortage of specialist oncology services outside the Dublin area would be eliminated, specialist palliative care services would be developed on a phased basis and a Cancer Research Unit would be established within the Health Research Board
Women's Health Plan Full implementation of the plan to develop our health services for women is a core objective
The current targetted Breast Screening Programme and a Cervical Screening Programme must be available on a nationwide basis
A BETTER DEAL FOR CARERS (Back to top)
Families and individuals who provide care for their loved ones are deserving of State support
The State also saves on not having to provide residential care in many cases
To give a practical edge to our support for carers we propose a number of specific initiatives
Carer's Allowance
We support the introduction of a Severe Dependency Premium on top of existing payments for carers who are caring for persons on the verge of needing residential care
We also favour an earnings disregard for carers and the unduly restrictive full- time commitments on carers should be relaxed
Monitor Care Facilities
The proposed Social Services Inspectorate should have a role in the registration and inspection of long-term care facilities
Examine introduction of a Partial Equity Release Insurance (PERI) scheme

We believe it is time to take a serious look at a Partial Equity Release Insurance (PERI) scheme to be run either by the private sector or in partnership with the State as a means of funding long-term care for elderly people
Such a scheme would be based on the fact that many elderly people are asset rich but income poor when it comes to meeting the high cost of long-term care

A person taking out PERI insurance would have no outlay upfront but would agree with the insurer that following the individual's death the first claim on the deceased's estate would be held by the insurance agency
This claim would more than likely be in terms of a percentage of the asset value
A degree of State support may be necessary to establish PERIs both to reassure potential insurees and to attract investors interested in long-term returns
It may also be necessary to introduce appropriate consumer legislation to protect the insuree
Incentives for the elderly to participate in PERIs may also be warranted
The option of recouping any Stamp Duty paid on the sale of a deceased persons property to the estate of that deceased person should also be examined
Extensive System of Respite Care
A more extensive system of respite care and ""breakaway"" services for carers and the caring families should be promoted through the health boards
Persons who look after elderly dependants at home should be enabled to have mid-week breaks, week-end breaks and holidays
Tax Allowances for Paid In-Home Nursing Care

The existing personal tax allowance for paid in-home nursing care should be improved and we also urge a relaxation of the regulations, subject to satisfactory anti-avoidance measures, governing the coverage of the present allowance to permit siblings to avail of the concession when the recipient of the care is a parent or another sibling
Summary Fine Gael has pro-actively promoted a caring approach to Families, Children, our Elderly and the health Service

Fine Gael has significantly reduced hospital waiting lists, given people option for private health cover, developed strong health policies for women and also for persons with physical and intellectual disabilities, tackled the drugs problem and launched the first National Plan for Cancer Services
Fine Gael cares for people
EDUCATION POLICIES ON EDUCATION AND TRAINING POLICIES ON EDUCATION AND TRAINING OUR PHILOSOPHY
Fine Gael has long believed that educating our young people to compete in a rapidly changing world has to be a priority
We also need to prioritise the importance of continuing education
However, in order to do both of these, it is essential that our education system constantly adapts to external changes
The education system at all levels offers the single greatest opportunity for Ireland to build a talented workforce which is able to compete on the international stage
We are now reaping the benefits of the far-seeing decision in the 1960s to abolish fees for second-level education
This has resulted in a direct contribution to our growth performance by producing a skilled and adaptable workforce
But this decision has also indirectly advanced our prosperity by being one of the pivotal factors attracting foreign investment to this country
It is perhaps fitting that 30 years after free second level education was introduced this Governmetn abolished fees for third level undergraduate courses
Fine Gael believes that it is essential to view education and training as complementary
A sound education at primary, second and third level should provide all students with a grounding in the fundamental and enduring elements of all knowledge
Training, which involves either learning by instruction or ""learning by doing"" provides for the needs of the present, while education provides for the needs which may arise in the future
A sound basic education early in life, supplemented by constant re-training, provides a platform for lifelong learning
A judicious balance between education and training is thus required to advance prosperity both for individuals and for the nation
So what did we do? (Back to top)
Cut the Primary School Pupil - Teacher Ratio
A key factor affecting the quality of the education our children receive is the number of pupils each teacher has in his or her classroom
The Rainbow Government cut that average number from 25 to 22
That means better education for all our children, and more time for teachers to concentrate on children who need special help
Launched a new programme called Breaking the Cycle

Breaking the Cycle, an innovative programme which involves highly targeted interventions in 50 Primary schools located in disadvantaged areas with the objective of combating disadvantage, was established
Class sizes were reduced in these schools to 15 pupils for every teacher
The results from this initiative should have important implications for how the problem of educational disadvantage is tackled over the new Government's term
Abolished third-level fees
We abolished third-level fees which were causing great hardship to many middle-income families and denying access to many children to this sector
This means that on average families will save £1,500 for every child at college each year
National Sports Strategy
We launched a National Sports Strategy which commits the Government to an additional expenditure of £1.6 million in each year up to the Millennium to improve the place of sport in all our lives
Education Bill
The Education Bill devolves the provision of educational services to Regional level
It would have established Boards of Management in all schools in receipt of public funding and would have placed the Department of Education's Inspectorate on a statutory basis
This Inspectorate would be charged with helping schools to plan change
It would have improved the quality of our educational services for our children
The bill will give a greater voice to parents
Universities Act
We enacted the most radical piece of legislation in the universities' sector for nearly a century
This will make universities more accountable to the public, to parents, to students and to the wider community, and thus make them more responsive to the needs of society
The Fine Gael Millenium Pledge for Education and Training
Every 12 year old should be able to read, write, have a basic command of maths and science, log on to the internet, speak a continental language
every 17 year old should have a satisfactory performance in at least the Junior Certificate
every school leaver, should, at the very minimum, have achieved a Post Leaving Certificate qualification
and every adult irish person should be encouraged to keep on learning for their entire lifetime
Fine Gael has six policy goals it will strive to achieve during the lifetime of the Millenium Government
They are to:
Emphasise the education of the whole person
Create a responsive education system
Increase participation and improve performance levels
Deepen the quality of our education system
Encourage more continuing education and training
Upgrade the quality and relevance of training courses
EDUCATION OF THE WHOLE PERSON (Back to top)
A sound well-rounded education calls for an approach which emphasises the education of the whole person
The role of non- academic activities should have a prominent and valued place in the curriculum of schools so as to promote the social, cultural, personal and physical development of young people
The provision of these activities in our school system should be evaluated with a view to significantly enhancing their delivery
In this regard the role of Guidance and Counselling services should also be developed
In respect of physical activity we believe that active involvement in sports play an important role in the formation of the young person
Fine Gael calls for the implementation of a key recommendation of the Sports Strategy Group by creating a Cabinet place for sport in order to elevate sports to a central place in Government activity
CREATING A RESPONSIVE EDUCATION SYSTEM (Back to Top)
Supporting diverse management structures We believe diversity of management structures is a quality which is intrinsically valuable in our educational system
Fine Gael sees the promotion of a statutory basis for parental involvement in the Education Bill as a major advance on the existing situation
Fine Gael believes there must be extensive consultation with the education partners before any new management structures are put in place
Involve the business community in third level institutions
An effective way to upgrade responsiveness is to involve the wider community, at both local and national level, in third level course planning and review
Third-level institutions need to be capable of flexibly responding to the needs of the economy without compromising academic standards
The management of colleges must anticipate developments in the job market place and respond speedily by adapting their teaching programmes
Of course, academic institutions must look beyond the immediate requirements of business for graduates with skills ""of the moment"", and provide for longer term needs too
The procedures laid down for assessment of performance in the Universities' legisaltion will provide additional checks and improve the level of responsiveness
Using educational resources as community resources Fine Gael believes our educational institutions need to be responsive to local need in terms of the use of educational resources
The logistical, insurance and other issues involved in making school and college facilities such as sports grounds, class rooms and assembly halls available to local communities should be examined
INCREASE PARTICIPATION AND IMPROVE PERFORMANCE LEVELS (Back to top)
All the international and national evidence shows that investment in education is the best investment an individual can make either for themselves or for their children
It is a tragedy, therefore, that each year about 13,000 students either drop out from second-level without qualification, or perform poorly in State examinations
Many of these children face a future of unemployment and are often placed at social risk
International evidence suggests there are important inter- generational and ""neighbourhood"" effects which influence educational choices

Even seeing one member of a particular family successfully complete second level school, or seeing one 18- year old in a disadvantaged area attend third level leads to imitation by others from the same family or neighbourhood
The State has a role in ""kick-starting"" this process in disadvantaged communities
By igniting the spark in even a small way, investment could take off through the compounding effects of these ""neighbourhood"" and generational effects
Divert resources towards disadvantaged children

We believe resources released by the so-called ""demographic dividend"" must be diverted, which will arise because of the anticipated decline in primary student numbers, towards disadvantaged children in all schools by investing in additional remedial teachers, home-school links, social and psychological support services and improved teacher training and school equipment
These freed-up resources should be used selectively to achieve consciously planned outcomes, and not just absorbed in a generalised way

Education and Training to Age 18 In Government, we would ensure that every child up to age 18 will have the opportunity to participate in second-level education, training programmes, Youth Reach, or other pathways to work
Establish two key aims
We favour the establishment of two key indicators on which to judge performance
First, by the age of 12, we will seek to ensure that children will have attained a minimum specified level in literacy and numeracy skills
Secondly, every 17 year old should have a satisfactory performance in, at least, the Junior Certificate
Expand the Youthreach Programme
Fine Gael is impressed with the achievements of the Youthreach Programme in addressing the problems of disadvantage
We demand greater coverage of young people in need and that participants progress to a tradable qualification
Promote participation in Post Leaving Certificate Courses

Steps should be taken to encourage progression in educational attainment beyond Leaving Certificate for those students who do not wish to attend third- level colleges or take up an apprenticeship by actively promoting participation in appropriately accredited Post Leaving Certificate Courses or the new National Traineeships' programmes
The extension of maintenance grants to students attending such courses as soon as resources permit,should be prioritised
DEEPEN THE QUALITY OF OUR EDUCATION SYSTEM (Back to top)
To maintain our competitive edge Fine Gael believes we need to move with some haste towards upgrading computer and language skills at primary and second level
Achieve computer literacy at all levels The attainment of a standard of computer literacy at all levels among teachers and students is an objective of Fine Gael
Specifically, we want all school- leaving students to obtain a thorough grounding in computer skills
The aim would be to integrate computers into the whole teaching and learning experience
Set a target pupil / computer ratio We believe there should be at least one Personal Computer for every 20 students at primary and second level
The private sector should be encouraged to support this investment

Promote cyber schools and colleges The concept of ""cyber schools and colleges"" and networking should be promoted through ensuring that every classroom is linked to the INTERNET, and to the extent that it is feasible, has ISDN capability

Introduce a ""Virtual University"" Pilot Project Fine Gael believes that there is tremendous scope for using modern telecommunications facilities to improve access, enhance quality and reduce the costs of delivering third-level courses from central locations to outlying community centres
The concept of a ""virtual"" institution of higher level learning is on the brink of realisation in Ireland
Fine Gael supports the development of a major pilot project to advance this concept
Innovative plans are well advanced by the Cork Institute of Technology and the Third Level Campus Group at Skibberreen, Co. Cork to develop a prototype of this concept
The local group have established links with similar projects at the University of Ulster at Enniskillen and at the University of Missouri at St. Louis
We believe this project has the potential to be a model not just for the innovative supply of third-level education in the 21st century but it also can serve to promote rural regeneration

By retaining those students who choose to stay close to their communities to be educated through providing a telematics resource, which can be used for the benefit of the business, cultural, social and sporting activities of local rural communities
Modern technology can help promote rural regeneration of recent years
Achieve a greater fluency in continental languages
It is absolutely essential that we improve our command of continental languages
While academic excellence may be the goal for some, basic literacy and conversational skills in these languages is the goal we seek to achieve for all
We believe the most effective way to build language capability is to commence a continental language programme at primary level
Fine Gael's aim will be to ensure that by the year 2010 every 12-year old primary school leaver should have attained a basic fluency in one continental language
This will involve significant changes in the timetable in primary schools, a significant investment in teacher training and the use of visiting teachers
Such a radical development will require full consultation with all interested parties
At third level, we believe that all graduating students should have a proficiency in applied continental language skills
To achieve this objective, a Commission should be established,in conjunction with the HEA, to recommend a strategic plan for the implementation of this objective
ENCOURAGE CONTINUING EDUCATION AND TRAINING (Back to top)
Education and training shouldn't cease when one joins the workforce
Fine Gael believes that everyone should be encouraged to take part in continuing education and training throughout their working life
We propose, subject to available resources, to allow all fees incurred for appropriately accredited courses to be tax deductible at the standard rate
Initially this should apply to certain IT courses and the learning of foreign languages
Fine Gael are committed to supporting, through suitable incentives, lifelong learning for all our people and we intend to extend the range of courses eligible over time
Greater investment in telematics
Lack of access to centres of education and training constrains the widespread participation in continuing education and training for working persons or persons with young families to rear
We believe that investment in telematics technology has the potential to considerably improve access and special priority should be given to this type of investment in future capital programmes
UPGRADE THE QUALITY AND RELEVANCE OF TRAINING COURSES (Back to top)
Supporting new initiatives for training Fine Gael calls for the rapid implementation of the Rainbow Government's White Paper on Human Resource Development
In particular, Fine Gael believes training for unemployed persons should be tailored to assist them prepare for the workplace through the Local Employment Service
The emphasis has to be placed on the supply of relevant and appropriate training programmes leading to accredited qualifications and the path to full-time employment
We support the implementation of intensive short courses on job search skills tailored to the long-term unemployed
Link second-level with traineeships
Fine Gael see considerable merit in linking the provision of traineeships provided by FAS with the second-level curriculum
We believe there is merit in examining the provision for student access to trainee opportunities after their Junior Certificate but as part of the school curriculum
As an alternative to completing the Senior Cycle, students should be able to opt for an accredited traineeship, apprenticeship etc

This option provides real alternatives for many students who may find it difficult to adjust to the academic emphasis at second level while at the same time allowing our economy to have the benefit of a wider range of skilled persons
In time, the qualifications gained through these traineeships, and other measures, could be recognised as appropriate for entry requirements to third-level Institutes of Technology
CRIME
Policies on Crime (Back to top)
Fine Gael identified crime as one of the major issues that the Government needed to tackle
We pledged that in Government we would devise and implement a comprehensive plan to fight crime
This plan involved: Major changes in criminal law
Reform of our penal system
Improvements in relation to the Garda Siochana
In December 1994, Fine Gael immediately set about implementing a comprehensive crime plan
In just 29 months, Fine Gael achieved all three of these pledges and much more
Any objective assessment must recognise the sheer breadth of reform across almost every element of the criminal justice system
For the first time since 1989, indictable crime decreased
So what did we do in Government? (Back to top)
1 Major Changes in Criminal Laws (Back to top)
Fine Gael in Government set about a major reform of our criminal law
We took the time to identify weaknesses and then acted decisively to eliminate those problems and tilt the balance of our laws in favour of the victims of crime and those who uphold those laws
Fine Gael enacted legislation which : Allowed for the detention for questioning of drug traffickers for up to seven days and restricted the right to silence in drug trafficking cases
Introduced new measures to tackle the problems of delays in the Courts, including the appointment of additional judges
By May 1997, 24 extra judges have been provided for by legislation, a 25% increase on 1994 levels

Given the Gardai new powers to search for evidence relating to serious offences such as murder and rape, extended the period for which a person may be remanded in custody, provided for the giving of certain Garda evidence by certificate and permits the use of ""stingers"" to tackle the crime of joy riding
Provided for stronger measures against syringe offences, stalking and combating drug abuse in licensed premises
Bail Referendum
We introduced the Bail Referendum which was passed by the people
This means that the scandal of convicted criminals committing crime while on bail was finally tackled
The Government also reformed our laws to ensure that bail money will be collected
Criminal Assets Bureau
The Rainbow Government established the Criminal Assets Bureau
This put a multi-agency approach to tackling crime on a statutory basis - including pro-active targeted measures by the Gardai, the Revenue Commissioners and Social Welfare
The Bureau can request the High Court to freeze and ultimately dispose of property which it is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, is the proceeds of crime

The choice before Ireland

For rarely has Ireland faced such a critical range of opportunities and threats

The choice before the people is as stark as that

Economically, we now have the opportunity to build on the current wave of success, laying solid foundations for a prosperous Ireland in the 21st century as a viable member of European monetary union and an effective player in an enlarged Europe
Or we can squander the benefits of our present position, condemning the future Ireland to be an also-ran always in need of support in a world much less ready to give it
Five years on, we will no longer have this choice

Socially, we now have the opportunity to act decisively on the cancer of crime by enforcing our laws effectively and even more importantly, by removing for ever the disadvantage in our society that gives rise to much of it
Or we can watch helplessly while lawlessness takes over our country, and the gap grows wider between the haves and have-nots
Five years on, we will no longer have this choice

Technologically, we now have the opportunity to catapult Ireland to the front rank of the information age, where we can for the first time in history use our strengths to full advantage in an environment where our historical weaknesses need no longer matter

Five years on, we will no longer have that choice

Politically, we have the opportunity to restore the peoples confidence in the process of government involving them in it as never before, making the administration of government genuinely responsive to their needs, and frankly addressing the demand to eradicate all unethical conduct from public life

Five years on, we will no longer have that choice

make prudent management of our national finances the overridng policy objective of government, as the best way to sustain a better life for all in the challenging times ahead

Fianna Fáil's track record in prudent management
Fianna Fáil's ability to manage the national finances prudently is well proven

Over the past decade our consistent policy has been to lay firm foundations for future growth, and at the same time improve vital services and bring down taxes by controlling costs and increasing efficiency
In 1987 we created the ground-breaking social partnership which became the framework for carefully-managed growth

Fianna Fáil's strategy protected our economy during the world recession that began in 1990, made it possible for us to meet the maastricht guidelines, and set the scene for the present remarkable growth which the rainbow coalition inherited and has been largely squandering for short-term gain

the top rate from 58% to 48%
the standard rate of vat from 25% to 21%
corporation tax from 43% to 40%

The national debt - a burden too far
the national debt now stands at over £30 billion

Some 15% of all current spending, equivalent to 56% of income tax revenue in 1996, still goes simply on servicing the national debt

Fianna Fáil make a further commitment: once we have eliminated further borrowing, we will adopt a deliberate policy of paying off the national debt

Time to balance the budget

no crime, no matter how small, is insignificant;

certain crimes will not be overlooked because they are not important,

Fianna Fáil will make public administration more relevant to the life of the citizen, for whom the service exists

Information

Revitalising the public service through best-practice management
Fianna Fáil will develop a new dynamic in the public service and foster a proactive and innovative spirit
Our policy on entering government will be to immediately legislate to remove the obstructions and barriers which have restricted the potential performance and job satisfaction of many public servants

Fianna Fáil will release this potential by ensuring that individual public servants are given every opportunity to use their creativity and personal abilities to provide a better service to the public
This will be done through structured management systems, based on best practice

This approach will carry forward the strategic management initiative, which was introduced by Fianna Fáil
Creating a system of real local government
Fianna Fáil believe that a central part of bringing government closer to the people is to reform radically our system of local government
Since independence our government has been over-centralised by international standards, with little real power devolved to local level
Previous attempts to address this issue have not been backed by a driving political will, and therefore nothing has happened
Fianna Fáil believe that the time has now come to grasp this nettle, and give the people control over more of their affairs at local level
Our aim is to develop a system of democratic decision-making which harnesses the energy of all citizens and maximises their capacity to shape the future development of their communities
To achieve this, the new local government system will:
be structured so as to encourage maximum participation by people in decisions that affects their lives;
respond flexibly to local needs, and have the financial capability to do so adequately;
operate the principle of subsidiarity, that is, provide services at the lowest level at which they can be delivered efficiently;
nourish a vibrant and healthy local economy;
allocate responsibility and resources, wherever practicable, to the people affected
As part of our local government financial package, Fianna Fáil will cap levels by which local authorities can raise commercial rates each year

Fianna Fáil in government will consult widely with all the interests involved, and within the lifetime of the next government begin this radical transformation in the structure of how we govern ourselves

As few as one in five young suicides give psychological treatment a chance before going to their deaths
Fianna Fáil aim to change this through better availability of information, and better treatment of those at risk through alcohol dependence, drug abuse or depression
We will bring in priority measures to research suicide
Better use will be made of the coroneris enquiry by extending the confidential report sent by the Gardaí to the central statistics office
We will consult with a view to developing media guidelines for reporting suicides
Alcohol problems
We will control the advertising, packaging and promotion of alcoholic lemonades, and consider imposing higher excise duties on these products
We will develop an effective joint approach between the public and private sectors to encourage moderate use of alcohol
We will give particular attention to advertising aimed at young people
Overall, Fianna Fáil will energetically implement the national alcohol policy in full, including the setting up of a national alcohol council
Aids
We will ensure that all sexually-active men and women are informed of the risk factors associated with aids and how these risks can be minimised
Asthma
Asthma is becoming the disease of the decade
We will introduce a high profile treatment and awareness programme, especially for young people who would benefit from early treatment

Fianna Fáil in government will
set up a commission for parents in the home
implement a strategy designed to reconcile work and family life
address the effects of divorce by appointing a commissioner for children and strengthening counselling and mediation services
facilitate adult adopted children and their birth parents who wish to make contact, and fully recognise foreign adoptions under Irish law
promote the status of women at work and in business
work to eliminate violence against women
create a fairer deal for charitable lotteries
parents in the home
there are 500,000 Irish women and a much smaller number of male parents working full-time in the home
It is a priority of Fianna Fáil to provide them with support to enhance the quality of life in the home and community
Fianna Fáil will establish a commission for parents in the home to recommend a strategy for the next millennium
Social isolation is a major concern
We will encourage the development of community-based groups and projects which help improve the position of parents at home
Work and family life
Fianna Fáil are committed to an overall policy designed to reconcile work and family life
We will encourage job sharing, flexi-time and flexi-place working arrangements as ways of facilitating women who wish to participate in the workplace and maintain a family/home life
There is a clear need for a co-ordinated programme to provide properly qualified child-carers and to maximise the use of community facilities for crche and childcare facilities
There is a need to develop programmes of after-school care and play schemes for holiday periods
Fianna Fáil will encourage individual schools to provide these programmes and will make arrangements to ensure that insurance can easily be put in place
Fianna Fáil will introduce paternity leave, following consultation with the social partners
A childcare policy unit will be established in the department of health
Fianna Fáil''s tax policy will make a contribution to the cost of childcare
Addressing the effects of divorce
a commissioner for children
It is estimated that 10,000 to 15,000 couples will apply for divorce in the first few years

To ensure adequate protection for children, we will appoint a commissioner for children, initially attached to the courts, who will be responsible for highlighting to parents the needs of children in marriage breakdown/divorce and for pressing the needs of children in court where necessary
Counselling
The initial impact of divorce may place a great burden on the available counselling service

Fianna Fáil in government will ensure that sufficient resources are made available to the existing marriage counselling services to enable them to meet the need for counselling that will arise in the next few years
We will also plan for the long-term future by creating a permanent counselling service supported by the state, to complement or augment the services provided by the churches
Mediation
In each divorce case the judge has to be satisfied that adequate provision is made for dependants

Obviously, if in advance of the court appearance the parties have worked out an agreement on the financial matters, either by themselves or with the aid of a mediator, this would save court time and cut court costs
A mediation service is now available only in dublin and limerick
Fianna Fáil on return to government will begin immediately to set up this service nationwide
We will look carefully at doing this in conjunction with the legal aid service as a one stop operation
Bringing our adoption legislation up to date
many adopted children wish on reaching adulthood to establish contact with their birth parents, but this has not been possible under our closed adoption system
Fianna Fáil have presented a bill which establishes a voluntary contact register, and on return to government will immediately enact this bill

A register of this kind will enable a great many adopted children and birth parents to establish contact with each other, if both parties are in agreement, and is an essential first step in making progress in this area

When Irish couples seek to adopt abroad, they very often are offered children only on a basis that is not yet recognised in Irish law, one that transfers parental rights and authority to the adopters but does not sever legal ties between the adopted child and the birth parents
The rainbow government have refused to extend recognition in Irish law to these adoptions
The result is that, for practical purposes, opportunities for Irish couples to adopt abroad have been hugely curtailed

as it is likely in the future that the numbers of babies available for adoption here will fall well short of meeting the needs of the many couples who wish to adopt, it is essential that the road block which the government have unnecessarily placed in the way of these couples is removed
Fianna Fáil in government will legislate to extend recognition in Irish law to adoptions effected abroad
Women at work and in business
Fianna Fáil will progress steps to eliminate discriminatory and prejudicial practices in the public service
We will amend the anti-discrimination (pay) legislation to allow the use of notional comparators
This will mean that workers in occupations which are overwhelmingly female will be able to base equal pay claims on the earnings of other groups of similarly qualified workers doing similar jobs
We support the expansion of the existing joint labour committees to tackle effectively the problem of low pay as well as a national minimum hourly wage
Fianna Fáil recognised the trend towards part-time work and expanded the social insurance system to provide cover for part-time workers
Some 70% of all part- time workers are female, many of whom will retire on a social welfare pension
However, the provision of occupational pensions is an outstanding issue and Fianna Fáil will seek to remove this discrimination on our return to government
A certain percentage of training, education and community employment opportunities will be made available to women in the home who wish to return to the workforce
Sexual harassment undermines an individualis dignity by bringing an unwanted and unwelcome connotation to working relationships
At present, there are no legislative provisions dealing with sexual harassment, although the current employment equality bill endeavours to address it
Fianna Fáil believe that separate focused legislation is required

Women are poorly represented at senior levels of responsibility in social partner organisations and are grossly under-represented on negotiating teams and on the central review committee of the national agreement
We will ensure that women are represented equitably on these negotiating bodies
It is also important that we reflect the views of parents working in the home in our social and economic planning
Fianna Fáil strongly support the establishment of quotas and targets for women as a medium term strategy and will work with the social partners to achieve realistic targets

Fianna Fáil support the incorporation into legislation of European court decisions which provide that discrimination on the grounds of pregnancy is direct discrimination on grounds of sex and is therefore unlawful
Fianna Fáil recognise that there are some internal flaws in the existing maternity protection legislation which require amendment to strengthen a womanis right to return to work after maternity leave
Fianna Fáil will wholeheartedly support the continuing success of now, the European union equal opportunity scheme

Fianna Fáil will end discrimination in car insurance against spouses of policy holders, who at present are not entitled to any no claim bonus, if their spouse dies, even if they have been driving safely for years
Violence against women
a recent survey revealed that 11% of women experienced physical violence and/or sexual violence
To address violence against women effectively Fianna Fáil will:
legislate for separate legal representation for victims of rape and sexual assault
Secure funding for womenis voluntary agencies
Set up a domestic violence resource unit
Put in place a treatment programme for sexual offenders, as well as a register of sexual offenders
A fair deal for charitable lotteries
many charitable organisations pursue causes which greatly enhance the quality of community life, and in many instances cater for the essential needs of disadvantaged families
But lotteries conducted by charities have been almost driven out of business by the impact of the national lottery and recently by new competition from the uk national lottery

The problem is that there is no limit on prizes in the national lottery, where the jackpot alone can rUN into millions of pounds, but the charitable lotteries are strictly limited to £10,000 in prizes a week
In addition, charitable lotteries are obliged by law to report to the garda the names of all prize-winners and the amount of each prize
This applies even to scratch cards and places a major cost on the charitable lotteries
It also takes up valuable garda resources which would be better spent in dealing with crime
Fianna Fáil will immediately remove the cap on prize limits and will also remove the unfair burden of accounting and reporting of all prizes of less than £1,000
Improve housing prospects for all Fianna Fáil in government will
continue our innovative approach to social housing
bring about better co-ordination and co-operation between agencies in the housing field
give greater support to the fast-growing voluntary housing sector
carry out research into housing and homelessness
extend the shared ownership scheme and the sales scheme
legislate for speedier eviction of anti-social tenants and squatters encourage rural resettlement
encourage home ownership and alternatives between renting and full ownership
increase the first-time buyeris grant to £5,000 for couples
enact our draft legislation to abolish ground rents
housing policy that adapts to change
in 1990 Fianna Fáil brought innovative concepts into our housing policy such as shared ownership
We created a framework for the growth of the voluntary housing sector
Fianna Fáil in government will continue to implement this policy, suitably adapted to meet the changing society in which we live
We believe there is an urgent need for better co-ordination and co-operation between the various agencies involved in social housing
We will work to co-ordinate all areas including rent allowances, social supports and caring
We will respond to the need for more research on housing and homelessness, to ensure a quicker and more flexible response to housing needs in the future
We will also monitor the implementation of social housing policy to ensure they do not have unforeseen adverse effects
For instance, we must take care that in buying existing houses a local authority does not distort the market or upset the social mix of areas
Key elements of housing policy
Fianna Fáil will continue our commitment to the construction and acquisition of housing units by local authorities, and will continue to put resources into upgrading and refurbishing
We will give greater recognition to the growing importance of the voluntary housing sector, with extra overall resources and financial improvements in the details of existing schemes
We will phase in a well-targeted scheme of house repair grants
We will develop and extend the shared ownership scheme, reflecting increased property values
We will develop the sales scheme, with greater discounts for long-term tenants
We will transfer the rent allowance scheme into local authority control, and co- ordinate it with the existing scheme of letting priorities
We will make the maximum use of existing housing stock, with incentives to encourage elderly people to move to smaller accommodation designed for senior citizens
We will complete the registration of private rented dwellings, and enforce standards and controls for the protection of both the tenant and landlord
We will improve to co-ordination between housing, social support and care, in view of the increasing number of older people in society
We will aim to introduce broadly similar housing supports in the various housing categories local authority, private rented, and the voluntary sector
We will improve and formalise estate management procedures
We will bring in new legislation for local authorities and private landlords, so they can speedily evict anti-social tenants and squatters
We will look at setting up a housing court to deal with all local authority and private housing issues
We will continue and expand the policy of social integration in local authority housing
We will extend this to the private rent allowance sector by introducing guidelines or limits to the number of rent assisted dwellings in any area
We will bring in tenant training for all new tenants, and create better awareness, implementation and enforcement of the tenancy agreement
To rejuvenate rural areas, we will encourage rural resettlement and bring in a £3,000 grant for those surrendering local authority accommodation to purchase in rural areas
We will improve the first-time buyer grant to £5,000 where the house is being bought in the joint names of a couple
We will terminate ground rents, in accordance with our draft bill
We will encourage individual home ownership and other arrangements between rental and full ownership

completing the transformation of our roads system
following new approaches in energy
focusing on learning needs, not bureaucracy Fianna Fáil in government will
give priority to computer literacy, science, languages and third-level research
commit the state to pre-school education
end the resource starvation in primary schooling
manage change effectively at second level, and search for a replacement of the points system
make a radical attack on the problem of students dropping out
