Work
True work is primarily desirable not because it serves to redistribute wealth but because it both provides useful goods and services to society and is creatively satisfying to the worker
As long as such work is ecologically sustainable, we consider it good; but much of what passes for work in contemporary society is mere drudgery, and often ecologically destructive as well

Our party therefore believes that there is an urgent need to replace such drudgery by good work, as defined above, and that this would be greatly facilitated by the provision of Basic Income to all citizens (See the next section)

Our Party sees many fields of activity which, especially in a decentralised society, could provide opportunities for far more good work than is enjoyed at present, and some of these will be mentioned in other sections
It is natural for people to provide for themselves either by selfsufficiency, a cash income or a combination of the two
In addition, everyone should have the opportunity to provide for him- or her-self, through access to land, covered space, tools and training, together with finance where appropriate
Basic lncome
As a result of the development of technology, most of our wealth is produced not by human labour but by machines
For this reason employment, never an entirely satisfactory way of distributing income, is now less appropriate than ever

In response to this situation Basic Income schemes are under consideration in several countries; these aim to guarantee to each man, woman and child the unconditional right to an independent income sufficient to meet basic living costs
Such a scheme was proposed in Ireland in 1979, under the title of the National Dividend, as a solution to the poverty trap; but it was not followed up

Had it been adopted at that time (when the cost could have been met from Income Tax plus Social Welfare contributions) the formerly unemployed would now be free to accept any full-time or part-time job that came their way, or to work for themselves, alone or in co-operatives

The alternative is our present system, under which an employed person is free to take on two or three extra jobs (time permitting), whereas someone labelled unemployed is not allowed to take even one: a ludicrous state of affairs
Basic Income could become a positive force in many fields
Women would be less dependent on men, and thus relate with them better; mothers would be free to be just that, if they wished it, instead of having to forsake parenthood for wage-earning
Basic Income would allow energetic young people to work for themselves in their native counties, thus halting urban growth
It would put the equivalent of a grant at the disposal of those who, at any age after leaving school, wished to take on further education
Above all, Basic Income would release an immense amount of good will, and result in far more good work being done: this is why money released to make it possible would more than repay itself
But Basic Income would also result in a great devolution of power from Government to ordinary citizens: perhaps that is why the authorities have not been prepared to try it
Agriculture
We reject the agri-industrial approach to farming prevalent today because it adversely affects our rivers and lakes, wildlife, the soil, and inpeed the very quality of the food itself
Since, in addition, the quantity of some items produced is vastly excessive (due largely to centralised decision-making) radical changes are necessary
We actively support the organic farming movement and wish to see it become the norm

We appreciate the faet that its methods are labour- rather than energy-intensive, and that it is more appropriate to the smaller farm: in view of the energy crisis and the large number of people who would like to work on the land if they could, these seem to us to be advantages
We believe that the land is a common resource and that all who wish it should be given the opportunity to earn a living from market-gardening or farming, whatever their background

For this reason, land should be made available to them as cheaply as possible; by restoring the Land Commission or a similar body, it would be possible to put to far better use farm land that is now lying idle
When large estates or farms come on the market, these should be purchased by the State and used for teaching farming methods to people from both farming and non-farming backgrounds
In poorer areas of the country, where small farms are finding it difficult to survive, the establishment of agricultural co-operatives should be encouraged
We maintain that each household and community, whether rural or urban, should provide as much of its own food as possible
More allotments should be made available for gardening and horticulture, and public and private waste space utilised for this purpose

We reject all forms of agriculture which treat animals as mere items in an industrial process, for it is profoundly unecological to exploit other species in this way; the damage to human health caused by the consumption of meat impregnated with synthetic hormones, antibiotics and other drugs is also to be noted

We further point out that any form of food production which involves obtaining protein by first feeding it to animals is an extravagant use of such resources in a world where so many people are starving
Although Ireland was once covered in forest, it has now the lowest tree-cover of almost any region in Europe
We therefore urge the establishment of an intensive tree-planting programme and the need for the rehabilitation of neglected broadleaf woodlands
In addition to environmental considerations, we must also remember the value of wood as a highly versatile raw material which for years we have been importing at enormous expense
lndustry
We believe that the starting point for industry must be local production for local needs, realising that this will be fully possible only as the need for decentralisation is understood and acted upon

Recognising the undesirable conflict of interests of management and workers in so much of industry (and nowhere more so than in large concerns), we urge the need for the establishment of workers' co-operatives, and for an end to the bureaucratic obstacles put in the way of small enterprises

It will be understood from statements elsewhere that we do not see employment as the only nor even necessarily the primary way of making work available; but in so far as people seek it, and as long as the redistribution of wealth demands it, employment should be shared as fully as possible, for example by two or more people sharing the same job; double-jobbing is the exact reverse of this
Labour-intensive industries should be encouraged as long as the work is not degrading, the product socially desirable, and the result not ecologically harmful
Import substitution projects, as well as providing additional work, are also usually in the planet's interest, as of course are the many jobs that would become available by taking recycling seriously
The activities of multinationals are seen as most undesirably centralised and unecological, as well as needing to be distrusted for other reasons
Services
What is sometimes known as the Service Industry plays an increasingly important part in our society

While we recognise the value of much of the work done under this heading, we cannot help noticing both that many important services do not seem to be done efficiently and that some of the most valuable services (for example, in the home) are best done by those who are not paid to do them at all

The Basic Income scheme, as previously defined, would be of enormous benefit to many kinds of service, especially those which, like help with the elderly and handicapped, depend as much on compassion as on skill.

Other services, such the tidying of litter-ridden areas and the beautifying of countless neglected gardens, would doubtless be done for a modest sum by the jobless if the substitution of Basic Income for the dole meant that to undertake them would not involve the loss of other benefits
Leisure

As good work replaces drudgery as the norm in an ecologically sane society, the rigid distinction between work and leisure will disappear: far more work will be done, yet it will be invigorating in a way that, for many, only leisure activities are at present
The growth of the so-called Leisure Industry, we consider to be a very temporary phenomenon, and something that will doubtless make as little sense to our descendants as it would to our ancestors
Finance and Taxation
We believe that a radical reappraisal is needed of the role of the banking system, and in particular that there must be an end to the monopoly that the banks have in the creation of credit

Ultimately we seek an inflation-free world in which people will not need an income from savings, and in which workers' co-operatives, small businesses and individuals will be able to get loans for productive purposes at very low interest rates, as will those in need of housing
We see banking, insurance and stockbroking as separate activities, which should not overlap since this causes increasing risk and losses
Regarding taxation, the present system is cumber­ some, inequitable and extremely complex
A totally new philosophy of taxation is needed, and the following is an outline of a syste we would like to see introduced
Whether collected locally or nationally, taxation should be based primarily on non-renewable resources and energy, and for social reasons on such items as alcohol and cigarettes
A tax could also be levied on the unimproved value of the land, including land already built on
The effects of this fundamental shift in taxation would be to encourage the use of labour and to husband our non-renewRble resources"
Until such a system is introduced, however, there are urgent priorities relating to the collection of taxes under the present one
In particular we recommend that failure to hand over PAYE and VAT on collection be treated much more stringently
Businesses should be required to lodge VAT and PAYE into a separate bank account pending payment to the Revenue Commissioners
Businesses which fail to comply with this requirement should be closed down
As a counterbalance, PRSI contributions by employers, which are a tax on labour, should be abolished

Concerning the enormous variation in income between the richest and the poorest, it needs to be pointed out that, while our Constitution guarantees the right to private property, it qualifies the statement by saying that this right should be "regulated by the principles of social justice"
It would therefore be reasonable to put an upper as well as a lower limit on the annual income of the individual
Regarding the International Debt, we do not believe the repayment of this external debt to be a moral imperative
Serious consideration should be given to the cessation of interest payments
At the very least, negotiations should be initiated to reschedule it, to enable the outflow of interest and repayments to be substantially reduced
If this were successful, the enormous budget deficit would be virtually eliminated
Energy
The knowledge that the resources of the Earth are limited is fundamental to our Party, and we realise that we, the human race, must act upon it
This means that eventually all our energy must come from renewable resources; only then will we be able to live in harmony with the planet that is the source of our wealth

We reject the ESB's centralist approach to energy supply, with its emphasis on gigantic, massively polluting showpieces; and we deplore its 66% overcapacity, its 35% thermal efficiency, and its continued reliance on ships like the 'Kowloon Bridge'
Instead, we propose: a) large-scale investment in energy conservation in homes and industry, since energy saved is cheaper than energy generated;
b) thermal efficiency standards for new buildings, and grants and incentives for thermal efficiency in old ones;
c) the immediate establishment of a wind energy programme, and investment in renewahle energy production techniques using solar, wave and biomass sources;
d) the setting up of District Energy Commissions to implement a rational energy policy for each district, including small-scale community generation of electricity
Nuclear Affairs
Our approach to this policy is comprehensive and unequivocal, and we were the first political party in Ireland to call for the closure of Windscale/Sellafield
Concerning nuclear weapons, we look for: a) a universal ban on the production and testing of such weapons;
b) the destruction of all existing stocks;
c) effective, independent policing, under UN aegis, to ensure these steps are carried out;
d) universal abandonment of SDI-type research;
e) prohibition from Irish air/sea space of any craft which are nuclear-powered, carry nuclear weapons or refuse inspection
Regarding nuclear power, we look for:
a) the closing of Windscale/Sellafield, and cessation of the construction of THORP (Thermal Oxide Reprocessing Plant) on the same site;
b) meanwhile, the immediate cessation of the discharge of radioactive waste from Windscale/Sellafield into the Irish Sea;
c) an open-ended ban, to replace the present moratorium, on the dumping of radioactive waste at sea;
d) much-intensified research on methods for the safe disposal of the waste accumulated to date throughout the world;
e) the phasing-out of nuclear power production, on a time-scale laid down and enforced by the UN;
f) an immediate end to the foisting of nuclear power plants on Third World countries;
g) a phased transfer of resources from nuclear power activities to research into, and production of, means of generating power from renewable sources of energy;
h) rigid control of radioisotopes used for medical or other research
Pollution
Modern society has come to accept pollution as an inevitable by-product of "progress"
It is still widely believed that the earth, sea and air can be treated as limitless receptacles for all kinds of waste materials, and that the natural balance cannot be tipped over by such practices
We reject this attitude as dangerously short-sighted, and believe that the only acceptable level of pollution is no pollution at all

We see three main areas of pollution - Domestic, Agricultural and lndustrial - and believe that in every case the costs of pollution control and of cleaning pollution up must be borne by the polluters themselves

Examples of domestic pollution include refuse (much of it in the form of unnecessary packaging), fossil fuel emissions, and motorcar exhausts; in agriculture, synthetic fertilisers, pesticides, and slurry from intensive animal farming are the chief offenders; industrial pollution takes many forms, of which toxic waste dumping, emissions into rivers and the air, and the noise and fumes produced by road haulage are among the most obvious.

We believe that individual solutions can be applied to many of these forms of pollution, and that the setting up of an Environmental Protection Unit would speed up their application; but we are convinced that, like so many of the problems facing us, pollution has become a major threat because of the centralised nature of our society
Health
We believe that we each have a duty as individuals for, maintaining our own health, using that word in its broadest sense
We see the person as a unity of spirit, mind and body, and believe in promoting the well-being of this unity rather than merely treating symptoms of disease
To promote this well-being we advocate the ready availability of wholesome food, free from harmful additives, good housing, and an unpolluted environment
Furthermore, we recognise the need for people to be more aware of the benefits of good nutrition, healthy exercise and positive relaxation
To this awareness should be added an understanding of the dangers of alcohol and drug abuse

We would like to see official recognition of proven alternative therapies, and a more holistic approach to the treatment of chronic ailments; and we believe that small, well-staffed community hospitals are more likely to respond to human needs than large high-technology institutions
Housing
It is natural for people to take best care of things they regard as their own

For this reason we support home ownership; and we believe that it could be encouraged by the formation of building co-operatives, and by the availability of low cost housing loans and of building land at agricultural prices (as is proposed in the Kenny Report)
Agricultural land itself, however, should not be used for building, except as part of rural development plans approved by the community for reasons other than financial speculation

Where possible, old property should be renovated rather than knocked down in the interest of speculators; indeed, the making of profits merely out of changing site values, as distinct from improvements to property would seem to be inherently against the interests of the community

Concerning council houses, while a sufficient stock of these should be kept for those needing permanent residence, it would certainly be in the interest of both decentralisation and the care of the fabric if these were to be bought by the sitting tenants
Planning restrictions should be revised to allow people to work from home
There is nothing intrinsically wrong about a suitable mix of shops, offices, light industry and houses, and such a situation both reduces commuting and adds to a sense of community
Where possible, future housing developments should contain a mix of differently priced houses, to assist the dismantling of the class system

Energy-conscious house designs and building materials should be promoted; and provisions should be made wherever possible for the communal use of labour-saving devices, in so far as these are really necessary
Urban Conservation
Many of the problems of modern urban living can be traced directly to the destruction of community spirit

Sensitive planning and an intelligent urban conservation programme are essential to the health and happiness of those who live in towns and cities, and these can only be achieved if decision-making is decentralised
We therefore propose that:
a) the power to deal with environmental matters be returned to local authorities through the provision of strong planning laws and an equitable local tax;
b) the growth of local groups be encouraged in order to give people a greater say in environmental matters affecting them, including the drawing up of Development Plans;
c) the preservation of the unity and integrity of communities be protected against pressure from the car lobby and commercial developers;
d) the whole planning process reflect the change from large scale to small scale development and provide for the growing recreational, artistic and educational needs of the people

We believe furthermore that the character of local areas and the architectural integrity of our towns and cities must be protected through the rigid enforcement of preservation orders on worthwhile buildings and valued aspects of the environrnent, while at the same time ensuring that all new buildings be required to blend in with the existing fabric
We therefore further propose that:
a) property speculation be eradicated;
b) owners be encouraged to preserve existing buildings through the provision of financial inducements and expert advice;
c) parks, harbours, canals, riverbanks, wildlife habitats and other amenities be protected and expanded where possible, with special emphasis on tree planting;
d) effluents that threaten the health of humans and the survival of animals, plants, buildings and monuments be strictly controlled and if possible banned;
e) laws dealing with the nature, weight, noise, routes, speed and time of movement of heavy loads be introduced to ensure that urban dwellers are not endangered or inconvenienced by these loads;
f) further growtn of Dublin be halted, and the proposals of the 1985 ERDO study be rejected
Transport
In accordance with our Principles, we aim to reduce commuting and promote walking and cycling, the healthiest and most ecological modes of transport

Walking and cycling should be encouraged by the creation of pedestrian zones in urban areas, permanent cycle-ways on main roads, and facilities for parking bicycles in urban areas and in all public buildings
VAT should be removed from bicycles and spare parts
The implementation of our Housing policy would further encourage walking; so too would financial incentives for those willing to live within walking distance of their work places
Public transport needs to be greatly improved
We urge that:
a) buses be given priority over private cars, and fares reduced;
b) local communities be involved in transport planning;
c) the trend to one-man buses be questioned, as they hold up traffic, cause stress to the driver, and deprive the passengers of help;
d) the railways be revitalised for the transport of both passengers and goods;
e) DART be extended to Tallaght-Clondalkin and, where feasible, to other inland suburban areas
Since road construction involves enormous capital investment, and as motorcars are energy-intensive and environmentally damaging, we recommend that:
a) social and environmental considerations be included in assessing all proposals concerning future roads and bypassers
b) the use of vehicles with a long life be encouraged
c) the present speed limits be rigidly enforced and not increased
d) dangerous and drunken driving be treated with the seriousness that it deserves
e) city-centre parking be strictly controlled, street parking severely curtailed, and the provision of parking space near certain suburban stations and bus-stops be considered
Irelands inland waterways should be used for transportation whereever feasible.
The use of horse-drawn traffic should not be forgotten, and facilities for this should be provided wherever there is a reasonable demand
Women in Society

In the history of Europe, society has virtually never acknowledged the importance of women, either as individuals or as a group that constitutes about 50% of the population (and indeed much more than 50% after each of those many wars that have been started and fought by men and in which men have sometime been the victors, but women never)
We strongly welcome the move away from this disastrous imbalance, and we condemn contemporary activities that run counter to it, and in particular sexist advertising and the pornography industry

Concerning the regrettably small part which women at present play in this country's decision-making processes, we believe that only when the latter have become properly decentralised will the balance be restored
Regarding the Green movement itself, women have from its beginning been as involved in its decision-making as have men
Discrimination
The human tendency to discriminate against certain groups normally results from ignorance, and it is heightened by fear of the unknown

When the discrimination is largely unconscious (as in the case of discrimination against women) much can be done by the passing of specific laws; but when fear of the unknown enters the equation (as in the case of discrimination against the Travellers), such laws on their own may actually increase prejudice
In fact the latter can wither away only as people from each group get to know one another as individuals, but this is unlikely to happen as long as the groups feel mutually threatened by each other

To take the case of the Travellers a step further: when there is a sufficiency of dwelling sites suitable to their needs, each with a caretaker whom they themselves have elected, the Travellers will feel less threatened by the rest of the community, and consequently vice-versa

The per- manency of such sites (offering the advantages of settled residence without any obligation on individual Travellers to become less itinerant) would gradually allow the majority population to know and appreciate the minority, and then willingly to share educational and other facilities with them
Language
We value the variety of cultutes and languages in the world as an expression of ecological diversity
Here in Ireland we are in a position to treasure a very ancient language, An Ghaeilge, through which most of our national identity, place names, music, mannerisms and so on have developed
Although English is now very widely spokern, a large majority would still nevertheless like to see Irish used more, and equity for speakers of our two languages
We propose political autonomy for Gaeltacht communities, and positive discrimination in favour of Irish generally

We believe that all public agencies such as An Post and libraries should foster the conduct of business in Irish by making it clear which members of staff are willing and able to do so; and further, that private businesses should be encouraged to provide similar bilingual facilities, and to use both languages on stationery, signs and packaging and in advertising
We fully support the recent rapid growth in Gael­scoileanna as an example of community-based initiatives in education
We urge that priority be given to establishing a Teilifís na Gaeltachta to serve Irish speakers throughout the country

On the international scene we deplore the linguistic imperialism which results from the importance attached to a few widely spoken languages, and we welcome the development of Esperanto as a language which allows speakers of different mother tongues to meet on equal terms
Foreign Policy
Ireland's foreign policy, indeed every country's, should be based on constructive non-interference
Most conflicts are caused or worsened by the interference of nations in the internal affairs of others
Where exceptions have to be made to this rule they should be carried out through the United Nations
Ireland's neutrality has amounted, in reality, to no more than non-membership of a military alliance
As a result we have been unable to fulfil our potential as a conciliator between developed and non-developed nations and between East and West
Any co-operation in foreign policy within the EEC can only draw us closer to NATO, at least as long as all the other EEC states are members of that military bloc
We are committed as a Party to the pursuit of change by peaceful means

We recognise that violence can often take the form of economic exploitation (in particular by multinational companies and by banks), and of the destruction of traditionel living patterns, not least through the bad example of our extravagant lifestyle
We believe that international bodies such as the Uni ted Nations and the EEC should be more active in tackling human rights violations and problems such as trans-boundary pollution
Their dealings in other areas should be based on co-operation rather than centralisation of decision-making,
To a Party committed to decentralisation the very existence of superpowers, whatever their actions, is ecologically unacceptable

In particular we deplore their tendency to treat bordering and other countries as puppets, and believe that Ireland should use its neutrality to pressurise both blocs to cease their interference in countries such as Nicaragua and Afghanistan
We insist that Ireland ratify, and act on, the UN International Convention on the Elimination of all forms of Racial Discrimination
Our Party supports any peaceful campaign to secure a democratic future for all in South Africa
Northern lreland

We welcome the positive aspects of the Anglo-Irish Agreement, in particular the willingness of the British Government to co-operate with the Republic of Ireland in an attempt to solve some of Northern Ireland's problems, but we regret the lack of consultation with the Unionists which has hindered progress

We recognise that the system of majority rule in Northern Ireland has been much abused, and we urge the need for a Bill of Rights guaranteed by some body outside Northern Ireland, London and Dublin, whether at European or United Nations level
We accept the concept of two traditions in Northern Ireland, and we have no desire to incorporate the people of Northern Ireland into a United Ireland against their will
We reject the narrow nationalism of the past which saw a United Ireland as essential to our cultural identity
We believe that the only long-term solution to the problems of Northern Ireland will involve compromise by both communities there

This could be arrived at by use of a Preferendum (ie a referendum in which the voter expresses support for several options in order of preference), which would oblige people to think beyond the straight yes/no answer to a United Ireland
A prerequisite to the holding of the preferendum would be a statement of intent by the British and Irish Governments that they would abide by the result
Animal Welfare
As a political party with humane principles we cannot accept without question the exploitation of other creatures
Other animals cannot be thought of as mere means to our ends
We must remember that for each individual animal its own life and welfare are paramount

We therefore believe that we cannot lightly continue to cause suffering to animals in the name of food production, of medical research and of leisure pursuits, but must learn, in the words of Albert Schweitzer, to extend the circle of our compassion to all living things
PROGRESSIVE DEMOCRATS

PROGRESSIVE DEMOCRATS
BLUEPRINT FOR JOBS, FAIR TAXATION AND SOCIAL JUSTICE
Feb-87
It's Time For Real Change!
It's time for change in Irish society - from top to bottom.
That is why the Progressive Democrats were formed just a year ago.
We are a party comprising people drawn from all walks of life who realise that the old ways - and the old political parties - have failed us.
This election offers you an opportunity to vote for real change for a new way of tackling our economic and social problems for a new kind of political leadership.
Only the Progressive Democrats present that possibility.
In just twelve months we have changed the political debate in this country.
We have spelled out a detailed plan to cut government spending.
That is necessary to reduce state borrowing, and to enable standard rate income tax to be reduced, on a phased basis, over five years to 25%.
A fair tax system will reward people who work, and will encourage others to start up new industries, or to invest in existing ones.
At present investors get a better return by leaving money idle in a bank or building society.
That is a recipe for economic stagnation:
stagnation that is now stalking the land.
A fair tax system is also the key to combating the black economy.
Ireland is in crisis.
Years of living beyond our means on borrowed money have caught up with us.
The weight of government debt is crippling.
Taxation is intolerably high, and Irish industry can provide only a fraction of the jobs that are needed to employ our workforce and offer hope to our schoolleavers.
All around we see the consequences.
A quarter of a million people unemployed.
Over 30,000 more - skilled, educated and willing to work, forced to take the emigrant boat and plane each year.
And thousands of others just biding their time in job training and work experience schemes.
With each passing month, the problems deepen.
People generally are growing fearful about our ability as a nation to ever recover.
State borrowing has now grown into a mountain of national debt, totalling over £23,000 million.
Simply to pay the interest on that debt, eats up almost all the money collected in income tax each year.
State borrowing has pushed up interest rates to a level that is crippling industry and agriculture.
This has also led to a £50 monthly increase in the cost of the average house mortgage, above what they need be.
We must get back to basics if we are to survive.
We must banish our dependence on borrowings, the emigrant boat and plane, and the awful problem of mass unemployment.
We have to begin living within our means.
To do that requires a government that runs the country efficiently, and gives real leadership.
Only when that happens will we begin realising our full potential.
The proper development of agriculture, food processing, forestry, fishing and fish farming, tourism and other service industries can provide thousands of new jobs.
But that will only happen in a competitive cost environment, where the price of products and the services they depend on in transport, telecommunications and energy match those in other countries.
In other words, we are back again to the necessity to cut taxes, direct and indirect, and to restore incentive.
The Progressive Democrats have spelled out the cure to our problems.
We have shown how taxes and government spending can be cut.
This can be done while protecting those on social welfare.
At present the state attempts to spread inadequate health and welfare services too widely, and the poor often lose out
The other parties have failed miserably.
Fine Gael and Labour have wrangled with one another for the past four years, and ignored the worsening economic crisis.
Fianna Fail seek to be all things to everyone, and are afraid to take any unpopular decisions.
The problems of the country, however, cannot just be talked away.
To pull us back from the brink of social and economic collapse will require tough decisions to be taken.
That will also require fearless and honest political leadership.
Only the Progressive Democrats have the policies to begin the task, the courage to stand by them, and the guts to see them through.
Only by voting Progressive Democrat can the Irish people be guaranteed that they will get the kind of government which the country needs.
Building A New Republic
The Progressive Democrats aim is to provide government based on the following principles:
- Government that is open and honest, and keeps the people informed;
- Government that is firm, but fair, and which works for justice for all;
Over the past year we have spelled out the fundamental change that must be made to make this country self-reliant, prosperous and proud.
To do this:
This is a formidable and complex agenda for action.
But the Progressive Democrats have demonstrated clearly in the past year that they can meet the challenge.
Success in dealing with these issues cannot be achieved by repeating the policies of the past.
Now is the time for Ireland to commit itself to clear and decisive policies, and to apply them consistently until we have accomplished the task of making this country great again.
We will only support other parties in government which are committed to action along the lines of the Progressive Democrats' policies.
By voting Progressive Democrat the people of this country will have a guarantee of the kind of government they want.
Leading By Example!
Politicians must lead by example, if they are to expect the people to accept the tough decisions that are necessary to make this country great.
The Progressive Democrats propose the abolition of Ministerial pensions for sitting TDs, members of the European Parliament, members of the Judiciary and the President.
The party introduced a Bill in the Dail last year to give effect to this, but neither Fianna Fail, Fine Gael, nor Labour would allow time to debate it, accordingly they prevented it taking effect.
The party also proposes:
- the abolition of the Senate;
- the reduction in the number of Ministers of State from 15 to seven;
- reduction in the number of TDs to about 120, as provided for by the Constitution.
Justice For All
The Progressive Democrats are committed to a major programme of law reform, and fundamental changes in the administration of justice.
Public confidence in the judicial system must be restored.
To achieve this, it is essential to tackle the slow, cumbersome and costly legal process; reform the courts, and make the system intelligible to ordinary people.
We propose a new courts system and a new system for appointing judges.
The structure of the Garda force, and the training system for members of the Force must be reformed.
The Prison system must be reformed.
The party supports the broad thrust of the Whitaker Report.
Alternatives to custodial sentencing must be expanded for less-serious offenders.
Custodial sentences should only be a last resort, or and where it is the only sanction sufficient to express society's abhorrence of the crime, and to deter others from committing the same crime.
It is also important that justice is seen to be done in the courts, and that for serious crime, the punishment fits the crime.
But prison must also be a place of rehabilitation, offering the offender the opportunity of a new start

The Progressive Democrats have also set down in their recent "Justice For All" document major reforms of the criminal law, including measures to confiscate the assets of drug dealers and racketeers; to toughen the law on bail, and to crack down on the activities of moneylenders.
We will introduce legislation to cope with the problems of under-age drinking and video-nasties.
Caring For The Disadvantaged
There are many disadvantaged groups in our community.

Social justice demands that they be given the best support and protection that the community can afford, along with opportunities to develop their potential and play a fuller role in the life of the community.
To ensure this, health, education, social welfare and housing needs must be provided in a comprehensive framework.
The Progressive Democrats are committed to protecting the living standards of those dependent on social welfare, and to creating the maximum opportunities for their improvement.

What the vast majority of social welfare recipients want most of all is the opportunity to work; to enjoy the dignity and self-esteem of having a job, and being able to look after their family by using their own skills.
The Progressive Democrats will insist on the payment of this year's social welfare increase in July, and the maintenance of the real value of welfare benefits.
We will carry out a major overhaul of the existing social welfare schemes.
At present there are 19 different social insurance payments, and 12 social assistance schemes.
These must be simplified with more emphasis on local administration.
We will also change the Appeals system, to speed up appeals and to prevent people suffering from very long delays.
Social services for the old, the sick and the handicapped reflect the capacity of the wider community to afford them.
That is why a thriving Irish economy is the surest foundation on which to maintain social progress.
The Progressive Democrats are also committed to:
- focussing welfare payments to those genuinely in need;
The physically handicapped must be accorded full equality of opportunity in the educational system, and in fulfilling their right to work.
Care for the adult mentally handicapped including residential facilities, must be provided in a local neighbourhood setting as much as possible.
Protecting The Family
Although many promises were made during the last General Election about new legislation to protect the family, very little reforms were actually introduced.
We propose:
(a) New legislaton to give the non-working spouse (generally the wife) who stays at home to rear the children joint-ownership of the family home and family property.
(b) To up-date our marriage laws by raising the minimum age of marriage to 18 for both sexes.
( c) To up-date the law on judicial separations in order to allow the Courts to grant a decree of judicial separation on the grounds of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
(d) The creation of a Family Law Court, with full jurisdication over most family law cases.
This should be staffed by Judges who have a particular expertise in family law matters, who would have a back-up team of counsellors, welfare officers and medical experts.
Putting Our Children First
During the last General Election there were many promises about new legislation designed to protect the welfare of children.
Again, very little of this has actually come into effect.

We propose to introduce new legislation to protect children, particularly the children who are vulnerable - those born out of wedlock and those children who are abandoned, neglected, abused, or in care.
We propose:
(a) New legislation to give equal rights and protection to children born outside marriage.
(b) New legislation to allow for the adoption of legitimate children who have been abandoned, or neglected by their parents where this step would be in the best interests of the child.
(c) New legislation to up-date the Children Act 1908 in order to allow Health Boards to take steps to prevent child abuse and neglect.
(d) To provide separate legal representation for children in any Court proceedings where their welfare is at stake.
Realising The Potential Of The Public Service.
The Progressive Democrats see a restructured public service being at the core of a national patriotic drive to bring the country back to solvency and prosperity.
We endorse the reforms set down in the White Paper "Serving the Country Better,' so far as it goes.
And would apply its proposals to the wider public service.
But much more needed.
Real responsibility must be devolved to civil servants for the work they do.
The myth of a the Minister being responsible for every single Departmental item must end.
We propose reductions in outside consultancy work in Government Departments.
Generally, the civil service has the capability, and where necessary can acquire the expertise, if given the opportunity.
We are opposed to any enforced redundancies in the civil service or the public service.
Such a policy would only exacerbate the jobs crisis.
Because of the Exchequer's financial constraints, there must be a two-year freeze on recruitment in the administrative and clerical grades of the public service.
Civil servants will be deployed, to the areas of greatest need, and this will ensure more rewarding career opportunities.
This will be done in consultation with the civil service unions.
Modern management systems and new technology must be efficiently deployed in the public service.
This will ensure greater efficiency in the use of public funds, and the most efficient delivery of service to the general public.
A rewards scheme for improvements in efficiency and productivity will be introduced.
We will introduce protection for public servants who report improper practices or questionable procedures.
Jobs and Living Standards

Because we are a small country dependent on trade with the outside world, the key to success in creating employment and improving living standards is our ability to have enough activities that can compete successfully on export and home markets with firms from other countries.
Agriculture, industry, tourism, forestry, fisheries, financial and other services all have the potential to increase their contribution to this national need.
They face many obstacles in this task, not all of which are within our control or are capable of being quickly removed.
There are, however, some major improvements we can make which would lead to the creation of thousands of extra jobs.
The two immediate steps we propose are:
- major tax cuts in PAYE and PRSI which protect and improve living standards of workers, without the need for large pay rises;
The essential step to achieve these two cuts is to reduce government spending and borrowing.
Once government borrowing is reduced, interest rates can begin to fall to the levels prevailing in other European countries, which are as much as 7% below Irish rates (or half our levels)
If government borrowing is to be cut, then the only way in which to finance tax cuts is by reductions in government spending.
There is no other way to achieve these two essential steps on the road back to increased employment and improved living standards.

We also propose to examine in the context of the 1987 budget the scope for tax adjustments in sectors such as construction and the motor industry, which could generate increased economic activity and jobs.
An Industrial Policy That Yields Jobs
Industry has been a major source of increased production in recent times.
It has not, however, contributed significantly to meeting our employment needs because older, more labour-intensive industries have given way to modern, high-tech.firms, which employ fewer workers.

While the contribution of these modern firms is valuable and welcomed, it needs to be reinforced by greater efforts· to develop industries based on Irish natural resources, and smaller scale businesses which can create jobs for thousands of people, especially our school-leavers.
Our policy proposals in this area include:
- Changing the present system of large capital grants for new industry to favour employment;
- A business development scheme to give smaller firms greater support and improved access to finance at lower cost;
At present, the Revenue Commissioners are operating what is, in effect, a self-assessment system for the self-employed.
We believe this should be formally regularised, and a comprehensive self-assessment system introduced.
The present system of tax enforcement via either the County Registrar or a Sheriff seizing goods is outmoded and ineffective.
The Progressive Democrats propose that the most effective enforcement measures against non-compliant taxpayers is through seizure of bank accounts and attachment of earnings.
Underpinning our entire approach will be the re-deployment of a significant number of civil servants into the Revenue Commissioners, and the waging of outright war on the black economy.
Creating A Tax Climate That Releases Enterprise.
The country faces a massive problem posed by the high levels of government spending and government debt.
Spending has been rising much more quickly than we can afford.
Taxes have shot up to excessively high levels, but even this extra money has not been enough to pay for the spending, so that more and more money has been borrowed.
There is no way in which this pattern can continue.
The Progressive Democrats are the only party to have committed themselves quite clearly to ending this vicious trend by a policy of cutting both spending and taxes.
Spending must be cut in order to end the need for borrowing.
Taxes must be cut in order to create the opportunities for employment, and to restore the incentive to invest, as well as rewarding effort.
Our policies in this area include:
- reducing the standard rate of income tax to 25% within five years;

We published a detailed programme last Autumn to indicate the scale and the nature of the changes to be made each year over a four to five year period to achieve this fundamental reform in the whole area of government spending and taxation.
This programme naturally needs to be updated to take account of the actual 1987 situation.
But the basic programme remains unaltered.
This year we propose to:
- abolish PRSI on the first £3,000 of employee earnings,
In addition we would also propose to implement the first phase of the public ownership programme.
The target would be to raise £100 million in this way in order to reduce government borrowing for 1987 by this amount.
By these steps we would make a positive start towards resolving our tax and debt problems in a manner that would assist the recovery of the economy, and the creation of employment.
The Wider Ownership of Public Assets
At present the effective power of the citizen and the employee in regard to the operation of state companies is limited to providing finance free.
The organisations are run by their executives and a small number of higher public servants.

The sale of these operations to the general public with provision for their purchase by the staffs involved, private citizens, Irish pension and life assurance companies, will create a stronger identification of the public with the bodies concerned.
The performance of the bodies would be improved by this change.
The subsidiary objective is to secure an improvement in the position of the public finances.

The improvement in the public finances would occur first in the receipts from the sale of the assets to the public; second, from the elimination of the need for annual operating subsidies and, third, in transferring the companies need for equity capital from the taxpayer to the capital market.
The latter change would result in a higher standard of investment and general operation than we have today.
The Dublin capital market at present could without difficulty raise up to £400m a year from the sale of public assets.
The Progressive Democrats in government will prepare a programme for the sale of assets to draw on the available funds.
In discussing the sale of assets it is important to distinguish state control and state ownership.
It is not necessary that the state owns assets in order to control them.
For example the Irish banking system is not nationalised, but it is controlled strictly by the Central Bank.
The sale of forests by the state likewise need not require any reduction in state control of these forests in terms of access for the public and controls on tree felling.
In the contracting out of state services, the state can still control the service by stipulating the conditions attached to each tender.
The state would also have the right to terminate any contract where the standard of service was unsatisfactory.
The Construction Industry
Construction activity must be matched to the needs of the economy.
As the economy recovers under our radical proposals, there will be a matching pick-up in construction.
Such a balanced approach will provide the best prospects for this sector.
The development of a modern roads network nationally is a pressing necessity, and one of the most economically viable construction programmes that must be expanded.
The private sector must be actively involved, especially on toll-road projects.
At present, much road construction is carried out by local authority direct labour schemes, without recourse to competitive tender.
In contrast, it is authoratively estimated that road building and improvement schemes carried out by private contractors are considerably cheaper than those carried out by local authorities.
Considerable investment is also required in the country's water supply and sewerage schemes.

The eastern region alone is estimated in the ERDO report to need circa £600 million for sanitary services, and the requirement for the country as a whole is estimated at between £1,500 and £2,000 million.

The difficulties in calculating rates of return on investments in sanitary schemes are considerably greater than in the case of roads but it must be appreciated nonetheless that high quality water supplies and effluent disposal systems are essential to many types of industry.
A Vibrant Agricultural Industry Producing For The Market-Place.
The Progressive Democrats have a comprehensive policy on agriculture and food.
Some of the key considerations of our approach to this vital industry are:
- Reduction of the level of dependence on Intervention commodity products;
- Necessity to develop a greater mix of revenue-yielding activities on the farm, to support the maximum number of farm familites;
The price paid by this country for industrial free trade in the Community must be compensated in our natural resource areas.
Our peripheral and economic handicaps as a Community member-state must be stressed.

- Through our wider economic and taxation programme, focussed on getting government to live within the country's means, to create the right environment for farmers to develop their farms commercially.
Developing Our Natural Resources:
Tourism, Horticulture, Fishing, Forestry & Services.
These are the sectors that hold they key to real economic recovery.
But a proper tax climate and industrial environment is essential.
Internationally competitive transport, telecommunications and energy costs are prerequisites to any significant development in these sectors.
Ireland cannot sell holidays, food or fish products, financial services, or any other product in the EEC, or other world marketplaces, unless our prices and quality at least match our competitors.

Giving Power To The People
The Progressive Democrats support:
Educational Priorities

The Progressive Democrats see the allocation of greater resources in pre-school and remedial teaching as the key to helping children in disadvantaged areas aspire to equal educational and job opportunities.
The party also supports changes in the school curriculum.
At primary level, it must more adequately reflect the child's environment.
At second level it must reflect the realities of social and economic life outside the classroom.

At third level the party will review the grants system to take account of family size, in addition to actual financial circumstances, and will also examine the feasability of a student loans scheme to supplement, but not replace, the grant scheme.
We support wider community use of educational facilities.

We support the development of education programmes and courses by means of television and radio - backed up by correspondence courses and some class work, and a more flexible approach than the present school or campus centred programme, with a particular emphasis on adult and second chance education.
A special assualt on standards of literacy in certain urban areas by assigning teachers to local communities to work with young people is supported.
Irish Language And Culture
The Irish language is perhaps the most unique and distinctive feature of our cultural heritage.
However, it is in grave danger of extinction unless positive measures are adopted to ensure its survival.
The Progressive Democrats affirm that the survival, preservation, development and extension of the Irish language is one of the fundamental principles of the party.
A new approach is needed if the Irish language is to survive in a healthy state into the twenty first century.

This party believes this aim can be achieved by a combination of idealism and realism, involving realistic and practical measures to preserve and strengthen the Gaeltacht areas and to encourage positively the greater use of Irish throughout the rest of the country.
Our policy document on the language and Irish culture spells out how the language can be developed, and the Gaeltacht regions can be economically expanded.
Working For Reconciliation in Northern Ireland
The Progressive Democrats are firmly committed to working for peace and reconciliation among the divided communities in Northern Ireland.
We believe that the coming together of people in some new form of government and administration calls for an open and generous spirit on the part of all.
True unity in a community must be built on the consent of the people, not imposed by violence and intimidation.

The Progressive Democrats support the Anglo-Irish Agreement because it represents a recognition by both the British and Irish governments of the need to work for the creation of new structures of administration.

The Progressive Democrats also believe that the practical work of building stronger ties of friendship and understanding between North and South should be promoted in areas such as education, cooperation in social services, development of trading and other economic links, as well as in the fields of culture and sport.
Playing A Role In The World.
Recent events have seen much questioning of Ireland's role in the EEC, in the UN and in aid to developing countries.
The Progressive Democrats are committed to a forward looking view of Ireland's place in the international community, and are committed to maintaining our policy of nuetrality.
We are also committed to our membership of the EEC.
We support its fundamental aims of working for a closer union of the European peoples.
We also believe that our membership of the EEC enables us to exercise a degree of influence on the shape of policy adopted by the other member states.

We recognise that membership will continue to give rise to issues on which the interests of the member states diverge, but the experience of the Community to date has demonstrated its capacity to resolve differences by negotiation.
We also support a policy of Ireland playing an active role in UN affairs.
We favour converting many of our Embassies abroad into trade and promotional centres, in line with an Ireland House concept.
The Progressive Democrats also favour providing maximum help for the development efforts of Third World countries.

We favour strengthening the links between voluntary and official aid programmes, so that we not only maintain the excellent reputation which Ireland has already achieved but enhance it in the years ahead.

INTRODUCTION
The election of February 1987, is critical for the working class.

It will decide whether the government of this country will once again be run by the representatives of the tax dodgers, those who take all and give nothing; or whether they will finally be challenged by serious representatives of the PAYE workers, those who pay all and get nothing.

It will also decide whether the profits of a few will continue to be protected, at the cost of savage cuts in public spending, or whether work and progress on social issues will finally become the major issues.
The Workers' Party is now seeking a mandate from the people (o fight back in earnest, We are asking for the increase in support we need to send a larger and stronger team into the Dail.
We will fight back against unfair taxation, low pay, the drain of our people to other lands in search of work, the cuts in health and social services.
This is a fight by workers and unemployed together, a fight by those who demand the right to work and live in peace and security in their own country.
Let us be quite clear about it: we firmly reject the establishment view that unemployment, exploitation, emigration and the misery of poverty are inescapable.
We do not accept that we must be helpless victims of 'blind economic forces'.
We have shown in the past few years what just a few determined public representatives can do in the Dail, On Corporations, County Councils, Health Boards or Vocational Education Committees.
In the Dail that is now out of office, our two TDs have made full use of Dail debates to confront the defenders of the status quo with genuine plans for changed
They have used Question Time to expose abuses of power, cases of neglect, public injustice, rather than indulge in the narrow local point-scoring of most Dail representatives.
They have made life awkward for the major parties time and again by using their votes to challenge the legislation that puts further burdens on workers and workers' families.
With your support we will do far, far more.
PROGRAMME FOR CHANGE
With more TDs in the Dail, The Workers' Party will change the political agenda of this nation,
We will make economic recovery, social Justice and job creation the priorities, and where necessary we will bring the full democratic power of the people to bear on the establishment.
We are putting before the people a progressive programme for political change.
We are a modem socialist party; we want a fundamental shift in the whole direction of the country.

It is now urgent to begin building a new economic order, one that is socially responsible and will offer all citizens the chance to work productively, not as emigrants elsewhere, but as citizens here.

That day will never come if we allow our affairs to be permanently controlled by those who have a vested interest in the continued emigration of young people, the continued low level of pay for workers, the continued under-development of resources - in short, in continued inequality.
The Workers' Party believes that most social and economic problems are political problems, and they can only be met with political action.
No economy can hope to prosper with hundreds of thousands forced to depend on social welfare, while State resources are left lying, untouched by development.
We are prepared.

In this manifesto we offer in brief outline the analyses of our party on the economic and social crisis in Ireland, and the basic principles on which a radical reconstruction of Irish society can ' be built, with the support of the Irish people.
* We propose the creation of a new and powerful Agricultural Development Authority to undertake the vital task of modernising our whole agricultural production system.

It must also develop the most effective use of our land resources, increase investment, and establish a complete series of industrial linkages between the produce of the land and the consumer products in the supermarket.
That body will also have responsibility for developing aqua-culture, fish farming and fish processing.
It will also assist in promoting increased timber production, processing and manufacture.
* We want an Immediate transfer of 10% of PAYE tax from workers to the farmers, self-employed and owners of capital.
We see such an initial shift as the beginning of a complete restructuring of the tax System to end the disgraceful System where PAYE workers now pay over 90% of all income tax.

* We propose a new 'social guarantee' for all our young people which will provide a guarantee of either full time education, job related training or worthwhile employment initially up to the age of 18 years.

That will be achieved by a series of measures to restructure the education and training institutions, expand recruitment in slate, semi-state and private enterprises where labour can improve performance and create new task forces to bring/unused resources into productive use.
* We will introduce a series of initiatives to eliminate all forms of sexual discrimination in employment, in social welfare, in the law, in sport and in society generally.
This will form part of a wider programme to eliminate aII forms of social discrimination against the poor, the unemployed, the homeless, the handicapped as well as part time workers and home workers.
* We believe that part of our economic recovery must include an environmental programme or urban renewal.
Such a programme makes both economic and social sense and offers tremendous prospects for employment generation in construction, tourism, services, arts and entertainment.
It provides opportunities for democratic community participation in planning and could bring substantial long-term savings in policing, maintenance, transport and public services.
This will be accompanied by control of the price of building land and a tax on derelict sites.
* We will work persistently both North and South to achieve peace and reconciliation between the people of this island.
We recognise the legitimate rights of Protestants, Catholics and Dissenters and reject the view that the Northern Protestant population can be bullied, bombed or threatened into a united Ireland.
We will develop dialogue, co-operation and common activity between workers as the means of uniting our people in a campaign for peace, work and class politics.
* We will build a series of community leisure and sports facilities in all working class communities to provide a resource centre for entertainment, leisure, sport, art and culture.
The creative artist will be accorded the same rights as other workers and steps will be taken to develop all creative talent up to its maximum potential.
Steps will also be taken to end the growing exploitation of the poor and unemployed in newly emerging amusement and entertainment sectors.

* We will continue to press the government to make our neutrality more positive in character by campaigning energetically for world peace and nuclear disarmament, by remaing out of military alliances, by giving support to developing countries and to those seeking to create democratic governments in place of racist and dictatorial regimes.
THE ECONOMY
Other parties looking for your support in this election can only offer policies of despair and defeat.
The Workers' Party owes nothing to the wealthy or the status quo and because of this can offer practical policies for full employment.
Unemployment is at the root of almost all of our social ills.
It is our worst social injustice.
The Republic has the resources needed to give a decent living to all.

The cause of poverty and mass unemployment is gross government incompetence, especially in the last ten years, and determined efforts by government in the last 10 years to confine profit-making economic activity to private industry.
The policies followed by governments in the last ten years mean that we have:
* The highest rate of unemployment in the industrialised world;
* The greater part of our farm exports sold into intervention;
* Half the workforce in that building industry is denied the right to work;
* One third of our population lives in poverty;
* One in eight of our manufacturing jobs have been lost in the last six years;
* Mass emigration is back;
* We pay one of the highest rates of indirect tax in the world.
It is obvious that the present private enterprise Irish economy can only remain solvent with the aid of massive government subsidy.
This is a crucial factor in our heavy burden of foreign debt.
THE NATIONAL DEBT
The scale of the national debt must be seen by all as a major economic problem.
All parties except The Workers' Party say that the way to deal with the crisis is to cut government spending.
They talk about tightening belts.
Whose belts?
The word "cuts" in the mouth of Fianna Fail, Fine Gael, the Progressive Democrats or Labour means cuts in social welfare payments and cuts in spending on health and education.
It is a policy of making the needy - the victims of the crisis - carry the burden of the crisis.
A policy of cuts in government spending on social services will only aggravate the situation by increasing the scale of poverty.
More will be thrown on the dole queue and emigration will worsen.
A brief examination of the plans of the establishment parties shows a repayments bill of £1,000 million a year until the end of this century.
It is impossible to find that amount of money every year by a policy of cuts.
They, of course, hope to reduce social welfare payments by a policy of encouraging emigration.
Some 31,000 emigrated in 1985.
The figures for 1986 will be double this.
THE WORKERS' PARTY PLAN
The Workers' Party puts forward a policy of expansion rather than cuts.
We must grow or go down.
The debt crisis must be met by massive growth in our Gross Domestic Product (the value of all we produce).
The way to end the crisis and to work towards full employment is:
(a) Change the "spending policies" (grants to the private sector in the hope that this will produce jobs) which was followed by all Irish governments for twenty years.
We must have "investment policies" (investment and grants given only on the basis of a firm plan to increase employment and output);
(b) A plan to develop the economy on the basis of planned output applies especially to production for export;
(c) We must commit resources to marketing our products.
This is a crucial area in need of investment.
We must have highly trained staff and develop popular brand names.
OUR INVESTMENT POLICY
In 1985 the overseas firms in Ireland called home the better part of £ l,000 million profits made in Ireland.
A large part of these profits were made as a result of the Irish State guarantee that profits made from manufactured exports would remain taxed at 10% until the and of the century.
The government should negotiate for the investment of the bulk of these profits in Ireland.
Public enterprise in manufacturing, marketing and profit-making enterprise should be greatly expanded.
All restrictions on State companies should be removed.
JOB CREATION
The Workers' Party calls for the creation of an additional 40,000 jobs a year, spread over the next 10 years.
We have explained in a number of publications how this can be done.
We published an extensive plan An End to the Crisis - when unemployment levels started to rise sharply.
We published a Farm and Food Industry Study when the EEC started to seriously re-examine its intervention payments policy.
JOBS FROM OUR NATURAL RESOURCES
Industry based on our natural resources is the only way to create dependable employment.
In our farming and food industry study we gave detailed plans for the creation of 150,000 jobs.
It is important to note that the Workers' Party regard productive jobs - jobs which produce a saleable, exportable product - as the foundation on which the whole economy must rest.
This policy means:
* The production of (food products in consumer-ready form and delivery guaranteed over the full twelve months of the year;
* The production of high-quality clothing manufactured from natural fibres like linen and wool, mostly for the export market;
* Supplying our need for paper by producing ourselves from our own resources rather than by costly imports;
* The development of a timber industry to produce timber and processed timber for the construction industry, and wood pulp for paper manufacture;
* Full development of the shoe industry which should be linked to the manufacture of leather from raw-hides now exported:
* The industrial development of our mineral wealth by smelting our lead and zinc;
* The development of fishing, fish processing and fish farming, on an extensive scale;
* The cultivation and processing of industrial crops like bamboo, flax, New Zealand flax and dwarf sumac;
* The development of an indigenous electronics sector with an emphasis on research and development and a capacity for regeneration.
OUR INVESTMENT POLICY ~ OVERSEAS SECTION
The overseas sector of the Irish manufacturing economy employs 80,000 industrial workers.
This sector of the economy is located in new and growing industries like electronics and chemicals.
We note that this sector of the economy imports massive quantities of semi-processed raw materials - £5,000 million in 1985.
It is in this area of great potential development that we believe that negotiations should take place for the re-investment in Ireland of profits made in Ireland by these firms.
We regard this as a fair return for the substantial tax concessions made 10 firms operating in the area of exporting manufactured products.
ENERGY
The Workers' Party has continually agitated against the high cost of energy to manufacturing industry.
It is next to impossible to develop competitive manufacturing industry based on the present 20% energy cost handicap.
We recognise that the handicap is to some extent compensated for by a lower rate of pay to the Irish manufacturing workforce.
This method of cancelling a cost handicap is a grave Injustice.
A part of the high cost of energy in Ireland is caused by a penal levy of indirect taxation on this essential.
ESB bills, for example, all carry a substantial tax levy.
It is an economically unwise aspect of government taxation policy.
THE PUBLIC SECTOR
Privatisation: The Workers' Party is totally opposed to privatisation of our State companies.
Demands to hand over our valuable public assets to private capitalists must be resisted and the motives of those who make such demands must be exposed.
The Workers' Party welcomes the opportunity presented by this election to debate the role of State industry in the Irish economy.
Those who suggest that selling off our publicly owned companies will help to solve the financial crisis are misleading the people.
The only people to benefit from privatisation would be the small clique of well-heeled financial speculators who would make a killing on the stock market.

It's almost ten years since the Workers' Party identified the potential of State companies, exposed the resentment against State industry among private enterprise politicians and predicted that attempts would be made to privatise these national assets.
Despite massive hand-outs of taxpayers' money, (a thousand million in 1986), the private sector has failed to deliver the jobs.
Now the same private sector wants to get its hands on the profitable operations within the public sector.
To auction off our public sector companies in order to satisfy the avaricious appetite of private enterprise would be the kiss of death for state industry in this country.
Starved of share capital by successive private enterprise governments, our State companies have been forced to borrow from private banks at exorbitant interest rates.

Despite the obstacles placed in the way of our State companies and the restrictions placed on their operations - for example being prohibited from competing with private enterprise - these companies have played a crucial role in the social and economic development of the State.

Contrary to the daily propaganda about "loss makers", in the last year our 17 main public enterprises had trading profits of £447 million, and net profits after financial charges of £85 million before tax.

The Workers' Party in declaring its outright opposition to privatisation of any of our State enterprises reiterates its long standing policy that our State companies be used as the engine of economic growth and recovery.
There is no time to waste if the full potential of our State companies is to be utilised to tackle the massive jobs crisis which is the legacy of decades of reliance on private enterprise.
The Workers' Party demands that substantial amounts of State funds presently being swallowed up by private companies be re-directed for Investment in the development and expansion of State industry.
Such initiatives are needed to lift the heavy burden of under capitalisation of our public enterprises.
An efficient and dynamic State sector generating wealth and creating jobs is a cornerstone of the Workers' Party plan for economic development and job creation.
The party will fight inside and outside Dail Eireann to oppose and expose those who would hijack the State's resources in the interests of private profit.
OUR PAY POLICY
There should not be one-sided restrictions on pay.
We believe, as does the trade union movement, in a pay policy, but it must include all incomes and be linked to an agreed policy of investment - a comprehensive national plan.
A pay policy to the establishment parties means restricting workers' pay.
Government should not prevent the payment of awards agreed upon by the machinery established for this purpose.
The Workers' Party believes in equal pay.
OUR TAXATION POLICY
The present tax System is glaringly unjust, It favours the wealthy, business and the prosperous end of farming.
We have long been active on this scandal as have the trade unions.
We have many times pointed out injustice in the present System of taxation, We now say that in relation to income tax the following facts are a grave scandal.
In 1981 the PAYE sector paid 87.7% of the total income tax bill.
In 1986 this percentage increased to 90.3%.
Over the same period the number of employees (PAYE taxpayers) fell by 8%.
It is a grave injustice, the PAYE sector was charged an increase of 2,6% in their total income tax bill while at the same time they suffered a reduction in numbers of 8%.
The employers and self employed suffered a reduction of 1.4% in numbers but received a reduction of 3% in their income tax bill.
The enormity of the injustice becomes clearer when explained in numbers:
Employees (PAYE taxpayers) 524,000 - who pay 90.3% of the total income tax bill.
Employers and self-employed 228,300 - who pay 8.2% of the total income tax bill, ,

The payment of this 10% should be transferred to employers, self-employed and farmers.
