INFLATION
Fine Gael aims to secure a more rapid fall in inflation than that projected by Fianna Fail.

The Fianna Fail targets imply cost increases in the immediate and medium-term future that would leave our goods and services uncompetitive, and would make certain a further and continuing decline in purchasing power and employment.
Fine Gael will set new targets for the reduction through the next four years.
The inflation target will be the subject of discussion with Unions and Management with a view to securing an orderly winding-down of the rate of income increases and price increases.
This reduction is possible; it was achieved by us in the mid seventies when the inflation rate was brought down by this process from 24% to less than 7%.

To ensure that increases in the retail prices of imports are held down to the now much reduced rate of increases in actual import prices, steps will be taken, by legislation to monitor and, if necessary, control import profit margins.
Fine Gael have dealt in greater detail with this subject in our Policy Document "Jobs in the '80s".
The Government cannot rule by edict in this area, but can negotiate from a position of strength.
Fine Gael now looks for a mandate from the people, to negotiate to achieve the following aim:
Interest groups must settle their arguments about income distribution without passing on inflationary burdens to the rest of the community.
The management of public sector pay increases so that they are related to available revenue.
The introduction of mechanism to allow variation in pay increases related to productivity growth.

Fine Gael will also consider the appointment of an expert body to be established to bring to Government and public notice, trends in our relative competitiveness vis-a-vis other countries, and the need, in the interest of jobs, to keep the costs in this economy below those of our competitors.
INDUSTRY
Fine Gael accepts the broad thrust of the Telesis Report on Industrial Policy.
In particular, and in line with the Telesis recommendations, Fine Gael will place greater emphasis on wholly owned home-based export firms in disbursing state grants.

In regard to grants to foreign companies priority will be given to those which will yield maximum advantage to the Irish economy in terms of the provision of skilled employment, supply linkages with Irish firms, and the setting up of a full range of operations especially marketing and research development.
Fine Gael's industrial policy in government will give particular priority to the development of the food processing sector.

This will be achieved by encouraging long term contracts between suppliers and food processors and by establishing the new National Development Corporation which will have special responsibility for promoting new enterprises in this area.
AGRICULTURE
In agriculture, Fine Gael's aim is to secure real income increases for farm families and sustained growth in the volume of farm output.
Farm income increases will be brought about by reducing inflation and securing the maximum rate of increase in prices at EEC level.
The alleviation of the present price/cost squeeze will in turn allow the volume of farm production to increase in a sustained manner.
This will produce expansion of output and employment in our food processing industries, leading to substantial export gains.
This approach will also allow us to make progress reversing the inroads made in our market by imported food products.
Agricultural expansion must be a key component of future development since its import content is low and the scope for adding value and increasing employment in the food processing is enormous.
We must therefore ensure that the maximum possible porportions of available development resources is channelled into agriculture.
It is only by consciously directing our resources in this way, that we can achieve the results we so urgently require.
Fine Gael will pursue its policies in such a way as to restore solvency and to bring profit margins on our farms to reasonable levels.
It is only by doing this that we can bring a new impetus to farm development.
The measures which we believe must be given priority are set out in our programme "Jobs in the '80s".
Such further measures will be defined in the framework of a four year development plan for the sector, which we will re-examine and define so that it corresponds to our principal objectives.
SOCIAL AFFAIRS
Fine Gael will ensure that the State provides for the Health and Welfare of those in greatest need.
Therefore we will protect them from the effects of expenditure cuts.
Fine Gael will develop community-based Health facilities and will introduce major directional changes and developments of Community Programmes.

In regard to Care of the Child, especially of those in deprived social circumstances, and the Care of the Aged Fine Gael will seek to maximise the potential to keep them living within their own communities.
Positive encouragement will be given to the development of voluntary agencies.
Fine Gael will review the medical card system and the drugs refund schemes.
Fine Gael proposes to review eligibility for Hospital Services for those with incomes in excess of £12,000 and private patients will pay more realistic fees for hospital back-up services.
In this context it is proposed to develop the Voluntary Health Insurance involvement in the provision of Health Services for the middle and higher in-care groups.

In addition Fine Gael will implement necessary expenditure cuts in such a way as to relieve the least-well off from the adverse effects of these cuts, and to spread the burden equitably between people at the various income levels.
Where charges for service have to be introduced, provision will be made, where possible, to relate these to means.
TAXATION

Fine Gael will gradually revise the taxation system and will increase its equity for example by - Substituting tax (which are of equal benefit to all) for tax allowances (which benefit better off people disproportionately and which give no relief to the lowest paid).
Re-introducing a family income supplement for the low paid; and reducing PRSI on incomes below a figure of around £6,000 as proposed in our policy document "Jobs in the '80s".
Fine Gael will further modify the tax system to increase the incentive to save.
In this connection it will sympathetically examine the Commission on Taxation's proposals.
In particular it proposes to give early consideration to an exemption from taxation of savings in the year in which the savings are effected.
The introduction of any change along these lines, will, however, have to be accompanied by measures to eliminate evasion of taxation.

We will reduce the disincentive to work that exists, at present in cases where after-tax income is as high as, or, in an important minority of cases even higher than, the after-tax income available to a person at work.
A first step in this direction will be the principle that income from all sources will be equally liable for taxation.
With regard to State benefits, this taxation will be applied to unemployment benefit, disability benefit and pay related benefit.
Fine Gael will examine the imposition of V.A.T. at point of import.
Fine Gael strongly opposed this measure in the Dail and is aware of the serious damage that it is causing to industry.

We also recognise, however, that an advance commitment to do away with V.A.T. at point of import, immediately on returning to office, would have a very serious effect on the 1983 Current Budget Deficit.

The financial situation of the country is so serious that we cannot make a pre-election commitment which could have such a bad effect in a year when our finances, and indeed, our capacity to borrow, are already very precarious.

Fine Gael will immediately on taking up office initiate discussions with the Confederation of Irish Industry and other importers' groups to work out the best possible way of dealing with this problem and if feasible having regard to the current Budget Deficit for 1983, reversing the existing policy.

OTHER POLICIES CRIME
The extent of crime is indicative of the social and economic difficulties facing our country.
Fine Gael recognises that the arrest, conviction and punishment of offenders cannot, and should not, be considered as the complete solution to a problem which is often the result of deprivation.
With some categories of crime, law and order will not be re-established merely by getting tougher with criminals.
Only a two-pronged attack through reform and tackling poverty, taken in conjunction with more effective measures against crime can ultimately succeed.

As a community we must, of course, deal with organised crime of the brutal and de-humanising kind which has become more and more prevalent in recent years and which is often but by no means always associated with illegal organisations.
Fine Gael believes that our present resources for dealing with crime are seriously inadequate.
Clearly there are insufficient man-hours of police time available and applied to the task.
Clearly also our laws have defects which make life easy for the hardened criminal, difficult for the hard-pressed Gardai.
Among the measures which will be introduced to increase the effectiveness of the criminal law will be the following:

A provision enabling evidence to be given at a trial of questions put to an accused before a District Justice or quasi-judicial personage such as a Peace Commissioner, and the answers given, or refused, by the accused.
A requirement that alibis to be advanced by the defence in a prosecution be notified to the prosecution a sufficient time in advance to enable them to be checked.
A provision that offences committed when on bail must be separately dealt with, and, if proved, that they be the subject of a sentence separate from that given for the original offence.

Fine Gael will also examine the possibility of introducing a provision which exists in some other countries viz shifting the onus of proof to parents of juvenile offenders that they, the parents, are not responsible by their neglect, for such offences.

At the same time Fine Gael will establish a Garda Authority to seal off the Gardai from political interference and will make provision for an independent complaints procedure in respect of actions by Gardai.
A judicial enquiry will be initiated to investigate all allegations of political interference with the Gardai during the last two years.

Such a course of events would threaten the economic and social stability of our society
Our economic potential, however, is great and our capacity to avert the unwelcome consequences, which now threaten us, is clear

OTHER COUNTRIES ARE FACING THE SAME CHOICE 1
Our problems are not unique

After two decades of exceptional economic growth and, in many countries, full employment, countries everywhere are faced with the need for severe adjustment and unpalatable corrective action to offset the effects of the worst and most prolonged recession to hit the world economy since the nineteen thirties
The defensive measures taken by other countries up to this period in the recession have been much the same as our own
Taxation and borrowing were increased so as to finance greater government expenditure, to maintain demand, and to finance balance of payments deficits
Otherwise, demand would have been lower and unemployment would have been greater
But in spite of these measures which could only last temporarily, the countries of the developed world are, almost without exception, still in profound economic difficulties
It has not been possible to maintain demand sufficiently to prevent unemployment growing
There are now 11 million persons unemployed in the European Community as compared with 5 million in 1977

The intimidating outlook is for continued increases in unemployment as countries give the necessary priority to cutting back on their high levels of borrowing and to lowering prices and interest rates
OUR SPECIAL DIFFICULTIES AND OPPORTUNITIES 1
We have special difficulties in adjusting our economy without causing excessive cutbacks in demand and output
Our population is growing at about four times and our labour force at about twice the European Community average
This measures our need for greater investment and for more new jobs at a time when we must curtail borrowing and correct our large and unsustainable balance of payments deficit

Many of the international economic trends are, however, now for the first time in three years beginning to offer us the prospect of increased exports to replace the internal demand we were forced to create temporarily at the height of the recession by internal and external deficit financing
Compared with a fall of over 1.5% last year, EEC imports are forecast to increase by 2.5% in real terms in 1982 and by about 3% in 1983
In the United Kingdom, our largest export market, the volume of manufactured imports, which was static in 1981, is expected to expand by 7.5% in 1982 and by 5% in 1983
International inflationary pressures are moderating
Our imports, which increased in price by nearly 21% in the first seven months of 1981, increased by just over 8% in the corresponding period in 1982
The international trend in interest rates is downward from the unprecedentedly high levels of recent years

Against this slowly improving international background, our economic strategy during the recession, in common with other countries, of deficit financing to sustain demand and employment, can now be modified progressively to remedy deep-seated defects in our economic structure
Our economy suffers from a number of serious defects which will worsen unless we avail of the improving international outlook to remedy them:
- we are losing jobs faster than we are creating them due to our increasing inability to sell competitively at home and abroad all the goods and services we can produce;
- we have lost a substantial and growing share of the home market to imported products;
- our higher inflation and interest rates are raising our production and operating costs faster than in other competing countries;
- our unit labour costs in manufacturing industry have been rising faster than those of our EMS narrow-band partners in the European Community;
- because we are consuming more than we produce, we have been running large deficits in our account with other countries
Such large deficits cannot continue without affecting our trade and the value of our currency

We must return to paying our way in the world; - our level of borrowing for public expenditure, including for current expenditure to finance public services, is unsustainably high and must be progressively curtailed; -we still have serious regional imbalances in economic and social growth and opportunity which diminish total output and reduce the efficiency of our economy

Existing basic trends in the economy cannot be allowed to continue without unwelcome consequences
Predominant among these trends are growth in public expenditure which cannot be matched by tax increases;
a high balance of payments deficit financed temporarily by borrowing annually to maintain our foreign currency reserves;
an uncompetitive growth in wages and incomes, and rates of inflation and interest which are well above the average European Community
The current budget deficit, if it were not corrected by increased taxation or by reduced expenditure, could rise to almost f3 billion or 13% of GNP by 1987

THE WAY FORWARD 1
The essential objectives of the Plan can be simply summarised:
- to halt and reverse the trend in unemployment so that, by the end of the Plan period, employment could be growing twice as fast as the labour force;

- by lowering inflation and interest rates and more moderate trends in incomes and taxation, to create a more cost-competitive economy which is the only basis on which we can expand output, increase employment and maintain existing jobs;
- to improve social equity in our society by reducing unemployment, making the taxation system more equitable, and ensuring that public services are provided in accordance with need;

- to create the kind of economy and society in which sufficient resources can be made available to protect the living standards of those who must rely on long-term social welfare benefits and in which fraud and abuse of the social welfare system are eliminated;

- in promoting the equity of taxation, to reduce over the period of the Plan, the burden of PAYE taxation which is excessively decreasing take-home pay, penalising enterprise and increasing inflation;
- to reduce Exchequer borrowing progressively to levels compatible with the long-term ability of the economy to borrow and repay;

- to effect this reduction essentially by eliminating the current budget deficit by 1986 through a combination of measures including eliminating wasteful and unjustifiable public expenditures, reducing the numbers employed in the public service and moderating the public pay bill, making working methods in the public services more efficient and charging those who can afford to pay for certain public services;

- to the extent that the over-riding requirement to reduce Exchequer borrowing allows, to increase public investment over the period of the Plan, and apply more rigorous investment criteria, so as to ensure the high investment which the development of a more productive and efficient economy requires;

- to create an economic environment conducive to private investment and to ensure that public aid to encourage private productive investment and innovation is more selective and linked to performance targets;
- to bring the balance of payments deficit under control by increased exports, more import substitution and abating the rate of increase in foreign debt service
These are the objectives of the Plan

They are the basic requirements to create a more competitive, lower-priced economy in which employment can progressively increase, the grim upward trend in unemployment be reversed and the realisation of a more equitable and expanding economy ensured
The objectives of the Plan are essentially economic, though certain basic social objectives are included
The full working out and development of social policy as such in the new economic context created by the Plan will be the next major task of national policy to be undertake
The succeeding chapters contain the details of the practical policies and measures proposed by the Government to give effect to the objectives of the Plan
CHAPTER III THE ECONOMIC FRAMEWORK INTRODUCTION 1
Our economic and social development over the period 1983 to 1987 requires a new firm economic and fiscal framework which is the essential purpose of the Plan
This framework must be one based on the capacity of the economy to pay its way at home and abroad
It must be the containing framework within which all economic and social decisions must stay during the period of the Plan
The framework proposed is explained in detail in this Chapter
INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENT 2

As a trading nation, with one of the highest ratios in the world between trade and total output, international developments in trade, prices, costs and exchange rates are fundamental to the management of our affairs
The trends within the European Community particularly influence our economic performance
It is difficult to forecast with certainty international economic trends
For the purposes of the Plan, a number of key assumptions have been made based on the assessments of international agencies
If these in time turn out to be pessimistic, the results as far as our economy is concerned will be more favourable than the Plan envisages either in total gains or in earlier gains

On the other hand, if the international assumptions turn out in time to be optimistic in any way, this could diminish or delay the results envisaged in the Plan or impose on us more austere domestic decisions than those already envisaged
Some key assumptions are necessary to form a Plan and the ones adopted are based on the best advice available
The following are the key international assumptions built into the economic framework of the Plan: - an increase in the volume of our export markets of just over 4% a year;
- average growth in unit wage costs in our trading partners of about 7.5 % a year; - an increase in import prices of 7.5% a year, including a fall in the relative price of oil;
- overall stability in the external value of the Irish Pound - industrial export prices to grow in line with those of our trading partners;
- agricultural export prices to grow in line with the level of inflation in the European Community as a whole
THE PUBLIC FINANCES 5

An essential part of the economic and fiscal framework of the Plan is restoration of balance between Exchequer receipts and current expenditure, the reduction of total Exchequer borrowing to manageable and economically justifiable levels and, to the extent that the borrowing constraint permits, the expansion of public capital expenditure to make the economy more productive and efficient
CURRENT BUDGET DEFICIT 6
The current budget deficit will be phased out by 1986 in accordance with the path set out in Table 1
This will progressively reduce the growth in the public debt and in debt service, the balance of payments deficit, the burden of taxation, and the rate of inflation and interest
This fundamental correction in our fiscal balance is essential for our credit standing and to permit greater investment in the capacity, efficiency and equity of our economy
Such a reduction in the current budget deficit cannot be achieved painlessly
Taxation is already extremely high at our level of output and income and priority in taxation must be given to greater equity

The measures to reduce the budget deficit must, therefore, fall on expenditure through, for example, reduced employment in the public service as a result of greater efficiency and economy, moderation in the growth of the public pay bill, cutting the non-pay budgets of the public service and transferring the cost of some services now paid for out of either taxation or borrowing to the users of those services

This general policy has already been given effect to in the public expenditure reductions set out in the Government statement of 30 July 1982, in the proposals put to the Public Services Committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions on the pay matters covered by that statement and in the Estimates for 1983 that will be presented to the Dail in the coming session
PUBLIC SERVICE PAY
The growth in public service pay will be curtailed in line with the restricted capacity of the Exchequer
Excluding carry-over effects from 1982, the Exchequer pay bill will have to be contained to an average growth rate of 5% a year to 1986 inclusive of general and special pay increases
If we exclude the cost of debt service, pay represents one half of current Exchequer expenditure
The Exchequer pay bill has increased by 24% in 1981 and would have increased by an estimated 20% in 1982 (before the proposals announced by the Government in its statement of 30 July, 1982)

WithoLt the measures taken in July 1982 and in determining the 1983 Estimates, and assuming a general increase approaching the 1982 level, it could have increased again by about 25% in 1983, including some £250 to £300 million for special increases alone
Such an increase would have been far beyond the capacity of the economy
The falling trend in inflation envisaged during the period of the Plan will facilitate the curtailment of the public pay bill
Within the limited funds available for increased pay, consideration will need to be given to ensuring that the greater proportionate benefits go to those most in need
The Government consider that National Pay Agreements which give across the board percentage increases followed by relativity awards are no longer tolerable in present circumstances

Special pay increases have been a substantial factor in increasing the public pay bill in recent years and their potential cost poses a particular threat to achieving and maintaining a better balance in the public finances not only during the period of the Plan but in the longer term
The Exchequer pay bill in 1982 contains almost £400 million extra due to special pay increases in the previous three years alone
The proposed level of pay increases in the public sector contained in the Plan could consist partly of general pay increases and partly of special pay increases within the overall limit specified
But a basic economic question is to what extent the process of special pay claims based on relativities can continue if the economy is to achieve its full potential
There appears to be no end to this process as each settlement triggers off another until the process starts all over again
In addition, there are special pay claims linked to productivity and technological change
If these have to be paid for in increased wages, what is the extent of the net benefit to the economy?

There is grave public disquiet also about the payment of special so-called "disturbance" sums for changing the location of employment nearly always to improved accommodation and sometimes by a very short distance
These issues are complex and involve the private sector as well as the public sector
Where special pay increases based on relativities have been terminated, there have been beneficial results for competitiveness and inflation

It is intended to explore with all interests the possibility of a Commission representative of Government, trade unions and employers to examine the entire question of special pay claims in the context of the long-term optimum development of our economy and employment
The Government to date have not filled about 2,000 vacancies in the civil service and non-commercial semi-state bodies
Similar restrictions are also in effect in the Defence Forces and in the health sector

By 1986, it is proposed to reduce the numbers employed in the public service by 4,000 by cutting back on low priority or ineffective programmes and through greater efficiency in the provision of services
NON-PAY EXPENDITURE

The measures initiated in the July 1982 non-pay expenditure cuts and in the 1983 Estimates will be continued to bring about a cumulative reduction of up to 5% in the volume of non-pay expenditure by 1986 as compared with 1982
To achieve this, it will be necessary to reduce the level of services by more than the equivalent of 5% of 1982 expenditure
This is because demographic or other trends would mean volume increases in expenditure on the assumption of no change in policies
The net reduction envisaged will be found either by restriction or cessation of programmes or by introducing new charges or increasing existing charges for public services
At least one quarter of the savings will be achieved by way of new or increased charges over the period to 1986 and the effect of these on prices has been estimated to average about 5% a year to 1986
Total transfer expenditure can grow by an annual average of only 8% in nominal terms over the period to 1986
The protection of the living standards of old age pensioners and other such recipients of long term social welfare benefits may well require restrictions on increases in other transfer expenditure
The amount available for subsidies can grow by an annual average of only 4% in nominal terms between 1982 and 1986
This will require a detailed examination of the social equity, incidence and effectiveness of the different subsidies currently being provided through public expenditure

While the necessary resources to deter and defeat crime and lawlessness will be maintained, a major improvement in effectiveness will be sought through the better employment of the large resources now being provided
Expansion of An Garda Siochana in 1983 is envisaged as an exception to the general reduction in numbers employed in the public service
The Government will shortly introduce legislation and implement other measures to give effect to certain changes in the Social Welfare system to deter abuse and to reduce unjustified cost
These changes are as follows:

- to remove the present disincentive to work, flat-rate unemployment benefit for short-time workers will be limited to ensure that it will be related to a five day working week and pay related benefit for those workers will be withheld;
- for disability benefit purposes, the overall benefit ceiling will be reduced from 100% to 80% of reckonable weekly earnings;
- pay related benefit for those entitled will be reduced from the current level of 40% to 30% for the first six months and to 20% for the remaining nine months;
- the Government will rectify the anomaly whereby employees by a combination of tax refunds and social welfare benefits can receive more than when they are wholetime at work;

- closer liaison between the Department of Social Welfare and the National Manpower Service including the location of placement officers at the larger Social Welfare Employment Exchanges and the availability of placement officers as required in the smaller local offices

For this purpose, amalgamation of administrative responsibility for the placement and benefit payments functions is being examined so that priority in placement is given to those on the Live Register;
- registration with the National Manpower Service of all those under 25 years on the Live Register

The very considerable expenditure now incurred by the local authorities and the Health Boards and the greatly increased numbers of professional and administrative staff employed by them warrant a rigorous examination of their structures and special measures to ensure the greatest possible efficiency and economy in the provision of services and to eliminate waste, duplication or overlapping

The Government, therefore, intend to establish, without delay, a special investigation team to go into the local authorities and the Health Boards to investigate their administration and finances with a view to ensuring the most efficient use of existing resources and providing full value for money to both the ratepayer and taxpayer
PUBLIC CAPITAL EXPENDITURE

The progressive reduction in the budget deficit amounting to the withdrawal from expenditure of about £900m by 1986 would have an excessive deflationary effect on economic activity and especially on employment, if not modified by capital expenditure proposals

The Government believe that over the period of the Plan, public investment policies must be continued and expanded to increase our productive capacity to generate employment, improve our economic infrastructure and enlarge our social capital to meet the needs of our growing population
Public capital programme expenditure by the Exchequer, therefore, will be increased substantially over the period of the Plan by an amount equal to 3% on average for the years 1983 to 1987
The Exchequer borrowing for capital purposes and the volume changes in public capital expenditure under the Plan are contained in Table 2
Public capital programme expenditure must be planned with careful regard to the strict limitation imposed by the capacity of the Exchequer to borrow

A further constraint on the amount of Exchequer funds which can be made available for new capital investment in the early years of the period of the Plan is the substantial amount which must be made available for the financial restructuring of semi-state bodies

As the current budget deficit falls, the volume of the public capital expenditure can grow provided the Exchequer borrowing requirement is kept witin sustainable limits given the already high level of national debt
The current budget deficit for 1983 will still be considerable in spite of the reductions being made in current expenditure

For that reason, the Plan and the 1983 Estimates must reduce the public capital programme in 1983 by 3% in real terms so as to reduce overall Exchequer borrowing, as compared with 1982, to a level which signals our firm determination to bring it down over the period of the Plan to a level sustainable over the long-term
There is no option any longer to increase overall Exchequer borrowing, it must be steadily and firmly reduced
The best way to do this in the interests of the economy and employment is to reduce borrowing for current expenditure so as to leave scope for investment expenditure
Falling interest rates will concurrently help to stimulate greater investment by the private sector

Full Employment and The Economy
The Workers' Party stands alone in this election in offering a comprehensive and positive alternative to the identical hairshirt economic plans offered by the other parties.

Our plan "An End to the Crisis" published before the election was called, is based on the central principle that the massive economic challenge facing country can only be solved by determined resolve on the part of the government to raise national production in industry, agriculture, and the new technology sectors by means of a production plan.
The spending plans produced by the other parties are born of the economics of despair, and are based on the indefensible proposal that we can deflate ourselves out of the recession.
No-one denies that tough action is needed to get us out of the economic mess produced by the free enterprise policies of the conservative parties.

But we say that the tough action must be directed towards the producing branch of the economy- to the private industrial sector, to the farmers, and by a broadly eased mobilisation of the state agencies and commercial state companies to cut the balance of payments and budgetary deficits by increasing exports and eliminating wasteful imports that can be produced just as cheaply at home.

The weak kneed and callous approach of taking tough measures only against the unemployed, the elderly, sick and the homeless would not be necessary if emphasis was on raising, national income rather then cutting spending.
The proposal of full employment by the end of the decade in our EconomicPlan "An End to the Crisis" is not "pie in the sky" as some have asserted.
Full employment is the demand of our society.
It is a massive challenge.
But if the will were there on the part of the Government it could be achieved.
We repeat our assertion that it is the duty of every political party that seeks to serve the people to formulate a realisable and realistic programme to creat full employment.
It is not enouch to talk, as the other parties do, of "creaing more jobs", of "reducing unemployment", of "stabilising unemployment".
The aim of full employment must not be shirked.
Our first economic policy priority is thus the creation of full employment.
This means the creation of an additional 300,000 jobs at the minimum between now and 1991.

Our secondary priority is the maintenance of living standards, wages and incomes, and to provide for these maintained living standards for the annual increase in our population of 37,000 that will occur every year through the rest of this decade, To meet those needs, national income must rise by an annual average of 5% for the rest of this decade.
As it happens this also is the target set in the Fianna Fail plan "The Way Forward" for the years up to 1987.

If the Government had faith in their own proposal for a 5% growth rate it would be entirely possible to meet its aim of eliminating the budget deficit without leaving recourse to the harsh cutbacks proposed in the public expenditure chapters of the "Way Forward".
This central inconsistency in the "Way Forward" reveals a lack of faith on the part of the government in its own proposals on agriculture, industry, services and exports.
The Workers' Part shares this lack of faith because the "Way Forward" places all the onus for creating this growth on the historically inefficient and bloated private sector.
Implicitly Fianna Fail have also revealed this lack of faith in the private sector by proposing unnecessary real and cruel cutbacks in the public service.
As deputy Joe Sherlock said in the debate on the confidence motion in the Dail, the second part of the "Way Forward" was only the dressing to sell the first expenditure cutback, part.

In voting no confidence in the government it was entirely appropriate for The Workers' Party to express its lack of faith in a government that demonstrably had no faith in its own proposals to "solve" the economic crisis.
The production plan put forward in "An End to the Crisis" sets forh a "sticks and carrot" approach to prod the economy into increasing its output by 5% a year.

As part of our "stick" approach, we propose to trim back on the £2,500 million spent - annually by the state on the private sector so that the most economically productive sections of industry get the use of these public resources - a central element in the approach recommended in the Telesis report.

As part of a carrot approach for the private productive sector, we propose a taxation strategy which would provide an incentive to companies to increase their production and exports in line with sectoral planning targets by means of a flexible adjustment of corporation tax levels through depreciation allowances.

The direct approach of establishing new state companies in the producing sector, such as Technology Ireland Ltd., An Bord Taluntais, and the new State Timber Board, and the capitalisation oil existing semi-state companies such as the E.S.B., Aer Lingus and Bord Na Mona to enter new areas of the economy will,however, be the main central plank in the production plan.

The financing of this development plan would largely come in the 4 year "recovery phase" of our 9 year strategy in the form of foreign borrowing through the European Investment Bank and in the open market.

At present the pitiful youth programmes now in existance or coming on stream are simply geared to keeping young people out of the official unemployment figures.

HEALTH
Introduction:
The Workers' Party is committed to the establishmentof a National Health Service.
This service would be free at the point of use and without discrimination.
We are totally opposed to thepresent cutbacks.
A National Health Service can be introduced, while committing very little additional resources to the health services.
All that is required is a reallocation of expenditure and a restructuring of the present service.
In Irelend, the Pharmaceutical and Medical professions have been allowed to serve their own interests.
They have not been compelled to serve the public interest as is now the case in most European countries.
Over the pariod of this plan the current level of expenditure will be maintained, in real terms, up to the end of 1986.
From 1986 to 1991 additional resources will be allocated to preventive medicine and to Community Services.
The aged need a much better Home Help Service - this means more care for a substantial number of people.
CRITICISM OF CURRENT POLICY:
Ireland, at present spends an unusually high percentage of its gross National Product on the Health services.

The paradox is that public expenditure of £900 million, over 7% of the GNP, provides very limited health care coverage, whilst a smaller proportion of UK Gross National Product provides 100 per cent coverage.
The main reason is, of course, that we have an illness service rather than health service.
Over 50% of health expenditure goes on general hospitals.
A high percentage of this goes to "Voluntary Hospitals" controlled by the Church and a variety of other interests.
Within the community health services, over 60% of expenditure goes on drugs.
Also the medical profession wants medical care, sold as a commodity on the market.
In such a situation, there is more money in private medicine than in public medicine.
We should recall the statement of Jack Massey, Chairperson of Kentucky Fried Chicken, who resigned to become head of the Hospital Corporation of America.
"The growth potential in hospitals is unlimited, its even better than Kentucky Fried Chicken".
Over the period of this plan, the stranglehold of doctors drug companies and voluntary and private hospitals on our health services will be broken and a National Health Service, established.
Development Plan:
Our present population structure, the piecemeal development of our health services, the competing demands for increasea in funds, all point to the need for a major re-evaluation and major change.
Without a radical rethink Ireland's health services face a crisis.
Planning in the health services is crucial so that the services may be developed rationally and efficiently.
Our Development Plan for the Health Services will
- Provide a complete divorce of public private systems - no private practice in Public Hospitals and no public subsidy to private hospitals.
Voluntary hospitals, 90% of whose funds comes at the moment from the taxpayer will be brought under public control.
- Provide full eligibility for health services for all citizens as follows:
a. A free General Practitioner Service for the entire population will be phased in over the five year period i.e. 1983 to 1988
b. A free hospital service for the entire population will be phased in by 1988.
c. Free medical services for all children under the age of 16 will be introduced by the end of 1984.
d. A free dental care service for the entire population will be introduced by the end of the 1988.
As an immediate priority, free dental care will be extended in 1983 to cover pregnant and nursing mothers.
e. The cost of a national health service without changes in the method of payments of doctors and consultants, would be explosive.
GP's will be paid on a capitation basis rather than on a fee-per-consultation basis.
Consultant specialists will be paid a salary than on a patient per stay basis.

Part of the reallocation of resources to preventive medicine and community care will involve the introduction of a comprehensive family planning service under the Health Boards, proper child care facilities, a comprehensive health and safety at work programme and a national health education programme.

The right to basic shelter is a fundamenal right and, accordingly, access to housing must be, ensured on the basis of a persons housing need and not on their ability to pay.
A national housing plan forms, therefore an integral part of our economic and social plan.

- There are 15,000 families living in unfit or overcrowded conditions.

TAXATION

The tax policy of theWorkers' Party entails a shifting of the tax burden from the PAYE sector on the property speculators, the holders of wealth, farmers and the business sector who are not paying their fair share.
There is no scope whatever for a reduction of the overall levels of and, indeed, the overall tax yield must be increased.
It is more essential than ever that the tax system should re-formed so as to simplify it for the majority of taxpayers and to ensure that the tax burden is evenly shared.
The working peopla of Ireland will no longer tolerate the, present levels of tax evasion, tax avoidance, and the simple refusal to pay taxes by business sector, the speculators and the farmers.
The only scope for real increases in indirect taxes is by way of levying VAT on clothing, footwear and food.

TAX COMMISSION REPORT
Some minor elements in the Tax Commission Report are to be welcomed but the "broad thrust" of the Commission Report is totally unacceptable to The Workers' Party.

The demands of The Workers Party and of the Trade Union Movement are for a more equitable tax system where the tax burden is shifted from the PAYE sector on to the farmers, the self-employed, the business sector and the propertied classes.

The Tax Commission's first report (on direct taxation) if implemented, would mean a reduction in overall business taxation, a massive reduction of over £400 Million in the employers' PRSI bill and no resource or wealth taxes.
The progressive elements of the income tax system would be abandoned and replaced by a direct expenditure tax of dubious practicability.
The burden on the PAYE sector would be increased and not reduced under these proposals.
The Commission proposals fail miserably to redistribute the tax burden.

A progressive and developing urban industrial society requires an educated population, adaptable to change and properly equipped to cope with the demands of that society.
We need to re-orientate education to provide for a population optimistic about industrialisation and urbanisation and motivated by the tremendous opportunities presented by developing technology.
Our system of education must play a positive role in harnessing this technology to our social needs.

The current middle and upper class domination of secondary and third level education needs to be challenged and effective policies must be introduced to give an equitable share in educational opportunities to working class people.

The Workers' Party's plan for education will use a comprehensive approach, covering the period from pre-school and nursery through to adult education and also recognises that the future economic development needs skilled and trained people.

EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT PLAN
- Expansion of pre-school and nursery education facilities under the control of the Primary sector.
- Priority for expenditure will be given to Primary level and junior cycle of Secondary level.
- An increase of over 3000 teachers at primary level and 4500 at Secondary level.
- Special educational allowances to enable working class children be educated beyond the minimum school leaving age.
- Positive discrimination to enable working class children participate in third level education.
- Additional resources for remedial education and declaration of educational priority areas.
- An overall plan for higher education, covering the NIHE's, universities, Regional Tech. Colleges, Colleges of Tech. and Teacher Training Colleges.
- Paid Educational Leave for workers.
Giving workers paid time off from work to attend training at any level, for general, social and civic education and Trade Union Education.

CONTROL OF EDUCATION
Over the period of the Educational Development Plan, the contradiction of public funding and private control of all schools will be ended and a democratic system of management will be introduced.
Most schools are currently denominational in ownership and management while the taxpayer, through the exchequer provides the bulk of the money.
The reorientation of our educational system towards the need of a modern urban economy would prove impossible while leaving control in the hands of religious authorities.

Cities in our culture have been devalued and the conservative parties have looked down on the capital city as "dirty Dublin".
Crocodile tears from the parties responsible for the crisis in our cities will not solve the problems.
Neither will a hundred Gregory deals.
Speculators and get rich quick merchants have been given a free hand by Fianna Fail and Fine Gael.
Labour's solution, as articulated by Justin Keating, is to get people out of the cities and back to the land.

The decline of Dublin, Cork, Waterford and other urban areas has resulted from the lack of social and economic planning in favour of the generation of private profits.

The Workers' Party demands fundamental changes in the approach of Government to Dublin and the rest of urban Ireland.
Jobs, houses and a decent environment must be planned for and provided along with a network of social and community facilities and amenities.
The free paly of market forces have no role to play in the development of out towns and cities.
To develop an urban environment geared to the needs of people who live and work there.

Its task would be
a. to establish the numbers and types of jobs required
b. to identify where the jobs should be located
c. to ensure that these jobs are created by public or private enterprise

The bias against Dublin and the East Coast generally in the IDA's incentive schemes must be removed immediately.

For The Workers' Party decentralisation means that every large working class area in all our cities must have a Community Services Centre.
This Community Services Centre would be linked into a central computer headquarters so that all information would be easily accessible.
The services available in these C.S.Cs. would include the following

b). Taxation
c). Manpower/AnCo. Information.
d). Car Tax and Insurance
e). Housing Department
f). ESB and Gas Office and Maintenance
g). Health Centre
h). Legal Aid Office.

At present working people have little or no say in the planning, administration or servicing of their Communities.

This is not enough.

- The establishment of a series of democratically elected Local District Councils throughout the region as a new tier of local government.

Proinsias de Rossa made some progress by persistent pressure on the Minister responsible for the oil industry, Albert Reynolds.

The health of children in urban areas, especially inner city communities, must be protected from the damage which lead causes.

An efficient transport system would ensure that workers, their families and the goods they produce or require can travel easily and cheaply.
For this to happen there must be an integrated transport plan.
The smooth and safe movement of traffic however, must not be at the cost of irreparable damage to living conditions, destruction of amenities, or the further depopulation of Dublin's city centre.
This means facilitating, developing, and extending public transport as the most efficient mover of people.
It means, also positively discriminating in favour of the old, the young, the discbled and the less-well-off sections of our community - in other words 80% of the population.
CIE's Electric Rapid Rail proposals would provide Dublin City and county with a sound basis for a fast, efficient public transport system suitable to a modern city.
It would have 47 stations with linking bus services, and over 200,000 employment plcces would be within a 10 minute walk of each station.

Many working class communities have to settle for vandelised car parks, tarmac patches and chip shop space invaders.

- the speculators, the bankers, the get-rich-quick builders and the tax-dodgers.

Urban planners must be compelled to take account of the needs of parents with small children through the provision of wider footpaths, ramps and additional pedestrian crossings and more rest rooms in public buildings.
THE LAW
A whole range of legal changes as well as radical changes in social attitudes are necessary to improve the status of women and end exploitation.
The Workers' Party is already committed to the introduction of comprehensive anti-discrimination which would make it illegal to engage in discriminatory practices against women in all areas of life.
This law would supersede existing legislation where this conflicts with women's rights.
A permanent commission on women would be established to oversee the implementation of this law.

The commission would have substantial powers of enforcement and its terms of reference would include the under-taking of an examination of the legal code to establish what further legislative change is in the interest of women.
The Workers' Party in Dail Eireann have already put down a bill to remove the constitutional prohibition on divorce.
This bill will be re-activated in the new Dail.
We will be also seeking greater legal protection for women in marriage through the strengthening of the family Home Protection Act.
The law relating to domestic violence needs stronger enforcement and rape within marriage must be recognised as a crime.
Most urgently great changes are required in the attitudes of those who handle such cases, for example the gardai and police doctors as well as those of the general public.
The training programmes of such personnel must be modified to promote a greater awareness of the needs and special problems of women.
It is our conviction that the building of a more just and caring society in this country requires the full and active participation of women as equal partners.
The Workers' Party is pledged to ensuring that participation.
We all have a great deal to gain from it.
NORTHERN IRELAND

The Fianna Fail and the Fine Gael Parties use the problems of Northern Ireland to divert public attention from the very real problem of crisis proportions of the area for which they have direct responsibility.

Our Party is organised in Northern Ireland and is engaged in working for the unity of the working classes there - so that class politics rather than sectarian politics can begin to solve the very serious problems of Northern Ireland.
We stand for democracy in Northern Ireland.
We are opposed to coercion in all its forms.
We are opposed to attempts by bankrupt politicians in Fianna Fail and Fine Gael to coerce the population of Northern Ireland into all island unity.
We say that their pretense to have a solution for the problems is untrue.

Our members are actively engaged in attempting to promote the unity of Catholics, Protestant and Dissenter through the political process for the common good of all.
This can only be achieved on the basis of class rather than sectarian politics.
In an atmosphere of mistrust ond suspicion this honest policy is not yet supported by all the working class in Northern Ireland - murder deepens the divisions between the communities.
In these difficult and deadly times we are much encouraged by the fact that our vote in Northern Ireland continues to grow.
We increased our vote very substantially.
A vote for The Workers' Party is, therefore, a vote for peace and understanding in Northern Ireland.
FOREIGN AFFAIRS
The danger of a nuclear armageddon is the greatest threat facing mankind today.
The Workers' Darty maintains that the efforts of Ireland's foreign policy representative abroad must be energetically directed towards achieving complete nuclear disarmament.
As a first step towards this end we urge the implementation of the Helsinki Accord on strategic arms limitation.
Ireland must be firmly seen to be a nuclear free zone.
Consistent with this aim, a primary purpose of Ireland's foreign policy must be the international relaxation of tensions between all power blocs and between all nations.
We embrace the United Nations Charter as a basic element in our foreign policy.
Consistent with this aim, Ireland's neutrality must be strengthened and reinforced, and with this end in view, it is our aim that Ireland should ultimately join the non-aligned group of nations.

Consistent with our support of United Nations Charter as the proper foundation of international relations we maintain that disputes between nations must be resolved through negotiation rather than through force.
We assert also the right of nations to self determination.
Thus we stand against all attempts by states to interfere either overtly or covertly with the sovereign rights of other states.
We thus stand for the right of the Polish people to solve their deep problems without outside interference or pressures from the Soviet Union or any other state.
We support the right of the Palestinian people to a state of their own, and likewise, we defend the right of the Israelis to a state of their own.
This position we believe, can be the basis of a lasting peace in the Middle East.
We reject attempts by the United States to interfere covertly in the affairs of Central and South America, and of South Africa to interfere outside its borders.

As socialists and democrats we defend the democratic rights of the working class, and thus we reject the suspension of the free trade union Solidarity by the Polish Government, and we reject military rule as a "solution".
We assert that Poland's problems can only be confronted through a deepening of socialism and democracy in that country.

Last Wednesday's budget proposals represented the completion of the first stage of the Government's action programme to deal with the threat to our national solvency.
I am not going to go back and describe how the present situation arose or who was responsible for it.
There is no point in raking over the past or reiterating the realistic analysis by Senator Whitaker a week ago to the US Chamber of Commerce.
Our need now is for national unity under this Government to face the future with greater confidence in our capacity to manage our own economy.
What this Budget is designed to achieve is the protection of our economic independence.
This means, essentially, the right to decide our own economic and social priorities and to determine our own policies to achieve those priorities.
The tough measures of July and January are part of the price we must pay for that independence.
That independence is of immense value to us.
I give only a few of our chosen priorities.
It is because this independence exists that we have been able to increase all social welfare payments by 25%.

This independence allows us to decide to make the income tax system fairer by introducing the Family Income Supplement which eases the burden on married people in the lowest income groups by as much as 25%.
Our independence has also enabled us to ease the burden of rates on farmers by halving the remaining rates payable and to provide the finance for a package of aid to help farmers bowed down by debt.

None of these measures of economic and social benefit helping hard-pressed sectors of our society* might have been permissible, or even within our power, if we had allowed our finances to get so out of control as to force us to seek outside guarantees for our solvency and credit worthiness
Such outside guarantees are not secured without paying a price and that price would be a certain loss in freedom to manage our own affairs.
This election, although unsought by us, presents the Irish people with an opportunity to endorse what are admittedly tough proposals, with a severe impact on many sections of the community.
This endorsement, of which I am confident, will show the world outside that we can manage our affairs and are prepared to do so.
Of course more still needs to be done.
But the back of the job is now broken.
The two budgets of this Government would have reduced sharply the prospective current deficit for 1982.
As a result of these actions it would amount to £715 million this year - a reduction by almost half of what it would otherwise have been.
The deficit in 1981 even after the 9% of GNP.
But for the action taken in July and proposed in the recent Budget, the deficit would have attained a figure of about 11^% of GNP this year our Budget cut it back from this threatened figure to 5.9%.
This represents firm and significant progress towards phasing the deficit out over 4 years.
The further stages in this process can, if expenditure growth is controlled be less dramatic and painfull although they will have to be taken with the same firmness and conviction in due course.

As regards borrowing in the Budget, last year's figure of 16.9% of GNP - which would have risen to about 20% this year if no action had been taken - was reduced to 13.8%, that is by almost one-third below what it would have been'. This is still too high/ but it makes considerable progress towards getting our excessive borrowing under control
We have had to take painful measures to cut expenditures.

These include cuts in the provision for local authorities to be met by additional revenue raised by these bodies and higher charges by hospitals to private and semi-private patients in public wards and reductions in the rate of subventions payable to.
Health Boards in the cases of persons who opt for treatment in private hospitals involving increases this year in VHI contributions as a result.
Moreover» action is being taken in the present year to secure reductions in the cost of drugs!
And the cost of food subsidies was halved - with compensation for the less-well-off.
In the pay proposals negotiated with the public sector unions we cut back the cost of special public pay claims under these proposals to £l6m this year.

Even allowing for carry-over of special claims from the period of the former National Understanding this will reduce the cost of special claims payable this year to less than half the average of recent years.
In addition, the public sector pay proposals negotiated will limit the year-on-year impact of the general increase to 8.5 % over what was already committed.
This is by any standards a moderate increase against the background of present inflation rates ~ notwithstanding suggestions to the contrary which have gained wide currency.

If in the private sector increases as close as these are to those recommended by the Committee on Costs and Competitiveness are negotiated/ (subject to any adjustments that may be appropriate to the different wage structures there), the outcome would represent a significant Step in relation to our competitiveness.,
All these measures have helped to cut or to hold down expenditure.

Issues of effective control of this expenditure and of increasing productivity in the public sector are now being tackled, but we took no financial credit in the budget for hoped-for improvements which have yet to be achieved.
What we have done is to demonstrate that the first serious attempt 'to curb the growth in public expenditure is at last under way.

At the same time, we have proposed painful tax increases, mitigated, however, for the less well-off in this Budget by introducing major elements of tax reform which protect those on lower income; and ensure that the burden is borne by those best able to pay.

The result is that after allowing fully for the impact of the Budget on the cost of living for low-paid workers, the Budget would increase the purchasing power of a person on unemployment assistance by 20% and that of a low paid worker by as much as 19%.
Such people will, therefore, be better off even in this difficult year.
No one can suggest that this Government has evaded the problem or shirked its responsibility r-.
Nor could anyone with a sense of- reality fairly say that we have over-reacted or over-corrected in the face of our deteriorating public and national finances.
In all we have done, we have been concerned to achieve equity, and to create confidence that the tax system is going to be much fairer as between different groups and their capacity to bear tax
This concern is clearly shown in our tax reform measures, which even in their modified form have/ as I have explained, significant redistributive effects.

We are, for example, remedying PAYE payers' grievances about being differentiated from other taxpayers by having to pay tax on the current year's income as we are providing that the other income tax payers will also have to do likewise and, thereby, in an inflationary period, pay more tax.

As we face into the uncertain future, let us remember that the country has come through worse times.
