THE REFORM OF THE DÁIL AND SEANAD
The Problem:
Because of out-of-date procedures the Oireachtas plays little effective part in either the making of laws or even the expert criticism of them.
It is the Government not the Oireachtas that exercises power.
National decision-making is in many instances the result of confidential bargaining by Government with representatives of major interest groups in the community.

Thus, in contrast to the democratic theory that decisions be taken in the open in a popularly elected parliamentary they are nowadays being taken in private in consultation with groups whose mandate is limited and not governed by law.
(3) The public does not get the full facts and simple issues are often made artificially complicated.
The Fine Gael Solution:
1. The status of all-Party committees should be raised, and they should play a far larger role in the legislative process.
2. On major Bills a special committee will be appointed to take evidence from members of the public and interest groups.

3. The present unsatisfactory procedure for the consideration of Government spending in the Dáil will be altered so that spending proposals for each year will be introduced and published in the September of the previous year.
4. The Capital Budget and borrowing plans for each year will be specifically debated in the Dáil in the same manner as Estimates.
5. Fine Gael proposes that written Questions to Ministers will be allowed while the Dáil is in recess.

6. A Joint Committee of the Oireachtas, with similar powers to the existing one on commercial bodies, will be established in relation to 57 State Sponsored Bodies which are currently classified as "non-commercial" bodies.
7. More Private Members' Bills will be afforded time for discussion.
It is proposed that any group of seven members be allowed to present a Bill and have it published.
Fine Gael will withdraw the power of the majority in the Dáil to vote down the order for the second stage of a Private Members' Bill.

8. In view of the enhanced powers of the Dáil its members will in future be required to enter in a special register a list of enterprises or activities in which they or their spouses have a financial interest.
9. The procedures for the presentation, format and debate of the Annual Reports presented to the Dáil will be tightened up considerably.
10. A code of practice of access to official information, to be applied to Government documents of the future will be drafted.
The enforcement of the code will be the responsibility of the Ombudsman.
11. Broadcasting of the proceedings of the Dáil will be introduced on an experimental basis, starting with the open sessions of All-Party Committees.
12. The procedures of the Seanad will be reviewed with a view to improving the joint operation of the Houses of the Oireachtas.

13. The panel system of election to the Seanad will be reviewed with a view both to introducing direct election by certain bodies and with a view to ensuring access to the Seanad for people who may not be qualified as candidates under the present system, e.g. housewives and young people.
ARTS, CULTURE AND LEISURE

A contributory factor in the neglect of art, culture and leisure is the division of responsibility among a large number of State Departments.
A concentrated and comprehensive plan is required to redress the neglect of these areas in the past.
The Fine Gael Solution:
A Department of Culture and Leisure will be established under the Taoiseach to be administered by a Minister of State.
2. The new Department will have transferred to it, from ten different Departments, responsibility for:

(f) Public records and archives.
(g) National Parks.
(h) The National Gallery and the National Museum.

NORTHERN IRELAND
The Problem:
The peaceful resolution of the problem of the relationship between North and South.
The Fine Gael Solution:

1. In government Fine Gael will pursue - as it has done in Opposition - the policy of establishing and maintaining relations with both sections of the community in Northern Ireland, which have been allowed to disintegrate under Fianna Fáil, as well as maintaining the momentum of the discussions and joint studies with the United Kingdom Government that have recently been initiated in accordance with 1979 Fine Gael proposals.

In line with its past policy Fine Gael will also continue to press British political leaders to give public expression to the private consensus that exists amongst most of them that the ultimate solution must involve a coming together of the two parts of Ireland.
This public expression would remove the illusions which at present bolster up intransigence amongst sections of the Loyalist population in the North.

Fine Gael will, however, be particularly concerned not to distort or exaggerate the significance of the Anglo-Irish discussions in a manner that could strengthen extremist forces in the North and increase tension there, creating additional risks in particular for the beleaguered Nationalist community.

2. Fine Gael (The United Ireland Party), is the only Party to have published a policy on Northern Ireland and the only Party to have made the objective case for the benefits that would accrue to Northern Ireland through political association with the Republic, for example in the form of a Confederation.
It is the only Party to have established and maintained contacts not only with the Nationalist community but also with sections of the Unionist community in Northern Ireland.

If a majority for a form of Irish unity is ever to emerge it can only be through a proportion of this section of the Northern Ireland community coming to understand and accept the benefits of political association with the Republic.

3. At the same time Fine Gael has maintained especially close and cordial relations with the SDLP and has been uniformly supportive of the efforts of this Party to maintain its role even in the face of a political vacuum in this area during the past five years.

Fine Gael has been recognised by leaders in both communities in the North as the Party that has shown the most consistent concern with the problems of Northern Ireland and has won the respect of people within both sections of the community there.
4. Fine Gael has always advocated peaceful unification of the country.
In 1969 it adopted and published its policy of Unity by Consent.
This policy has since been adopted by the other two main Parties.
Fine Gael has further developed this approach culminating in its 1979 Policy document "Ireland, Our Future Together".
5. Under no circumstances will Fine Gael seek to use these negotiations or other issues relating to Northern Ireland as a weapon to secure political support in the domestic area.
No Party pursuing such a course of political expediency deserves the support of the electorate.
6. Fine Gael advocates a pluralist society.

Such a society in the Republic can alone provide the kind of environment here that would eventually attract support from that minority of the Unionist population on the scale required to create the necessary majority in Northern Ireland for an agreed Ireland.
Fine Gael will remain true to the tradition of Tone and Davis and will seek to establish in the Republic a State founded on just principles common to the peoples of both parts of the island.

Our Objectives
NORTHERN IRELAND 7
Our first political priority is the achievement, by political means, of a united Ireland, in harmony and in peace.
We believe that we will not achieve the level of economic and social progress to which we aspire as long as the Northern Ireland question remains unresolved.
Recent events have dramatically proved that we are right in regarding Northern Ireland as the most urgent political problem and in seeking a solution to it as a matter of very great urgency.

Through the search for a political solution of the underlying problem through security measures and through efforts to effect a humanitarian solution of the hunger strikes of recent months the Government have sought to end violence, avoid deaths and injuries, ease tension and bring about a lasting peace based on justice for all.

We have made clear from the outset our belief that Northern Ireland has failed as a political entity and that attempts to bring about a settlement solely within a Northern Ireland context could not succeed.
The Taoiseach has asserted that it was essential to raise the problem to a new intergovernmental plane.
That objective has been achieved.

At the meeting with the British Prime Minister in Dublin last December there was agreement on the need to bring forward policies and proposals to achieve peace, reconciliation and stability and to improve relations.
Joint studies were commissioned and are proceeding on a number of key issues including possible new institutional structures, security matters and economic co-operation.

These studies represent the firs steps in a process which will help the two governments to see in a clearer light the possibility of a solution based on new political arrangements acceptable to all traditions.
The Government have made extensive and successful efforts to secure support internationally for this new and hopeful approach towards resolving the northern problem.
It enjoys the full support of the SDLP in Northern Ireland and has been welcomed by world leaders in Europe, the United States and elsewhere.
The continuing success of the Government's efforts to develop the economy is helping to make Irish unity a more attractive prospect, economically, for all the people of the country.
Particular emphasis has been given to cross-border economic co-operation with significant results.
In relation to the hunger strikes, the Government have done everything they could that was likely to be effective in resolving the situation and preventing loss of life inside or outside the prison.

They have urged their humanitarian concern on the British Government and urged on all concerned the view that every effort should be made to resolve the situation through a flexible application of the prison rules.
The Future
A Fianna Fáil Government, conscious of the urgency of a just and lasting peace will press forward the political process now in train towards that end.
A Fianna Fáil Government will promote and uphold the rights of all minorities and safeguard and guarantee the interests of all the different traditions in Ireland.
A Fianna Fáil Government will continue its efforts to bring about a humanitarian resolution of the situation at Long Kesh and to avoid further loss of life.

A Fianna Fáil Government will act firmly and resolutely to defeat those who avail of the instability of Northern Ireland to seek by violent means to overthrow democratic institutions and the rule of law in this part of Ireland.
Our ambition is to make participation in a new Ireland the most attractive basis for political, economic, social and cultural for all the people of Ireland.
Economic Policy and Planning

The Government's economic policy has been to bring the economy safely through the recession while pursuing the fundamental long-term objective of expanding and developing the economy so as to provide better living standards for all.
We believe that the present development level of the economy can be greatly raised by sound economic policies and by coherent economic planning.
The need to continue to develop our economy is particularly urgent because of the unprecedented increase in our population and, therefore, in the number needing jobs.
The Government's economic policy has, therefore, been based on a comprehensive and coherent series of objectives:
-To increase the rate of economic growth;
-To make the necessary investments to achieve faster economic growth;
-To expand and improve our productive capacity in industry and agriculture;
-To modernise and make more efficient the economic infrastructure on which our economy depends;
-To provide sufficient employment to absorb our growing labour force;
-To increase the rate of regional development so as to mobilise all national resources for economic and social progress;
-To provide throughout the country the technological and skills required by modern industry and agriculture;
-To improve our scientific and technological resources generally so as to develop fully our natural resources;
-To maintain the credit and standing of our currency;
-To moderate the effects of world inflation on our economy;
-To maintain our balance of payments within sustainable limits;
-To reform the taxation system so that it is more equitable and gives more incentive to enterprise and effort;
-To provide a coherent planning framework for the implementation of economic policy;
-To ensure that the expansion of the economy and employment is maintained even in times of recession;
The Government's economic strategy has been successful in achieving these objectives despite the special difficulties caused by the recession.
The economy over the past four years has grown by over 15.7% and by an annual average of 3.7%.
This is the fastest rate of economic growth in the entire European Community.
Our economy will continue to grow this year - by about 2½% - while the economy of the European Community as a whole will decline.
These comparisons show that we have defended our economy better against the effects of the world recession than any of our Community partners.
We are, as a result, coming out of the recession with a greatly enlarged and expanded economic capacity as a result of the positive economic policies of the Government.
The exceptional rate of economic growth achieved has been due to the policy of the Government to raise substantially the rate of investment in our economy.
Over the past four years we have been investing about 30% of GNP, by far the highest investment rate we have ever made in the development of our economy.
It is the highest investment rate in the Western World except for Japan.
It increases productive capacity, enlarges and makes more efficient the economic infrastructure and provides essential social capital.
Without this high investment our economy would stagnate.
We would be unable to provide sufficient new jobs for our young people and our living standards would sharply decline.
We have brought about this high investment rate by enlarging the public capital programme and by providing the facilities and services to attract and encourage private investment.
A recent survey showed that Ireland is now regarded by overseas investors as the most attractive European location for industrial investment.
New opportunities have been provided to private sector funds to participate in the provision of economic and social infrastructure.
Under the Investment Plan for 1981, £1,700 million is being invested in the economy the highest investment ever made in the development of the economy in a single year.
This expansion of investment and of the economy is being financed through the mobilisation of domestic and international resources.
Without borrowing, an economy, at our stage of development, cannot be expanded.
In relation to our growing earning capacity and exceptional rate of economic growth the level of borrowing is not excessive.
Repayments on foreign borrowing represent less than 5% of our foreign earnings and less than 3% of our gross national product.
Because of our basic capacity for economic growth Ireland enjoys the highest credit rating with all international banking and financial institutions.

The development of a modern technologically-advanced industrial base is being achieved by increased provision of industrial grants, by better tax incentives, by providing an extensive network of advance factories and industrial estates and by increased aid to scientific research and development.
Last year industrial investment was the highest in our history.
This industrial investment is providing new jobs in record numbers in new industries based on advanced technology and science including electronics, computers, chemicals, health care and engineering.
The successful measures to promote manufacturing industry have also stimulated the growth of the services sector of the economy.
The development of manufacturing and service industry has provided new jobs in unprecedented numbers.
Between April 1977 and April 1980 employment has increased by 80,000.
Despite the recession 30,000 new jobs were provided in 1980 and, in this year, the number will rise to 40,000.
The record numbers of new jobs have helped to protect our level of employment against the effects of the recession.

Unemployment has risen in the last year mainly because new jobs have been offset by temporary job losses in older industries vulnerable in the restricted and more competitive market conditions created by the recession.
Unemployment has now begun to stabilise as new jobs in new industries come on stream and as the older industries begin to recover as we emerge from the recession.
Special measures have been taken to protect employment in the older industries.
These include grants and tax concessions to aid restructuring and re-equipment.
State investment in companies requiring financial assistance and the provision of low-interest loans.
The particularly vulnerable industries of clothing, textiles, footwear and leather have benefitted from special employment contributions arranged with other employers.
Within the European Monetary System the credit and standing of our currency has been maintained because of the underlying growth and strength of our economy's capacity.
The effects of world inflation on the family and on the economy have been reduced by progressive Social Welfare policies by consumer subsidies and by tax concessions.
Through the exceptional expansion of exports and through import substitution measures the balance of payments deficit has been kept within sustainable limits.
Our exports have increased in the last four years from £1,859 million to £4,134 million, a rate of increase above that of the OECD and EEC averages.
Special measures have been taken to manufacture in Ireland the components and products required by new industries.
All oil importing countries are currently suffering high balance of payments deficits.
Our deficit last year was roughly equivalent to our oil import bill.

The European Commission has emphasised that the adjustment of external deficits, due mainly to the increase costs of oil, can only take place gradually if economies are not to be plunged into deeper recession.
The level of interest rates has been kept among the lowest in the European Community.
Mortgage interest rates have been subsidised where necessary and special low-interest loans have been made available to industry and agriculture.
Measures have been taken to increase the productivity and prosperity of agriculture.
This has ensured rising living standards for our farmers and ended the steep decline in farming employment so characteristic of previous periods.
So that our growing labour force will possess the skills necessary in a more developed economy our scientific, technological, management, training and education facilities have been greatly expanded.
Even the most advanced scientific industry is now able to find the skilled manpower to enable it locate in Ireland.
Over half the jobs now being provided in new industry are in domestic firms based on our own developing technological and entrepreneurial resources.

The National Board for Science and Technology has been established to develop in coordination with the State research and development agencies a national programme for scientific and technological development.
This programme is particularly concerned with the development of our national resources.
The Government's economic policy is implemented in a framework of economic planning and development which matches our resources coherently with our needs and opportunities.
It is this coherent economic planning which has enabled us to provide record levels of new jobs and to achieve the highest economic growth rate in the Community over the past four years.
There are those who maintain that there is little this country can do to influence its economic destiny because of the small size of our economy and our dependence on foreign trade.
We do not share that view.
Our Investment Plan for 1981 provides the planning framework for the measures we are taking to maintain the momentum of the economy despite the world recession.
This plan, prepared after consultation with the social partners, represents a comprehensive series of inter-linked and carefully planned investments.

As a logical extension of the Investment Plan, we will shortly publish a longer-term comprehensive economic and social development plan which will provide the framework and focus for the growth and expansion of the economy in the coming years.

This plan will ensure that the achievements of 1981 are built on and, as the world recession ends, a firm foundation provided for further rapid overall growth and an acceleration to an even higher level in the number of new jobs created each year.
It will concentrate on a vigorous and programmed expansion of the productive base of the economy with particular emphasis on industry, agriculture and tourism.
It will continue the expansion of infrastructural development in line with the Investment Plan 1981.
Within the framework of the Plan, social investment will be greatly increased.
Industry and jobs
During the past four years the Government have devoted special attention to industrial expansion.
The result has been a new dynamism in the provision of many more jobs both in industry and in modern service activity needed to support rapid industrial development.
Since 1977 the major achievements speak for themselves.
Between 1977 and 1980 total employment has increased by a record 80,000 compared with the highest three year total of only 18,000 between 1961 and 1964.
A total of 40,000 new jobs will be provided this year.
These jobs will come, mainly, from technologically-advanced and science-based industries which give high earnings and the assurance of permanent employment.
In the electronics industry alone employment has doubled since 1977.
Between now and 1985 it will increase two-fold.
The Government's job creation record is soundly based on their commitment to increasing investment.
Past investment has led to a doubling of industrial production manufacturing in exports increasing two and a half times since 1977.
Because of Government policies on industrial grants, taxation and training industrial investment this year will reach an all time high record.
Because of Government action the future of industry in Ireland has been assured.
Ireland is now regarded as the most attractive European location for industrial investment.
We have the largest share of Japanese investment in Europe.
Most telling of all are the results of the recent survey which showed that three-quarters of foreign firms intend to increase even further their investment in Ireland.
The Government have shown their special concern for the development of a strong domestic Irish business sector.
Again, the record since 1977 speaks for itself.
Over 68% of total IDA job approvals now come from domestic sources.
Small industry approvals have been substantially increased and a new enterprise development programme has been funding young Irish businessmen with sound ideas for profitable new projects.
The new 10% rate of Corporation Tax from January 1st this year will give a particular incentive to further domestic investment.
The Government have also acted to ensure that the scientific, technological and training resources for rapid, industrial development are provided.
Under the coordination of the National Board of Science and Technology, our scientific and technological resources have been expanded by the State Research and Development Agencies.
Our industrial programmes have also been greatly expanded.
ANCO's funding has been increased from £15 million in 1977 to nearly £40 million in 1980.
Since 1977, ANCO training premiums of £13.4 million have been paid to 4,500 employers covering a total of over 27,000 additional employees.
For rapid industrial growth expanding market opportunities are essential.
Here again the Government have acted to ensure the continuing development of Irish firms.
The funding of Córas Tráchtála (CTT) has been substantially increased.
Grants schemes have been further improved and group promotion programmes have been stepped up to the highest level in the history of CTT.
The result can be seen in the growth of 22% a year in our exports.
To ensure the home market for Irish products, the Irish Goods Council has increased participation in the "Guaranteed Irish" scheme to cover 90% of firms producing consumer goods.
Import substitution efforts on all fronts have meant at over £100 million of new business has gone to Irish manufacturers in the last two years.

During the past four years the transition of the Irish economy into the new industrial age has been given a new momentum so as to expand export activities and to support the efforts of all those participating in industrial enterprise.

With some of the most modem techniques in Europe, with a solid base established for the new growth industries of chemicals, electronics, and pharmaceuticals, the results of this effort can now be clearly seen.

We now have an economy which provides challenging and worthwhile employment opportunities for our rapidly growing young population, an economy in which young Irishmen can experience the best international management practices and technological developments; an economy in which they are being encouraged to set up their own companies and to develop overseas markets for new and innovative products.
To ensure that that momentum is sustained the Government have taken a number of very important steps.
The new Sectoral Development Committee, representing Trade Unions, Employers and Government Agencies is exploring the full potential for growth of all sectors of industry.

So that the combined expertise of employers, trade unions and Government can develop new commercially profitable projects particularly in natural resources, the Government have established a National Enterprise Agency to utilise to the full our domestic research, scientific and technological resources.
A further scheme of employment aid by employers in the textile, clothing, footwear and leather industries has also been introduced.
Finally the Government are committed to the introduction of a new dynamic industrial development policy in the light of the recommendations of the National Economic and Social Council.
At the request of the Government the Council has undertaken an in-depth study of the requirements necessary to accelerate Irish industrial development in the 1980s.
Regional Development
Fianna Fáil believe that overall national economic progress can best be achieved by the comprehensive development of every region of the country.
By improving the economic infrastructure of the regions, by improving their efficiency and by increasing their productive capacity we will achieve greater total national development.
We have won special recognition from the European Community for our policy of accelerating regional development.
We have made special arrangements with the Community under which grants from the Regional Fund to our regional industrial and infrastructure programmes have been greatly increased.
Last year we obtained over £46 million and this year we will obtain over £50 million from the Regional Fund as compared with only £8 million in 1976.
We have also negotiated greatly increased allocation from the Community's Social Fund to accelerate our regional technological training programmes.
This year our allocations from the Social Fund will amount to over £70 million as compared with only £13 million in 1976.
By our regional development policies we are mobilising the talents of all communities, large and small, throughout the country for national progress and advancement.
Our regional policies enable the economy to be developed at lower overall cost than policies which concentrate development in a few favoured places.
Excessive concentration increases development costs, creates uneconomic and environmentally-damaging congestion and, by encouraging migration, adds to expenditure in new social capital.

Our policies, by retaining population and improving economic and social opportunities in the regions bring a new vitality to communities which heretofore have suffered population decline and economic and social deprivation.
The cultural and social life of the nation is enriched and enlivened by the resultant renewed diversity and vitality of local and regional cultures.
The success of the government's regional policy is clear.
Population is increasing now in all urban areas and in the great majority of rural areas.
New technologically advanced industry has been established in all regions.
The economic structure of all regions is being changed fundamentally to give the wider economic and social opportunities formerly available only in the larger centres.
Differences in income between regions have been significantly narrowed.
A comprehensive and coherent series of measures have been taken to ensure this economic and social transformation in every region.
Investment in the regions has been greatly increased.
The Investment Plan for 1981, which raises overall investment by one-third, is the largest regional investment programme in our history.
Telecommunications, roads and sanitary services which are the essential basis for increased regional economic activity and efficiency are being rapidly improved under the Investment Plan.
Investment in industrialisation of the regions last year was the highest ever in our history.
The Investment Plan for 1981 provides for even larger investment in regional industrialisation.
An industrial development plan is being implemented for each region based on advance construction of factories and provision of modern fully-equipped industrial estates.
Employment in the services sector in the regions is being rapidly expanded.
The Government have initiated a new programme to transfer major sections of the public service from Dublin to the regions.
This year construction will commence on Government Offices in twelve towns throughout the country to which Civil Service sections employing nearly 3,500 persons will be transferred.
These measures will give young people for the first time full opportunity to obtain Civil Service posts in their own regions.
This will add significantly to the economic and social diversity of life in the regions.
Our policy is to ensure that public administrative posts are distributed equitably throughout the country and that local involvement in public administration is increased.
Employment grants are being made which will encourage the development of private sector service industry in the regions.

Our regional development policies include the many measures to ensure a prosperous and progressive agriculture, to raise living standards in the regions and to provide rewarding and permanent employment in farming.
The technological skills of the regions are being improved to keep pace with the demands of modem industry and agriculture.

The Regional Technical Colleges and other higher institutes, the Universities, the ANCO industrial training centres and ACOT training and education services have been enlarged and expanded to enable the regions to raise their levels of technological and scientific skill.
The Public Service
Policy Objectives
The Government are committed to creating a modem, efficient and responsive public administration which really serves the public.

The size of the public service and its remuneration must be kept in proportion to the resources of the community, but in a country with expanding needs, a growing population and a demand for higher standards of service, an indiscriminate freeze on public service recruitment or pay would lead to a deterioration in the quality of the public service as well as being contrary to the Government's employment objective.
The Government are committed to a policy of decentralising Civil Service post so that this type of employment is available in centres throughout the country.
Progress achieved
-Appointments of young people to the Civil Service nearly doubled from 4,989 in 1977 to 9,629 in 1979.
-Preparations for the transfer of over 3,300 Civil Service posts to 12 provincial centres are well advanced;
-A programme of implementing a target of 3% for the employment of disabled persons in the public service is being carried out;
Computer services in the Department of the Public Service and other Government Departments have been introduced so as to provide major improvements in administrative efficiency;
-An Ombudsman is to be appointed who will act as an effective source of appeal for members of the public;
the Government have acted as a good employer in the public service.
The standard terms of the national pay agreements and understandings have been awarded to all public service staff, including Gardaí, teachers and nurses.
In addition, the Government have honoured all special pay increases awarded to public servants by arbitrators and other independent bodies.
Further measures being taken
-Administrative Officer posts open to graduates and serving Civil Servants will be created in all Government Departments;
-Further decentralisation of Government Offices will be undertaken, once the current phase is complete;
-Greater mobility within the Service and between the public and private sectors will be encouraged;
the Government will promote the spirit of commercial enterprise in semi-State bodies and encourage them To play a more active role in future development.
Industrial Relations and the Safety and Welfare of Employees.
The Government has pursued a policy of dialogue and partnership with employers and trade unions in order to secure industrial peace and progress.
The two National Understandings represent a major social advance by providing a broad and comprehensive framework in which agreement on economic and social progress can be reached.
A major improvement in the over-all industrial relations climate has been achieved.
A major reduction has taken place in the level of industrial disputes.
Days lost in 1980 were half the 1976 level and the figures for the first quarter of 1981 show the favourable trend continued into this year.
The Government supports, in the strongest possible terms, progressive labour policies embracing employers, trade unions, and all other consultative bodies.
Such policies are a prerequisite for the success of the economy, and their formation and implementation has been a major element of Government strategy for future development.

As part of Government policy the Taoiseach and the Minister for Labour have regular meetings with the Irish Congress of Trade Unions at which economic development, employment, labour relations and other issues are discussed in a constructive and friendly atmosphere.
An extra Division of the Labour Court was recently appointed, and as a result the time lags between the referral of cases and hearings and between hearings and recommendations has been cut.
The Court has also been able to deal with a greatly expanded work load.
This new development has been welcomed by employers and trade unions alike.
In 1980 the Government set up a Commission to enquire into the whole field of safety, health and welfare at work and to make recommendations on any new legislation required.
The National Manpower Service has been greatly expanded over the past four years.
In July 1977 there were 26 Manpower Offices throughout the country with a staff of 100.
Today there are offices in 39 cities and towns nationwide with total staff in the region of 300.
There are also 60 part-time offices in smaller towns and the Occupational Guidance Section has been doubled in the same period.
The future role of the Manpower Service will be further expanded and enhanced.
A Manpower Consultative Committee of Trade Unionists, Employers, Representatives of Government Departments and other interested parties was set up.
Under the chairmanship of the Minister for Labour the Committee identified a shortage of skilled key workers as being one of the most important factors impeding industrial expansion.
Other steps taken by the Government to improve industrial relations included:
The full implementation of worker participation by the Government in designated State enterprises, and the encouragement of worker participation throughout industry.

The preparation of a draft voluntary code of practice on the disclosure of company information for discussion designed to improve trade union and employee knowledge of company affairs and to facilitate collective bargaining.
The introduction of regulations protecting the right of employees on the transfer of a business in which they are employed to new ownership.
A Commission to enquire into industrial relations - publication of its report is imminent.
Substantially increased grants to the Irish Congress of Trade Unions Education, Training and Advisory Services.
It will continue to be the policy of Fianna Fáil to expand further activities that will be of assistance to employers and, trade unions alike.
There will be full consultation on matters of mutual interest, on legislation and measures to assist in the advancement of the economy as a whole.
Taxation
In regard to personal taxation the Government's objective is to ensure that each individual will pay a fair and reasonable amount of tax having regard to his or her circumstances and no more.
Our aim is to establish an equitable system of taxation which will provide the necessary revenue, and at the same time give an incentive to work, to investment and to savings.

As evidence of the Government's determination to achieve these objectives, a Commission on Taxation representative of all tax-paying interests, was set up in April 1980, to carry out a comprehensive review of the taxation system.
The Commission are expected to report before the end of 1981.
We have eliminated many inequitable features of the tax system, and are committed to continue this process.
The total cost of income tax relieves provided by the Government between 1978 and 1981 is about £500 million.
If these reliefs had not been introduced, income tax payers would now be paying about 50 per cent more tax.
The Income Tax Allowance for married couples was raised to double the single person's allowance in 1978.
In addition, 750,000 people have benefited from the special allowance of £600 introduced for PAYE taxpayers.
Full equality of treatment for married couples was achieved in 1980, so that a married couple are now taxed on the same basis as two single persons.
This has brought substantial savings for married taxpayers.
This year a married couple earning £4,000 or less pay no tax; the comparable figure in 1977 was £840.
For the first time total exemption was introduced in 1980 for all those on low incomes.
An additional special provision was also introduced for the elderly.
A number of important beneficial changes were made in Capital Gains Tax.
Most of the thresholds for Capital Acquisitions Tax were doubled, and the special agricultural relief for farmer beneficiaries was increased by 50 per cent.
Wealth tax was abolished.
The Government will not introduce penal forms of taxation which discourage investment and reduce the volume of funds needed for productive purposes.
We introduced, with effect from the beginning of this year, a special low rate of Corporation Tax of 10% for manufacturing industry which applies to profits whether earned on home or export markets.
This is a very valuable incentive which will stimulate the creation and expansion of greater investment and more jobs.
Rates on private houses are abolished in 1978, bringing a saving to the average householder of between £250 and £400 a year.
In the interests of tax payers generally strong measures are being taken to combat tax evasion.
Special enquiry units were set up during 1979 for this purpose and these succeeded in identifying 14,500 new cases up to the end of 1980.
So as to ensure that the tax burden is fairly shared by all, the staff of the Revenue Commissioners has been significantly increased.

Fianna Fáil accept that the burden of personal taxation paid by some sections, notably the PAYE sector, is too heavy and they intend to continue to reduce the impact of direct personal taxation as economic and financial circumstances improve.
Price Control and Consumer Protection
Fianna Fáil are deeply conscious of the basic importance to families of the prices charged for essential goods and services.

By the strict enforcement of price control and the provision of subsidies the Government have acted to protect the housewife and the family from the worst effects of the increase of prices caused mainly by the price of oil and world inflation.

To keep down domestic inflation the Government have pursued a pay policy which strikes a fair balance between protecting living standards and paying what firms and the public service can reasonably and competitively afford.
They have also taken major steps to safeguard the position of the consumer through new legislation.

Under the impact of the massive increase in oil prices, inflation rose to 18.2% in 1980 but is now being brought down again, and the annualised rate of inflation from May 1981 onwards will be in the order of 10-12%.
The Government's resolve to reduce the rate of inflation was given effect to by the recent introduction of special additional consumer subsidies.
The Government is by this means seeking to accelerate the downward trend in inflation.
They will continue to act to ensure this trend continues and by taxation policy by intensified import substitution, and by energy conservation to reduce the impact of imported inflation.
The National Prices Commission has had a significant impact moderating the rate of inflation.
Over the past 4 years they have dealt with over 1,700 applications and reduced the level applied for in 50% of cases.
In 1980 alone, the Commission saved the consumer from over £125 million of proposed price increases.

The Government have introduced a continued flow of important legislation which will safeguard the rights of consumers, especially the Consumer Information Act, the Occasional Trading Act and the Sale and Supply of Services Act.
Further legislation will be enacted as necessary to ensure that consumers' rights are fully protected.
Agriculture
Fianna Fáil believe that a prosperous and expanding agriculture is vital to national economic growth.
Our policy has been, and will continue to be, directed towards maximising farm output, increasing exports and expanding employment on the land and in related industries.
In this way we will improve the incomes and living standards of farmers and the viability of family farms.
Fianna Fáil are committed to full consultation and close co-operation with the farm organisations in working out agricultural policy and planning future development.
The Government have had an unprecedented level of consultation with the farm organisations in the past few years.
Our agricultural objectives are directed primarily to ensuring higher income and living standards for farmers through:
-Expanding the national livestock herd;
-Increasing the area under tillage;
-Modernising our agricultural production and marketing systems;
-Introducing a comprehensive new land policy;
-Developing our national food industry;
-Ensuring high quality home-produced foodstuffs for Irish consumers;
Fianna Fáil is fully committed to the Common Agricultural Policy of the EEC.
This Policy has been the basis of our greatly improved rural prosperity of recent years.
It will continue to be the aim of the Fianna Fáil Government to ensure that the basic principles of this Policy are strengthened and fully implemented.
The Government have already achieved major improvements in this Policy for the benefit of Irish farmers.
We successfully opposed suggested changes, such a super levy on milk, which would have damaged the CAP and seriously weakened its advantages for Ireland.
Fianna Fáil Achievements
EEC Farm Package
Despite the grave economic problems in Europe we negotiated major price improvements and a series of special measures for Ireland which no other Member State of the EEC has secured.
The increases in support prices this year average over 13%.
On top of this we secured a special £50m package covering livestock improvement, lime, silage and A.I.
subsidies and higher grants for beef cows.
The EEC have also undertaken to provide further help for Ireland by mid-July and work on this is already well advanced in Brussels.
A comprehensive market system for sheepmeat has been negotiated to give sheep producers assured price support and free access to the European market.
The Disadvantaged Areas have been extended and livestock headage grants have been substantially increased.
New Deal for Western Farmers
A new deal for Western farmers was also negotiated.
The major benefits secured are:
-Comprehensive drainage measures, including both farm and arterial drainage;
-Improvements in the basic services of water supply, electricity and roads;
-On-farm improvements aimed at raising the incomes of small Western farmers;
-Additional facilities for agricultural education and training;
-Higher grants for marketing and processing of farm products;
-Aid for calf-to-beef production;
-Commonage improvement;
Direct Government Aid

Having fully recognised the difficulties being encountered by farmers over the past two years the Government, in consultation with the farm organisations, took major steps to help farmers to overcome these difficulties and to improve their economic and social position.
A series of measures was introduced in the autumn of 1980 at a cost of £40m.
Including:
-A new winter fodder scheme to encourage silage making and the use of fertilisers;
-A new suckler scheme to expand the beef herd;
-An additional £23m. for the Farm Modernisation Scheme;
-The removal of the second moiety of 1980 rates on medium-sized farmers (small farmers were already receiving substantial relief on their rates bills);
-Special arrangements through the banks and the ACC to help farmers in financial difficulty;
-Increases of up to 100% in grants under the cattle and sheep headage schemes.
Further support for the farming industry was provided in the 1981 Budget:
-Full relief from rates for all farmers under £50 R.V. and halving of rates on farmers of £50-£70 R.V.;
-Abolition of resource tax;
-Suspension of levies for disease eradication;
-Adjustment of the tax code to encourage investment in livestock;
Recently further new measures to expand livestock numbers and increase output were announced:
-A grant of £60 for each additional calved heifer.

A beef farmer qualifying for the headage grants in the Disadvantaged Areas will now be able to get as much as £119 in respect of an additional calved heifer while a beef farmer elsewhere will be able to get £87 extra.
These compare with 1980 rates of £30 in the Disadvantaged Areas and £13 in other areas;
-A fertiliser subsidy aimed at encouraging grass production;
-Further aid for farmers who made silage for the first time in 1980.
Disease Eradication.
ACOT
The rationalisation of the agricultural advisory, training and educational services under a new authority - ACOT.
New Land Policy
Marketing
Credit
All these measures taken by the Government show our commitment to a thriving agricultural sector and the full development of the potential of the country's soil resources.
Since last autumn the total value of the new measures introduced by the Government and the improvements negotiated in Brussels amount to as much as £300m.

These improvements will generate a substantial increase in farm incomes this year and are a positive indication of Fianna Fáil's determination to promote agricultural development and help farmers to overcome the difficulties caused by the economic recession.
Fianna Fáil Plans for the Future
The strong commitment already shown by the Fianna Fáil Government to the agricultural sector will continue to underlie our policy in the coming years.
In particular, we will continue to work at home and in the EEC to bring about:
-The further improvement of farm incomes;
-The raising of the living standards of farm families;
-The expansion of farm output;
In addition Fianna Fáil in Government will:
-Introduce a scheme of interest rate subsidies to aid farmers especially those in financial difficulties;
-Implement the new land policy to ensure the viability of the family farm and the encouragement of younger progressive farmers;
-Continue to work in the EEC for the full development of the Common Agricultural Policy and the availability of adequate finance for it;
-Negotiate further special EEC help for Ireland;
-Continue to work in the EEC for the full development of the Common Agricultural Policy and the availability of adequate finance for it;
-Take steps to increase the processing of domestic farm produce;
-Continue to ensure, that Irish consumers are supplied with home-produced food of the highest quality at reasonable prices;
Fisheries
Policy Objectives

It is Fianna Fáil policy to achieve the modernisation of the Irish fishing fleet and a major expansion of the fish processing industry, within the framework of an EEC Common Fisheries Policy, and to provide a secure and prosperous living for Irish fishermen.
Progress Achieved
Landings of fish in Irish ports by Irish registered vessels have increased by 64% since 1977, and exports of fish have more than doubled.
The Hague Agreement target for doubling our catch was reached in 1980.
The number of boats has increased from 2,700 to 3,000 in the same period, and the number of full-time fishermen has risen from 2,600 to 3,500, an increase of 31%.
This year £17.2 million is being invested as part of the plan for the expansion of the fishing industry.
This expansion has been achieved at a time when the fishing effort in other member States is contracting.
EEC funds are being received for purchasing new boats, for Irish fish farming projects and for compensation for unsold fish.
Training facilities for fishermen have been expanded.
Major investment has taken place at the five chief fishery harbours at Killybegs, Castletownbere, Howth, Dunmore East and Rossaveal.
The Fishery Protection Service has been strengthened.
Since 1978, fines of up to £100,000 and forfeitures of catch and gear by foreign vessels can be imposed.
78 prosecutions have been brought under the law against skippers of foreign vessels.
Improved conservation measures designed to protect the interests of Irish fishermen have been introduced.
£4 million in State aid is being made available for the establishment of fish processing enterprises.

The Fisheries Act, 1980, setting up the Central Fisheries Board and seven Regional Fisheries Boards provided a new regime for the conservation, management, and development of valuable inland fisheries.
The Galway Fishery was acquired by the State in 1978, and the Cong Salmon Hatchery has recently been extended.
Negotiations are well advanced for the acquisition of Clarenbridge Oyster Beds for the nation.
Special measures were taken to transport slurry from the Lough Sheelin catchment area, so as to protect valuable trout fishery.
15 fish farms have been constructed since 1977 with technical advice and State aid for the cultivation of salmon and trout.
Further measures being taken

Fianna Fáil will continue to seek a reserved coastal zone exclusive to our fishermen and will insist on quotas in accordance with the spirit of the commitments made to Ireland by her EEC partners which will provide further opportunities for expansion.

The Government will also continue to press at EEC level for improved marketing arrangements, so as to provide safeguards against Third Country import and to ensure adequate incomes for Irish fishermen.
In the interim the introduction of a fish price subsidy scheme is being considered.

The Government will in conjunction with BIM consider arrangements to deal with arrears of repayments on fishing boat loans and will seek further Community aid for the restructuring of the fishing fleet and the development of fish farming.
Important improvement works are to be undertaken at smaller harbours, such as Greencastle, Burtonport, Schull and Portevlin.
New helicopters and vessels are being provided with EEC aid for fishery protection.
A new fisheries research vessel is being built at Verolme Dockyard and this is backed by a new Fisheries Research Centre at Abbotstown.

The Government will continue to consult closely with all Irish fishing interests so as to help achieve common aims of security and prosperity for fishermen and promote the development of the industry in the interests of the nation.
Forestry and Wildlife
Policy Objectives
Fianna Fáil is committed to expand forestry production and to provide for our own needs from home grown timber.
Progress Achieved.
An extra 36,500 acres were acquired in the three-year period 1978 to 1980 and about 76,000 acres have been planted since 1977.
There is now a total of 244 State forests embracing over 900,000 acres, employing nearly 4,000 people.
The State has taken a major share in the chipboard factory at Scarriff to provide an outlet for thinnings and to help sustain employment.
A new fibreboard plant in Clonmel will be operational in 1983 and will utilise all our available thinnings and pulpwood.
This will provide five hundred extra jobs and coupled with the present optimum expansion in the sawlog sector is proof of the success of Fianna Fáil planning.
The future of Irish forests is assured.
Development continued in the forest parks and an additional forty areas for public amenity and recreation were added to the existing 360 open forest areas to bring the total up to 400.
A Wildlife Advisory Service was set up in 1979 to protect flora and fauna, and a corps of 49 wildlife rangers has been appointed.
Sanctuaries and nature reserves are being expanded and negotiations have commenced for the purchase of Pollardstown Fen in Co. Kildare.
Further measures being taken
Incentives are being given to the development of forestry, particularly on marginal land in Western areas under the EEC Western Package.
Private investment in forestry will accelerate in the next decade and vast new areas will become productive.
The full potential of our forests is now being realised and utilised thanks to the systematic and continuing Fianna Fáil commitment to forestry.
Tourism
Policy Objectives
Because of the direct importance of the industry to the economy, especially to the balance of payments, and in the creation of employment.
Government policy gives a high priority to the tourist industry.
Tourism earned £563 million in 1980.
It provides one in every eleven jobs and has considerable potential for creating new jobs.
Progress Achieved
Since 1977 tourist numbers have increased by one-third (34%) and revenue by 73%.
The Government have introduced a number of important measures to help the development of tourism and, in March 1980, appointed a Minister of State with direct responsibility for the tourist industry:
-The investment, through Bord Fáilte, of £29 million in promoting tourism which resulted in cumulative foreign earnings of £l.2 billion, with a further £500 million earned in the Home Holiday Marked;
-The introduction of cross-Channel duty-free facilities;
-The introduction in 1980 of a new hotel bedroom grant scheme to meet estimated future needs;
-The introduction in 1981 of a self-catering scheme which will be of particular benefit to underdeveloped areas with tourism potential.
Initially, this will enable the provision of 2l6 self-catering units;
-The doubling in 1980 of the annual fund (increased to £200,000) for the development of farmhouse, town and country home holiday accommodation and the extension of the scheme to the country at large;
-The introduction in 1978 of a 100% capital allowance for hotel developments;

-In the period 1977-1980 tourism projects (other than accommodation) have been grant-assisted by £5.7 million, which has resulted in the introduction of many new tourism facilities, including cruising and waterway facilities, historic and cultural projec
-In addition, in 1980, tourism projects were grant-assisted by the Tripartite Committee on Employment by a further £900,000.
The Government have also acted to ensure that young people joining the tourist industry are well trained.
-By making a capital grant of £129,000 to CERT for the development of its training centre at Roebuck, Co. Dublin;
-By enabling CERT to introduce a re-organised Regional Training Service backed up by specialists in kitchen, dining-room, reception, housekeeping and management training;
-By increasing financial resources provided to CERT from £460,000 in 1977 to £935,000 in 1981 allowing CERT to increase the number of trainees from 3,310 in 1977 to almost 7,000 in 1981.
The Government have been successful in securing a total of £10.7 million under the European Regional Development Fund for projects in the Border areas:
-The North-West Tourism Cooperation Group was set up in 1979 to identify the tourism development and promotional needs of the combined areas of Donegal and Derry;
-The undertaking of an East Border regional study to determine the tourism potential of the area;
-The completion of the Erne Catchment Area Study;
-The introduction of the Derry-Dublin air link;
Further Measures
-The Government will continue to provide adequate funds to Bord Fáilte for the promotion of tourism to ensure the continued growth of the industry;

-The Government are committed to accelerating improvements to the infrastructure necessary for the development of tourism such as roads, telecommunications, water and sewerage systems and regional airports;
-The Government will also continue, through capital development grant schemes, to ensure the development of necessary tourism projects and amenities;
-The Government are carrying out a review of the Regional Tourism Organisations to decide on the structures best suited to their future needs in harnessing local support;
In addition, the Government will introduce measures to control indiscriminate development, such as the proliferation of illegal caravanning and camping sites in scenic areas.
Roads and Transport
Policy Objectives
Fianna Fáil regard a choice of modern and efficient transport facilities as essential for the functioning of the economy and for the freedom and mobility of the individual.
Fianna Fáil's main objectives in this area are:
-To achieve an efficient, free flowing and well maintained road system into, around and between major cities, ports and towns;
-To facilitate in every way possible the movement of freight;
-To discourage heavy lorries from using residential roads and to encourage bulk traffic and dangerous goods to go by rail;
-To encourage a higher standard of vehicle maintenance and safety;
-To tackle with determination and in a planned and integrated way the problems of urban traffic and congestion, giving a new emphasis to the role of public transport;
-To provide new rolling stock, both buses and trains, for suburban and inter-city services;
-To maintain a modern access transport service by sea and air;
-To develop a network of new small airports as an innovative addition to our transport infrastructure;
Progress Achieved
The Government have already embarked on major improvements in roads and transport as an essential part of its development programme.
Further substantial progress will be made over the next five years.
Almost £200 million has been allocated for investment this year as part of this programme.
The Transport Consultative Commission was set up in 1978 to advise the Government on the priorities in the transport area:
-The Road Development Plan for the 1980's.
-A milestone in road planning in Ireland and the first of its type since the foundation of the State - provides for major road improvements costing a total of £1,500 million.
Full support for the Plan is provided in the Government's 1981 Investment Plan.

The £87 million in road grants allocated to local authorities this year brings investment in our road network to new level and contrasts with total allocations of only £68 million in the Coalition's last three years;
Work is proceeding on ring roads, bridge and urban clearways in Dublin, Limerick, Cork, Galway, Athlone and other provincial towns;
-Private sector involvement in the provision of roads has been facilitated by the enactment of the local Government (Toll Roads) Act, 1979;
-The Road Transport Act of 1978 was a further step towards the liberalization of the road freight system;
-Ten Bi-Lateral Agreements have been concluded with major European countries;
-Following the Report of the Transport Consultative Commission on the traffic problems of Dublin, a Dublin Transportation Task Force was set up to initiate immediate action;
-Bus lanes have been successfully introduced in Dublin and will also be introduced in Cork to ease traffic flow and provide a faster service;
150 new buses will come into service in Dublin alone in 1981;
Services have greatly expanded over the last few years and will continue to improve;
-Modernisation of port facilities is taking place at Dublin, Cork and Foynes at a cost of £15 million this year.
A major development at Rosslare Harbour has been virtually completed;
A scheduled Dublin/Derry air service commenced recently with the aid of a Government subsidy;
-A new headquarters for the Meteorological Service was opened in 1980 with facilities for the direct reception of weather satellite pictures.
The Met. Service has extended its specialised facilities for farmers, fishermen, off-shore oil rigs and other relevant groups.
Further measures being undertaken
The Road Development Plan for the 1980's will be progressively implemented over the next few years and major improvements to trunk routes and urban roads will be undertaken:
- the Government are waiting a Report from the transport Consultative Commission on Further Road freight liberalisation.

The Government are actively pressing for increased participation by Irish road hauliers in the carriage of goods to and from Ireland by concluding bilateral agreements with other European countries and supporting increases in the EEC community quota of authorisations for multilateral and, road freight transport:
-Separate driving tests will be introduced for drivers of articulated lorries;
-Annual roadworthiness tests will be introduced from 1982 initially for all goods vehicles, buses and taxis;
-Electrification of the Howth/Bray railway, providing an 18 hour per day service with brand new rolling stock, will be completed by the beginning of 1983 at a cost of £65 million;
In addition, the services to link Tallaght and Clondalkin are being actively examined;
-A Dublin Transportation Authority, with planning and co-ordinating functions will be set up later this year with similar bodies in other large cities;
-The Government will implement on a phased and balanced basis the Cork Land Use and Transportation Study;
-124 new mainline rail carriages to come into service between 1983 and 1985 are to be built at Inchicore, creating 200 new jobs and using Irish materials to the greatest extent possible·
The existing passenger rail network, however, will be maintained as it forms an integral part of our overall transport system;
-Private bus operations will continue to have an important role to play in the provision of transport services;
The Government remain committed to Shannon as the sole transatlantic gateway and is extending the facilities at Cork and Dublin.
A major priority will be accorded to improving marine safety by:
-The provision of a Coastal VHF Network;

This Government have shown the will and courage to take the fundamental financial decisions to embark on this massive Transport Development Programme in order to provide better facilities and to create new opportunities for all our people.
Posts and Telecommunications
Policy Objectives

The Fianna Fáil Government have embarked on a radical and highly ambitious programme to modernise the telecommunications and postal services and to bring the standard of the telephone service in this country up to E.E.C. standards within five years.
These services play an essential part in making all our lives better and easier in the future.

No Government has ever given such a commitment to the rapid improvement of every aspect of Ireland's telephone and postal services, which will be of immense benefit to industry, tourism, agriculture, local communities and the individual and the family.
The Government aims to complete the telecommunications programme by 1984, giving Ireland one of the most modem and best systems in the world.
Progress Achieved

An accelerated telephone development programme costing £800 million to bring the standard of the telephone service in this country up to the level of other E.E.C. countries within five year and using the latest digital technology was embarked upon at the beginning of 1980.
To finance these major developments the Government have allocated a total of £343 million in 1980 and 1981.
Average capital expenditure in the years 1973-1976 was £36 million a year.

A new investment company, Irish Telecommunications Investments Limited, was established in April, 1981 to enable up to £100 million for the development of the telephone service to be financed by the private sector.
As a result of this programme, more than 2,000 highly skilled jobs will be created during 1981 with a spin-off in the service and construction industries of an additional 4,000 jobs.

In order that the future of these services will benefit from the most modern marketing and management techniques the Government decided to establish the separate semi-State boards - an Bord Telecom and an Bord Poist.
Sixty two thousand telephone connections were made in 1980 and 80,000 are planned for 1981.
Two thousand new telex and 500 new data lines will also be installed this year.
S.T.D. dialling was extended to over fifty centres in the last four years.

International dialling has been extended to all cities in the Republic and now covers more than 60% of subscribers and dialling of trunk calls to Belfast and major cities in Britain has been extended to all S.T.D. areas.
New trunk exchanges are being provided in 24 centres this year and next.
A special building and development programme of ultra-modern Post Offices is also under way.
Further measures being undertaken
-A 100,000 telephone connections are planned for 1982 and connection on demand will be available by 1984.
-The remaining 450 manual exchanges will be converted to automatic working by 1984.
-International dialling and dialling of calls to all areas in Northern Ireland and Britain will be extended to all subscribers by the end of 1984.
A new data service providing access for computer users in this country to European data banks was opened in 1980 (Euronet)
-A new earth station for satellite communication, linking up with the European Communications Satellite System, will be opened at Midleton in 1982.
But this is only the beginning of a brighter future for all our people who wish to avail of the most modern methods of Telecommunications and Postal services.
Our programme for the future, based as it is, on an already successful series of achievements will lead on to a better quality and to an acceleration in telephone installation.
Energy
Policy Objectives
Following the setting up of a separate Department of Energy at the beginning of 1980 significant progress has been made in formulating and implementing a national energy policy.
The major objectives of this policy are:
-To reduce dependence on imported oil and to lessen the disruption caused by supply interruptions and steep price rises;
-To increase energy investment so as to reduce significantly during the coming decade the share of oil in total energy consumption;
-To promote continuing extensive exploration for oil around our coast and to encourage the early development of a commercial oil field;

-In the event of a commercial oil find to make every effort to refine as large a portion as possible in Ireland and to create additional employment in oil handling, distribution and processing; also to achieve the maximum input into off-shore servicing;
-To increase security of energy supplies by strengthening the national capacity for stock holding and refining;
-To obtain a significant portion of our oil needs direct from the oil producers;
-To develop the use of natural gas for the maximum benefit of the economy;
-To build up the E.S.B. generating capacity on fuels not based on oil, such as coal and peat, and to reduce the share of oil in electricity production;
-To establish interconnections with other energy systems;
-To step up further peat production;
-To research actively and to develop alternative energy sources such as biomass and wind;
Progress Achieved
-A major programme of investment to achieve these objectives has already commenced, and this year, £290 million is to be spent on energy investment - a four fold increase since 1977.
-Oil imports has been reduced from 6.2 million tonnes in 1979 to 5.9 million tonnes in 1980;
-Since 1977, 25 exploration wells have been drilled, and significant oil flows have been registered from wells in the Porcupine Basin;
-£5.2 million was earned by the Irish off-shore servicing industry in 1980;
The INPC is now able to supply 16% of Ireland's needs;
-The natural gas field at Kinsale has been found to be one third larger than previously thought, and can now be exploited to supply a much larger proportion of our energy needs;
Natural gas will be supplied to towns on the selected route.
A development plan for the Dublin Gas Company has been drawn up and is being implemented.
Natural gas is already flowing to Cork homes.
Financial help is being given to the Limerick Gas Company to enable it to operate pending a decision on the supply of natural gas;
-Natural gas for the new Aghada station in County Cork will save the nation at least £150 million on its oil bill in 1981 and 1982;
-Construction work has begun on a 900 MW coal fired generating station at Moneypoint, County Clare.
It will start producing electricity in 1985.
Two new turf burning stations are also being built.
A major coal shipping harbour which could be utilised by other coal users is also being constructed at Moneypoint;
-Investment in generating capacity has already reduced the share of oil in electricity production from 75% in 1979 to 64% in 1980;
-An E.E.C. aided programme for the provision of new electricity supplies and the augmentation of existing supplies on farms in Western counties is being undertaken by the E.S.B.;
-Ireland is at present the world's second largest producer of peat after the Soviet Union, and it supplies fuel for 20% of our electricity production.

-Legislation to provide financial and technical assistance for private bog development has been enacted;

-In 1981 a further eight wells will be drilled.

-Negotiations with a Greek company to build a £300 million refinery on the West coast have reached an advanced stage.
