Environment
Policy Objectives
Fianna Fáil see the creation of an attractive and integrated living environment as a vital accompaniment of economic and social growth.
Our physical environment must be equipped to provide pleasant housing conditions and amenities accommodate and sustain industrial growth and cater for expanding services of all kinds.
These goals involve action on many fronts.
-An adequate stock of privately owned, rented and local authority accommodation must be provided to house our growing population;
-The supply of serviced land for the construction of new houses, factories, schools and hospitals must be accelerated by intensified water and sewerage programmes;
-Our fire services must be renewed and modernised to secure protection of life and property in an environment influenced increasingly by new industry and technology;
-A balanced policy for the environment must be developed to preserve and enhance our outstanding natural environment and allow for the requirements of industry and services;
-To ensure the orderly and forceful execution of these policies, the organisation of local government generally must be geared to the needs of the 1980's.
Progress Achieved
Housing
-More than 103,000 new houses have been built in less than 4 years of Fianna Fáil administration including the all time record of nearly 28,000 completions in 1980 alone.

The provision of housing for those unable to do so from their own resources is an essential element of our housing policy and some 24,600 local authority houses have been completed between 1977 and 1980;
-A grant of £1,000 to first time buyers of new houses was introduced in July 1977;
-A major Housing Package was announced by the Government in April 1981 including in particular.
-A new mortgage interest subsidy of £3,000 to first time buyers of new houses which is wholly additional to income tax relief on mortgages;
-An increase in local authority house purchase loans from £12,000 to £14,000.
Loan eligibility limits were increased from £5,500 to £7,000;
-A new loan facility of up to £18,000 for tenants and prospective tenants of local authority houses;
-An increase in the maximum grant for adapting accommodation for the physically and mentally handicapped to £4,000.
Since returning to Government in 1977 we have increased:
(a) Local authority loans form £4,500 to £14,000, and
(b) Income limits from £2,350 to £7,000
-The "claw-back system" for local authority tenant purchasers was abolished;

-The Government are committed to encourage rented houses through private sector re-development in major urban areas and have introduced a capital allowance to provide a special stimulus to the building of private rented accommodation;
-Total Government investment in housing will amount to over £240m in 1981 which is roughly two and a half times more than the 1977 level.
Water and Sewerage

A dramatic increase in the supply of serviced land for housing, factories, schools, hospitals and other development made necessary by our growing population has been brought about by the Government's intensive programme of investment in water and sewerage facilities.
-A record £67.3 million in capital provision has been made for public water and sewerage schemes in the present year nearly 3 times more than for 1977.
The Investment Plan, 1981 guarantees that investment in this area will continue to be a priority.
The overall provision for these has increased from just over £1m in 1976 to £7.4m in 1981.
- the Western Package of FEOGA Aid now agreed with the EEC has enabled maximum grants for Group schemes To be doubled for schemes in Western areas
-From £300 to £600 per house for domestic supplies and from £200 to £400 for farm supplies.
Higher grants are available in Gaeltacht areas (£750), Non Gaeltacht Islands (£840) and Gaeltacht Islands (£975).
Fire Services

-Fianna Fáil have maintained capital investment in fire services at 3 times the level of 1977 and have introduced a new subsidy on loan charges to encourage capital investment in new fire service facilities by local authorities.
Environment Policy
-The Government established an Environment Council in June 1978.

The Council has produced reports reviewing the current environmental position, the pressures and the issues involved and setting out proposals for an initial broad policy statement on the environment.
Further measures being undertaken
-We intend to increase the number of new houses built each year progressively to 30,000.
Maximum fines are being increased from £10 to £500.
A key feature of the new strategy will be the provision of a central depot to arrange for the export of toxic wastes unsuitable for disposal by other means.
Fianna Fáil's record in the environment area has been consistent and progressive.
Our present plans pave the way for conditions which will sustain industrial growth, preserve and promote amenities, and generally ensure an attractive living environment for all of our people.
Health, Welfare and the Family.
Fianna Fáil is committed to caring fully for the health and welfare of every member of the community young and old.
It is our aim to bring our health services to a level equal to the very best available elsewhere.
Fianna Fáil has always protected those in need in our society and we have consistently tackled the problems and hardships with which they are faced.
Our aim is to ensure that all persons especially the elderly, widows and the disabled share in increasing national prosperity and are able to live in comfort and dignity.
HEALTH
We have introduced many worthwhile developments in our health services over the last 4 years.
We expanded, developed and modernised the services in a way unprecedented in the history of the State.
We increased expenditure from £328 million in 1977 to £800 million this year.
We created 7,000 extra jobs - doctors, nurses, social workers and others - to improve the quality of health care and its availability to all the people.
Free Hospital Services
Fianna Fáil in 1979 extended free hospital services to everyone in the country.
This means that every sick person has access to a free hospital bed and out-patient clinics.
Furthermore, from June 1 this year, only those earning more than £8,500 a year have to pay consultants' fees.
Hospital Development Programme
The Government are vigorously pursuing a nationwide hospital development programme.
We increased capital expenditure from £11 million in 1976 to £47 million in 1981.
The hospital plan of the last Coalition would have resulted in the downgrading of a number of our County Hospitals and the withdrawal of specialist services from them.
We rejected this plan and made a firm commitment to preserve the role of the county hospital.
Our aim is to provide the most modern facilities throughout the country.
As part of this programme Cork Regional Hospital, the largest and most modern general hospital in the country, was opened two years ago.
More large new general hospitals at Beaumont in North Dublin, Tralee and Letterkenny are almost completed.
Others are going ahead at Cavan, Mullingar, Castlebar, Ardkeen, Sligo, Blanchardstown and Tallaght.

There will also be major extensions at Galway Regional Portlaoise, Wexford, Kilkenny, Tullamore, Nenagh, Limerick Regional and Our Lady of Lourdes, Drogheda and there will be major improvements at many other centres.
Services for the Mentally III
Fianna Fáil pioneered the development of modem psychiatric services and brought in legislation over the years to make more human the treatment and care of the mentally ill.
We will continue to improve and develop these services.

It is Fianna Fáil policy to develop community-based psychiatric services, to provide acute psychiatric beds in all our new general hospitals and to enhance existing long-stay accommodation for the mentally ill.
Services for the Handicapped
The Government have played a very active role in promoting the welfare of the handicapped and their full involvement and participation in the community.
This was achieved in co-operation with the many voluntary agencies in different fields of handicap throughout the country.
We are pledged to continue this co-operation and development.
In the last four years we provided an extra 580 residential and community places for the care of the mentally handicapped.
Our present programme will provide a further 1,200 residential places and 700 places in community-based facilities including hostels, day care units and sheltered workshops.
The high standard of this work, done in co-operation with the health boards and voluntary agencies, has attracted increased funds from the European Social Fund.
This year alone we will receive £12 million, an increase of £4 million over last year's allocation.
Teenage Drinking, Drugs and Tobacco
The Government's programme to educate the public, particularly our young, about the risks and dangers from alcohol and tobacco will be maintained.
Through the Departments of Health and Justice we are increasing our activities to deal effectively with the growing menace of narcotic drugs.
The development of our treatment and counselling services for drug abusers will continue.
We plan to extend the range of advice and information on drug and alcohol and their abuse to parents and those with special responsibility for teenagers and children.
WELFARE
The Fianna Fáil Government, not withstanding the international economic difficulties, raised long-term benefits by 25% in each of the last two budgets.
These increases amount to a 56% increase in little over a year.
Short-term benefits, like unemployment and disability benefit have also been increased substantially.
The Elderly
Better Benefits
When Fianna Fáil assumed office in July 1977 an old age pension couple received £24.40 per week.
Since April last that same couple receive £53.55.
We also gave pensioners a special bonus of a double week's payment last Christmas.
Under a Fianna Fáil Government pensioners and others can look forward to another bonus this Christmas.
Means tests have been progressively eased and this policy will be continued.
Farm Transfers
We have modified the method by which land transfers are treated for Non-Contributory Pension purpose.
This improvement has considerably reduced the waiting period for non-contributory pensions for farmers.
Free Fuel
Last October the Government introduced a National Fuel Scheme which was the first such scheme to apply to the whole country.
Over 115,000 pensioners and others are benefiting under the new scheme this year.
The value of the vouchers over the past year has been increased by 100% to £90 and will be further improved for the coming winter.
Free Travel
Fianna Fáil first introduced this scheme which has given the elderly the opportunity to keep in touch with their families and to travel widely throughout the country.
In the last two years we have improved the scheme by removing restrictions on travel over holiday periods.
Widows
Fianna Fáil have raised widows' pensions consistently.
In 1977 a widow with 3 children received £25.35 per week.
Under a Fianna Fáil Government she now receives £52.90 per week.
We will continue to improve the financial and other supports the widow needs to raise a family and maintain a home.
The Handicapped
Disabled Persons Maintenance Allowance

We increased the disabled persons maintenance allowance by 25% in each of the last two budgets and, for the first time ever, allowances are being introduced for dependants at the rates of £14.35 per week for an adult and £5.80 per week per child.
Mobility Allowance
We introduced a mobility allowance for severely handicapped people in September 1979.
We recently increased this allowance to £200 per annum.
Free Telephone Rentals
This year we extended the free telephone rental scheme to those receiving the Disabled Persons Maintenance Allowances
Blind Pensions
We also reduced the qualifying age for blind pensions from 21 to 18 years.
Domiciliary Care
This year we increased the allowance paid to parents who care for their handicapped children at home from £35 to £45 per month.
National Pension Plan
The Government are aware of the need for adequate pension cover for all worker and the self-employed.
The Government will shortly issue a White Paper setting out a new national pension plan for employees and the self-employed.
The Family
Fianna Fáil will continue to cherish the family as the basic unit of our society.
By providing education, housing, jobs, hospitals, community and welfare services we plan to positively support those who undertake the task of raising a family.
We have established a Working Party to make recommendations on family support systems and to indicate the steps needed to further improve the position of the family in our society.
Family Welfare Services

Since 1977 we have constantly developed community based health and welfare services reflecting the Government's policy of caring for people, particularly the elderly, the handicapped and children, in their own homes and communities rather than in institutions.
Our aim is to provide a fully comprehensive range of services and facilities, including health centres and day care centres in every community care area throughout the country.
Expenditure on community services has increased from £68 million in 1976 to about £153 million in this year.
Children's Allowances
We recognise the importance of children's allowances as form of direct support to mothers.
For this reason we aim to continue our policy of increasing these allowances.
We increased children's allowances by 30% in each of the last two budgets.
As a result the monthly children's allowance for a 3 child family has been raised by us from £14.50 to £24 since July 1980.
Working Mothers
We have introduced a radical new scheme of paid maternity leave for working women.
The new scheme is pay-related and a woman will be paid a weekly sum equal to her average net earnings for 14 weeks.
To protect women on low wages we have included a guaranteed minimum weekly payment of £47.75.
This new scheme is a major advance for women at work.
For the first time a Pregnant woman can now leave her job for 14 weeks with the comfort of knowing that her job is guaranteed.
Family Medical Care
Choice of Doctor - Medical Cards
Fianna Fáil have always given a high priority to the medical needs of the family in the community.
In 1971 we abolished the degrading dispensary system and replaced it with the choice-of-doctor scheme.
This scheme gave access for poor families to medical care by family doctors on the same basis as for the rest of the community but without charge.
It also includes for them the complete cost of drugs.
This scheme covers over a third of the population.
Drugs Refund
Fianna Fáil have introduced a number of other schemes to make drugs available where necessary either free or at moderate cost.
There is no charge for drugs for those with certain long-term illnesses.
For others, there is a refund of the cost of drugs for the family in excess of £8 in any month.
New Scheme - Drugs and Doctors Bills
Family doctors' bills can often be a hardship for those without medical cards, particularly for parents of young children and for large families.
The present drugs refund scheme does not cover doctors' fees.
As our next step in the development of family medical care, Fianna Fáil will bring in a Bill to provide for a refund of doctors' fees as well as drugs.

This scheme will work on the basis of a guarantee that no family will have to spend more than 5% of its monthly income to meet the combined cost of the family doctors' fees and of the drugs prescribed.
Dental and Ophthalmic Services
Dental and ophthalmic services have been much improved by the introduction last year of schemes allowing medical card holders to choose private dentists and opticians.

Fianna Fáil's next priority will be to widen these schemes, first to cover children in the 12 to 16 age-group who are not covered by the present free school dental and ophthalmic services, and, secondly provide for the wife working full-time in the home.
Fianna Fáil is not only committed to maintaining the living standards of those depending on social welfare payments, but also to improve them in a very real way.
We will continue to improve the position of those receiving social welfare benefits and to simplify the necessary procedures involved.
We will also continue to extend all our health care services so as to meet the increasing needs of our expanding community.
Status of Women
The Government are firmly committed to equal rights and opportunities for women.
We have introduced a number of major initiatives to improve significantly the position of women working outside the home and at home.
Most important were:

-The introduction of income splitting for income tax purposes which has meant a fundamental improvement in the financial position of married couples whether or not the wife is working outside the home;
-The system of paid maternity leave introduced from April of this year which secures the position of women who wish to return to paid work following the birth of their child;
-The review of the provision of child care services and facilities for working parents;
-The progressive improvements in Children's Allowance paid direct to the mother from 1977 to 1981.
Increases amounted to over 100% for the first two children and to 85% for the third and subsequent children.
The Government will consult the Council for the Status of Women on all draft legislation or discussion documents of special concern to women.
We have requested the Council to report to them as soon as possible on how the position of working women in the home can be further improved.
The Government will continue to allocate to women an increasing share of public appointments.
In co-operation with the Employment Equality Agency we will remove any remaining discrimination against women in employment.

To help achieve this aim AnCO Training schemes to prove positive opportunities for training women in new skills, whether they are starting work for the first time or returning after a number of years, have been greatly expanded.
Progress in Education
Fianna Fáil, the Party of Investment in Education has continued to develop its policy, of promoting equality of opportunity in education for all citizens.

Handicapped Children.

Youth and Recreation
Ireland has a rapidly rising population with half of our population under the age of twenty-five.

Government policies are designed to provide employment and work experience for our young people, to ensure that their ability and enthusiasm is used to its best advantage here at home, to provide them with the opportunities to achieve personal fulfilment not only at work but in recreation and sports activities at all levels and thus to enable them to play worthwhile role in the development of the country.

The Government have provided employment, training and work experience for school leavers through the special training and youth employment schemes available through AnCO - the Industrial Training Authority - and through the National Manpower Service.
For example 12,500 school leavers have participated in the Work Experience Programme and over 80% have got jobs as a result.
Almost half of the 27,600 who secured jobs through the Employment Incentive Scheme were young first time job seekers.
In 1980 the number of apprentices recruited reached a record total of 21,500.

Over 5,000 young people have taken part in projects aimed at improving local amenities carried out by youth and sport organisations with the help of Government grants from the scheme for Youth Employment.
The Government has provided this year £100,000 for a National Award Scheme to recognise exceptional achievement by our youth.
A national plan costing £8 m. was introduced in 1980 to provide community recreational facilities on a nationwide basis.
Over £5.6 m. has been allocated by the Government and the Tripartite Committee on Employment.
Following the implementation of the Government's policy on "Sport for All", COSPOIR, the National Sports Council was set up in February, 1978.
Direct youth service grants to voluntary organisations including Foroige (formerly Macra na Tuaithe) and the Scout Association of Ireland will be more than four times their 1977 level this year.

Funds have also been made available since 1978 through the Vocational Education Committees for sport and youth work and this year the total of almost £500,000 is five times the amount provided in 1978.

Young people will benefit from other Government expenditure, for example the mortgage subsidy for first-time owner occupiers, amounting to £3,000 over three years and not to be taxed, the increase of one third this year in capital expenditure for national and post-primary schools and most important the Government's Investment Plan totalling £1,700m for 1981, which will create the highest ever number of productive jobs at 40,000 and give employment this year to many young people and strengthen the foundations for a more rapid economic and social progress in the years ahead.
The Government commitment to youth is clearly illustrated in discussions recently held with the National Youth Council.
The Taoiseach undertook that the Council would be afforded consultative status on legislation and discussion documents affecting youth.
The Taoiseach agreed to meet the Council on a quarterly basis to discuss issues of mutual interest.
The Taoiseach also indicated the Government's commitment to greater participation by young people in Government bodies.

Fianna Fáil aims to provide a comprehensive broadcasting service for the nation, including a wide range of choice and a service for local communities that reflects the ideals, the heritage and the preoccupations of Irish people as well as providing entertainment and information service of a high quality.

-A second television channel, R.T.E. 2 was inaugurated in November, 1978 and second channel Radio, R.T.E. Radio 2 in 1979.

Culture and Community Life
An important and integral part of our overall policy of improving standard and the way of life of ordinary men and women is our policy for culture and recreation.
We fully understand that to an increasing extent people everywhere, particularly young people, seek more from life and work than simply material satisfaction.
To satisfy these needs better forms of physical recreation and intellectual and cultural amenities are required in our increasingly industrialised society.

We are investing heavily in the development of community centres and recreational facilities all over the country and the grants for youth services have been substantially increased to levels regarded as satisfactory by the youth organisations themselves.
The Office of Public Works and the Forestry and Wildlife Service are providing a growing number of wild-life sanctuaries, nature reserves, and national parks in every part of the country.
Local authorities are encouraged to acquire as public amenities, houses, gardens, and estates of special value and importance.
The Department of the Environment is developing a comprehensive policy for the protection and development of our natural environment.

Because we are deeply conscious of the fact that much of our natural, historical and architectural heritage is now being threatened by the spread of new technologies urban expansion and changes in farming methods we decided to set up a National Heritage Council which would take into its care historic monuments, national parks, heritage houses and gardens, the canals and museums.
It will ensure a nationwide approach to archaeological survey and excavation and under its auspices there will be a great new expansion of museum activities and facilities.
In this way we believe the preservation of the nation's heritage can be fully ensured.
We have also an active policy of fostering and encouraging creative artistic activity so that the full cultural artistic and intellectual potential of our people can be achieved.
The Arts Council has been provided with the necessary funds to promote a full range of cultural and artistic services.
Recently a new scheme, Aosdana which will enable the Irish writers and artists to pursue their vocations in reasonable security has been initiated.

The Government fully accepts its responsibility to enhance the everyday life of the individual and will continue its efforts to create a community in which physical recreation and intellect and cult al facilities will be readily and easily accessible to all.
Justice
Policy Objectives
The Government are determined to use every lawful means to protect the safety and security of the State.
We will continue to provide proper protection for all our people so that they may go about their daily lives in peace and safety and without intimidation.
We are also determined to stop wanton violence and damage to property.
We will firmly and impartially uphold the law of the land, constitutional democracy and the rights and liberties of the citizens.

The Government have taken positive action to reinforce the Gardaí who are succeeding in containing the growth of serious crime.
Extra resources have been made available to the Gardaí and a redeployment of strength carried out.

a temporary release scheme has been provided for offenders not representing a danger To the community.

Family Law Reform
Policy Objectives
The policy of Fianna Fáil is to reform and up-date Family Law in all areas where it is necessary, so that it may continue to promote and protect family life in modern conditions.
In this it is necessary to uphold the rights both of the family unit and of each individual member of it.
Fianna Fáil is particularly anxious to protect the rights of children including the rights of the unborn and to improve the legal position of women in modern society.
Fianna Fáil intends to give quicker and more convenient access to the Court so that a real protection of rights is afforded.
Progress Achieved
The discriminatory right to take an action for criminal conversation has been abolished in the Family Law Act, 1981.
Breach of promise actions were also abolished by the same legislation and engagements to marry are no longer enforceable by law.
The Government have simplified recourse to the Courts in Family Law matters.

Under the Courts Act, 1981 the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court has been extended to cover cases where the legal separation of married persons is sought, thus avoiding the enormously costly and difficult procedure which was previously necessary under the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1870
Access to the Lower Courts has also been substantially improved in the Courts Bill in cases of maintenance and barring orders under the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouse and Children) Act 1976.
The maximum maintenance order available in the District Court was increased from £50 to £100 a week for the spouse and from £15 to £30 per week for children.
A Bill to protect spouses and children from domestic violence by the introduction of preventative orders and by a more effective enforcement of barring orders has been introduced.
It enables a spouse to obtain a Protection Order, the breach of which will be a criminal offence.
Under a family Protection Order the children are automatically joined with the parent making the application.
The Family Law (Protection of Spouses and Children) Act, 1981 restricts a spouse from disposing or removing household belongings while an application for a Barring Order is being heard.

The existing law on rape has been reformed and the Government have recognised that rape victims should be afford the right to anonymity and protection that would enable them to report instances of rape in a private and sensitive manner.
Civil Legal Aid was introduced in December 1979, and there are now seven centres in operation at Lower Gardiner Street and Aston Quay, Dublin and in Limerick, Galway, Waterford, Cork and Sligo.
Legislation regularising the availability of family planning has been passed and will remain in force.
Emphasis will continue to be placed on promoting natural methods of family planning.
Further measures being taken

Recognising the serious and damaging implications that abuse of alcohol consumption can impose on family life, legislation will be introduced later this year to deal with the problems which are aggravated by the enormous increase in the number of exemptions, the increase in under-age drinking and the crease in violence in the home.
In addition the Law Reform Commission is studying a number of further key areas of Family Law.
The Law Reform Commission will shortly make its final recommendations on marriage nullity.
Having examined their conclusions the Government will have full consultations with all religious interests so as to ensure the introduction of acceptable and workable legislation.
The Government will also take any other measures that may help to prevent the breakdown of marriage and to promote reconciliation.
The Law Reform Commission is also examining the Law relating to illegitimacy including the succession and other rights of illegitimate children.
Having examined its report, the Government will take whatever steps may be necessary in this direction.

The Law relating to the domicile of married women (at present determined by the domicile of the husband) is being considered, in particular the idea that domicile should be replaced by habitual residence.

Consideration is being given to the form legislation might take to curb international child abduction in Ireland, to prevent the kidnapping of children out of the jurisdiction, and to secure the immediate return of children under 16 who are wrongfully removed from the country where they are habitually resident.
The Government are totally opposed to abortion, and an appropriate constitutional amendment to give effect to the position will be brought forward as soon as circumstances permit.
The Government will also continue to take the necessary steps to prevent abortion referral and seek to alleviate the causes which may lead women to seek abortions.

A substantial rise in the Unmarried Mother's allowance was contained in this year's Budget and Fianna Fáil will seek to ensure that adequate housing facilities are provided for single parent families.
A further Legal Aid Centre in Dublin at Ormond Quay will be opened later this year, and a countrywide service involving the opening of a large number of centres is planned.
The Government intend to improve courthouse facilities particularly those required for the parties in family law cases.
Defence
Policy Objective

The Defence Forces have a vital role to play in defending our sovereign independence, freedom and security, protecting our natural resources, and in making a contribution to international peace-keeping.
The Fianna Fáil Government will continue to see that they have the necessary personnel training and equipment to fulfil this role.
Progress Achieved
A major re-organisation of the Defence Forces was completed to fit the forces for their tasks within the defence arrangements and with a view to developing the reserves.
A programme of modernising defensive equipment was instituted and is being continued.
New artillery and armoured vehicles and helicopters have been provided.
The Defence Forces have been equipped and trained to provide support for Gardaí and other services in emergency situations when this is required.
The protection of the new 200 mile limit in particular has meant an unprecedented expansion in the fleet and manpower of the naval service and in air support.
A woman's service corps was established which is giving women the opportunity to join the Permanent Defence Force.
The first group of officers for the corps were commissioned recently.
Pay and allowances for the forces were reviewed on a continuing basis to ensure that remuneration is maintained at adequate and acceptable levels.
In the three year period 1978-1981 over £l4.6 million will have been spent in the provision of new accommodation including living quarters and the improvement of existing premises.
Out-dated living accommodation is being replaced and conditions of services generally improved.
New sports facilities have provided at a number of camps and at the naval base at Haulbowline.

Pensions and Special Allowances for Veterans of the War of Independence have substantially increased and concessions (free electricity, T.V. Licence travel, phone etc.) for these veterans were expanded and improved.

Specifically a new scheme of allowances was introduced for the widows of Special Allowance Holders to bring them into line with the widows of Military Service Pensioners who were already in receipt of an allowance.
These pensions and allowances are now exempt from Income Tax.
Further measures being taken
The Government will ensure that army personnel going abroad on UN peace-keeping missions are provided with the most modem equipment and facilities to enable them to discharge their role effectively.
Further modernisation of equipment will take place in keeping with the expanding tasks of the defence forces and with the country's changing defence and security needs.
Foreign Policy
Policy Objectives

The aim of our foreign Policy is to promote and protect the interest and ideals of the Irish people to uphold the sovereignty and independence of our State and to promote a more peaceful and stable world order.
Our election to the United Nations Security Council acknowledges our dedication and commitment to the work of the United Nations and to world peace and security.

Irish foreign policy is based on committed membership of the European Community, friendly relations particularly with our European partners and the United States, development of relationships with our nearest neighbour Britain (see under Northern Ireland), support for the aspirations of the Third World and improvement of East-West relations.
We will maintain our policy of military neutrality and will not become involved in military alliances.

We will continue to make our contribution to international peace and security through political co-operation with our partners in Europe, through our membership of the United Nations, our participation in its peace-keeping operations and our current membership of the U.N. Security Council.
We will continue to participate constructively in the European Communities.
We will seek to safeguard existing Community achievements and principles, especially the Common Agricultural Policy and the Regional and Social Funds.
We will try to ensure that economic convergence between the wealthy and the less well-off nations continues to be a central objective of the European Community.
We believe it is essential that more funds are made available to tackle the problems of the less well off regions and major Community problems such as unemployment and energy.

Towards this end the Government will continue to press for a substantial enlargement and improvement of the Social and Regional Funds so as to ensure that they can make a real and meaningful contribution to Ireland's future prosperity.

The Government will continue to seek an urgent and just solution to the Middle East problem and will co-operate with other nations towards the ending of apartheid and the accession to full independence of Namibia.

Effective arms control and disarmament measures are key aspects of Government foreign policy and respect for human rights throughout the world is a paramount objective which will permeate all policy attitudes.

Ireland will continue to show understanding in the problems of the Third World and to advocate a positive response by the industrialised countries of the Northern Hemisphere in what is called the North/South dialogue.
Achievements and Prospects
The Government are continuing to ensure that the country as a whole and every section of the community continue to derive the maximum benefit from E.E.C. Membership.
The Government have extended Diplomatic representation in the Middle East, in Africa and in Asia.
The Irish Foreign Service will be streamlined so as to provide a more effective voice of Ireland abroad, and to provide efficient back-up to promotion abroad of Irish trade, investment and tourism.

The diversification of our exports throughout the world, the stimulation of investment in Ireland and the encouragement of tourism are essential factors in the economic progress of the nation and our embassies abroad are a basic element in this drive.
Ireland's overseas development assistance programme has more than doubled from £6m. to £l6m. since 1977.
Ireland's bi-lateral programme is concentrated on African countries, Lesotho, Tanzania, Zambia, the Sudan.
Development offices have opened in Lesotho, Dar Es Salaam, Lusaka.
A Fianna Fáil Government will continue to expand the share of development aid as a percentage of GNP.

The Government have contributed towards many disaster relief programmes and have re-settled 229 Vietnamese refugees and will continue to work in close co-operation with international and voluntary agencies.
The Government have taken positive steps to unify Irish-American public opinion so as to mobilise their support for the Government's economic and political objectives.
A new Croup "The Friends of Ireland" has recently been established in the American Congress.
The Government have extended Irish cultural activities and co-operation abroad.
The Treasures of Ireland Exhibition has toured America and Europe.
Four new cultural agreements were concluded with Greece, Spain, the Netherlands, and Belgium in 1980, and further agreements with Germany and Italy will be concluded in the near future.
These aspects have a practical as well as cultural perspective and our trade, investment, and tourism organisations fit their plans into such activities.
Finally it is the basic function of Ireland's foreign policy to take a measured and balanced stance in international affairs and in this manner to take our place truly among the nations of the world.

ELECTION PROGRAMME 1981
Section One: INTRODUCTION
National Crisis
(1) In this election the electorate is of one mind.
The country is in a stats of crisis.
(2) The problems that really matter multiply and intensify.
But there is no national leadership to guide us through this crisis.
There is no sense of rational purpose.
Instead, the nation's mood is one of disillusionment, almost of despair.
The Path to the Future
(3) In this election the Labour Party presents its own independent policies as the only coherent answer to that crisis.

It believes that another four years of incompetence and indecision will but ruin the economy, destroying whatever social progress has been made and blighting the hopes of our people - above all, our young people.
(4) Labour offers this Election Programme as the basis of economic reconstruction and social renewal, as the only path to the future.
Old policies, no matter how well disguised, will not solve new problems.
We need a new way.
Economic Crisis
(5) Are things really that bad?
The honest and objective answer must be yes, and getting worse.
(6) Unemployment is at a peace-time record.
Inflation is the highest in the European Community.
The State's finances are in chaos and a cause for real alarm.
Agriculture is in its worst depression for decades.
The crucial tourist industry is in decline.
The gap between our imports and exports widens with each passing month.
The forced devaluation of the Irish pound is unavoidable unless present policies are changed.
Social Crisis
(7) Irish society too is in a deep crisis.
Crime and vandalism are on the increase.
Real poverty persists.
But many of the social services designed to eradicate it have been cut back.
The housing shortage worsens and is of crisis dimensions.
Land speculators make fortunes while young couples go homeless.
The inner cities decay and crumble.
The suburbs are starved of amenities.
Transport is a nightmare.
Roads remain inadequate and unrepaired.
Traffic congestion chokes our cities and towns, stifling economic and social life.
Reform Ignored
(8) Necessary reforms are ignored.
The causes and consequences of poverty remain untackled.
Existing programmes are either reduced or scrapped.
Education continues to support privilege while being unsuited to the new needs of the economy.
The legal system is archaic.
The law is in urgent need of reform in many areas which affect our children and family life.
(9) But nothing happens.
Except for the occasional public relations stunt.
The North
(10) And the problem of the North continues unsolved.
If anything, that crisis grows deeper.
The path towards reconciliation and peace is blocked.
Violence has taken on a renewed and dangerous vigour.
(11) Nowhere in our national life is the gap between rhetoric and reality more ominous and menacing.
Background to the Election
(12) This is the background to the 1981 General Election.
Tragically all this is happening at a unique moment in our history.
At what should be a time of great hope and inspiration.
(13) Our population decline has at last been reversed.
Emigration has ended since the mid seventies.
We have the fastest growing population in Europa - and the youngest.
(14) Labour sees this not as a problem but as a great opportunity.
The opportunity to build a new Ireland, freer, more equitable, more committed and a better place in which to live.
(15) But tragically at that very same moment the collapse of current policies has caused a crisis in existing social values.
Our young feel alienated from a society which cannot give them jobs, proper education, adequate social facilities, enough homes, and above all, a real purpose in life.
(16) This is the central issue which must be addressed in this election.
The Will to Create a New Future
(17) Election Programmes can be fantasies of the passing moment.
Clever but cynical, creations of an advertising agency with one single aim
to put a party in power no matter what the cost.
(18) Or they can be serious and committed, based on long held principles and directed towards the present and immediate future.
(19) Such is Labour's course.
Labour's socialist principles are spelled out in detail in its Party Programme adopted in 1980 which deals with the long-term problems of the eighties.
This Election Programme, focussing on 1981 and the years immediately ahead, is firmly based on the principles and the long-term policies of that Party Programme.
(20) There are no empty promises here.
There is no flight from reality.
(21) Labour accepts the fact that the nation is in crisis.
Labour recognises we need policies on the issues that really matter.
Labour is committed to matching policies with problems.
This Election Programme sets out to do that.
(22) Only Labour has the will to do it.
Labour's Role in the Next Dail
(23) The problems of today and the immediate future must be matched by realistic policies.
But those policies must contain more than realism;
they must also have a moral purpose.

That purpose must be to rid this country of poverty and unemployment, to end injustice and discrimination and to instil a new meaning into the national life so that individualism and materialism are replaced by humanity and common concern.
(24) As the only major political party with a coherent philosophy based on the inherent dignity of every individual, Labour has a key role to play in formulating the policies of the next Dail.
The aim of the Labour Party is to ensure that it exerts a decisive influence on all legislation.
(25) The aim is to match problems and realistic policies;
but to do so with clear, consistent moral goals constantly in view.
(26) That is the socialist way and this is the Socialist Alternative.
Section Two: GENERAL STRATEGY
(27) There are so many social and economic problems to be solved in the next few years that there must be great clarity as to the objectives, priorities and solutions.
All the problems cannot be solved at once.
While many desirable improvements could be introduced without any increased cost to the tax payer there are others which depend entirely on our economic circumstances.
(28) In reality, Labour begins by recognising that a serious and protracted economic crisis exists.
The Party goes further.
Unless strong action is taken immediately the economy will slide into total chaos, sooner rather than later.
(29) Those whom Labour seeks to represent will suffer most in that situation.
Unemployment, inflation, reductions in essential services, cut backs in social welfare;
all these are in prospect for even greater numbers unless the present crisis is dealt with.
That is why Labour has the will to act, and to act decisively.
(30) Labour's strategy is based on this central principle.
Action must begin with the economy.
Any plan for recovery must start here.
(31) Accordingly, this Election Programme commences with a series of proposals on the economy.
They are designed to regenerate an economy in serious and deepening decline.
They are also designed to commence the necessary process of its restructuring along socialist lines.
(32) The proposals are based on an unflinching acceptance of facts.

They are not founded on wishful beliefs in favourable external factors solving our current problems without any effort on our part - or on the gambler's desperate hope that oil will suddenly pay for everything.
Neither are they predicated on dishonest allegations that buoyancy in the economy will provide money which is presently non-existent.

(33) Above all, these proposals are based on the moral responsibility of this society to provide an acceptable minimum standard of living for all and to provide employment for every person eligible to work.
(34) In particular, the responsibility to provide work for all our young people dominates this Programme.
Section Three: THE ECONOMY
The Crisis Outlined
(35) The economy is in crisis.
The extent of that crisis is visible everywhere.
(36) Unemployment has climbed to 126,000, according to official statistics.
The real level is in excess of 150,000.
The numbers out of work are rising remorselessly and the official statistics will reach 140,000 by the end of the year.
(37) Unemployment among young people has reached catastrophic proportions.
Thirty three thousand young people under twenty-five years are officially counted as unemployed, although the true figure is in excess of 40,000.
A further 60,000 young men and women will leave full-time education in the coming summer months.
Their prospects of finding jobs are bleak.
(38) Irish inflation is the highest in the European Community and is forecasted to remain so.
Prices rose by 21% in the year to mid-February last.
For 1981, it is forecast that inflation will be at least 18%.
The result will be further inevitable cuts in living standards, a further loss of competitiveness and, therefore, more redundancies.
(39) Our balance of payments deficit has reached frightening proportions.
It will amount to over £ 1,300 million or 13% of our Gross Domestic Product, ten times the EEC average.
It is by far the largest in the European Community.
If nothing is done to correct this deficit, then devaluation of the currency within the EMS is inevitable.
And this will only lead to more inflation.
In the meantime, our external reserves have fallen to the equivalent of two months' imports only, compared with cover for four months in 1977.
(40) To add to the crisis, public borrowing is rising inexorably.
Servicing the public debt this year is estimated to cost £ 984 million, equivalent to four-fifths of all income tax collected.
About half of all public borrowing in recent years has been squandered on current expenditure and will show no lasting benefit for those who will have to repay it in the future.
In addition, foreign borrowing is dangerously high and is set to exceed £ 1,000 million in 1981 alone.
(41) The current budget deficit is out of control.
It is likely to exceed £ 800 million this year, compared with the £ 515 million forecasted in the last Fianna Fáil budget.
Immediate Policy Aims
(42) The immediate policy aims are clear if catastrophe is to be avoided:
Agricultural output must be restored.
(43) But above all, Labour's central priority is more jobs.
Employment must be protected and created.
All economic policy must be sub-ordinated to this aim.
Restraint in private consumption and a coherent approach to the rise of all money incomes is therefore essential.
Section Four: LABOUR'S ECONOMIC PROPOSALS
Inflation
(44) The key question is how to protect and create jobs.
The answer must be to conquer inflation.
(45) Most assuredly, a major contribution can be made by incomes moderation.
But that in itself will not be forthcoming unless there is a decisive and dramatic initiative in bringing down prices.
(46) The actual and expected level of inflation is of crucial importance to incomes determination.
It has a vital bearing on the competitiveness of the economy in general, on the structure of the budget, and on farm incomes.
For these weighty reasons, Labour proposes the following course of action on prices to the extent that the operation of an open economy will allow.
(47) Labour proposes to lower the rate of inflation by 4% through continuous subsidies on food items such as bread, flour, milk, butter, margarine and sugar;
and on public transport, electricity, gas and household coal.
(48) These subsidies will be maintained for the period of the three year plan outlined in paragraphs (57) to (64).

(49) These subsidies will only be introduced provided that the pay norms which emerge from the planning process, which are spelled out in paragraphs (53) to (56), are consistent with Labour's priorities for job protection and creation.
(50) These subsidies will only be maintained for such period as the pay norms are held.
(51) This programme will have an immediate favourable and beneficial effect on the economy, on the expectation of consumers and on the breaking of the inflationary psychology.

It will facilitate a fall in interest rates, and, therefore, in the level of Government debt service, create savings in public service pay and on Government purchases, modestly contribute to overall growth and tax buoyancy through increased employment, and save on transfers for social welfare and other inflation linked expenditure.
(52) To the extent that the programme is not self-financing, revenue will be raised by adjustments in the higher rates of income tax and by increased capital taxation referred to later.
Recouping the benefit of the subsidies from the higher income groups will meet most of the traditional arguments employed against subsidies.
Labour's Economic Proposals: Income Determination
(53) The introduction of price subsidies to reduce inflation will be inseparably linked to a new approach to incomes determination throughout the economy.
(54) The determination of money incomes is of critical importance to the competitiveness of the economy, to job creation and to the structure of the public finances.

For these reasons, incomes, jobs, taxation, prices, public and private investment, and social policy on health, education, social welfare and other areas, must be evaluated together in the context of the budgetary and balance of payments situations.
Free central wage-bargaining must be the foundation of this process.
(55) The critical part of this process will be the central pay norms established between the trade unions, employers, and the Government as employer.

But the norms must be established having regard to the protection of existing employment, the cost of creating new employment, the stats of the Exchequer finances and the size of the Balance of Payments deficit.

They must also be established against the background of Labour's policy of holding back price rises, of thereby increasing the social wage and, not least, of its moral commitment to a maintain the living standards of those on social welfare.
(56) Pay policy must be geared to salvaging the economy.

But it must be a policy freely accepted by the unions in particular and with a clear understanding on everybody's part that it is the key to beating both unemployment and inflation - and of restoring rising living standards when the crisis has been successfully overcome.
But there can be no doubt as to the necessity for sacrifice all round if these national objectives are to be met.
These are the issues that really matter;
Labour hare offers a strategy to deal with them.
The National Plan
(57) It has for long been Labour's socialist policy that the economy must be planned.
It is evident that the economic strategy outlined hers is the first real attempt to plan the Irish economy.
But this planning process must be based on new institutions invested with all the authority of the Stats and community-wide support.

(58) In order to achieve the coherent planning of the economy while avoiding the social disruption which results from a lack of real involvement in decision taking, Labour will take the following steps.

(59) Firstly, the establishment of a National Planning Board to be presided over by the Taoiseach of the day and involving all the senior economic ministers, together with representatives of the Trade Unions, Employer Organisations, Farming Organisations, as well as other social and public agencies.
(60) Secondly, the introduction of a three year National Economic and Social Plan to cover incomes, prices, employment, taxation, social expenditure, budgetary policy and economic growth.
The Budget will become the mechansim for implementing the Plan on an annual rolling basis.
Thus its broad outline will be the subject of discussion by the National Planning Board before it is enacted.
(61) A Department of Economic and Social Planning will be established to oversee the planning process and to ensure its implementation.

(62) Thirdly, all estimates of public expenditure, both current and capital, and of revenues and resources will be made available to the National Planning Board covering both the period of the plan and, in more detail, for each year in advance.
(63) Lastly, the setting up of a new Dail Committee on Public Finances to monitor and evaluate all estimates of income and expenditure.
The absence of such a mechanism at present is a serious deficiency in the management of the economy.
(64) If it does not prove possible, in any single year, to reach agreement on central pay norms on this basis, pay will be determined in the private sector by normal free collective bargaining.
In the public sector, pay will be determined later by bargaining in the context of Labour's priorities for job creation, investment, social policy and management of the economy.
The planning process will continue, in these eventualities, and decisions will be taken in the light of the outcome of overall pay negotiations.
Planning will remain, of course, the final responsibility of Government.
Saving the Irish Pound

(65) The introduction of food subsidies, the determination of incomes on the basis of protecting and creating jobs and the new planning process are all preconditions to winding down the rate of inflation.
(66) They are also essential preconditions for putting the public finances in order.
(67) These in turn are the necessary preconditions for future growth and development.
In other words, of more jobs and rising living standards.
(68) But even at that, before Labour unfolds its employment programme, equally decisive action is required in dealing with the Balance of Payments deficit.
Unless this is corrected, swiftly and substantially, it could undermine the strategy already outlined as well as the policies on employment which will follow.
(69) The paradox is that a general improvement in our economic performances would automatically lead to a corresponding, and very heavy increase in our import bill.
This would hasten a devaluation, in turn causing increased inflation and probably unemployment. This prospect must be prevented by the following exceptional measures.
(70) The Protocol to the Treaty of Accession to the European Community, negotiated in 1972, should be invoked for the very first time.
It should not be left dormant.
(71) The Protocol was negotiated in response to Labour Party criticisms that the economy could not withstand full free trade in the short run.
It provides for possible exceptional measures by this country to protect its vital economic interests in the event of a serious economic crisis.
(72) The whole point is that there is now a serious economic crisis.
(73) Labour, therefore, proposes a temporary import surcharge of 10% on selected consumer goods from other countries of the Community.
The import value of these goods in 1980 was just £ 1,100m.
(74) Such a surcharge would apply to about half of these imports and would last for one year only at the full rate.
It would be phased out over the subsequent years of this plan.
Goods manufactured in Northern Ireland would be excluded from the provisions of the surcharge.
(75) The objects will be:
(a) To ease pressure on the balance of payments;

(b) To generate a switch in demand in sensitive industries, such as parts of food processing, clothing, footwear, furniture, other household goods, in order to protect jobs while domestic costs were being brought under control;
(c) To prevent a devaluation of the Irish Pound inside EMS;
(d) To support the "Guaranteed Irish" Campaign;
(e) To provide a source of revenue to the Exchequer in the short-term.
(76) The surcharge will have a temporary adverse effect on consumer prices.
That is unavoidable and must be faced.
However, this will be far more than counter-balanced by the subsidies on basic items as stated earlier.
The alternative to measures such as this will be forced devaluation of the Irish Pound which would lead to a far greater increase in prices.
(77) Basic foodstuffs will not be subject to the surcharge.
Domestic price control will be strengthened on key items covered by the surcharge produced in Ireland.
Compensation for the price index effects of the surcharge will not be considered as relevant to the income determination process.
The main reason is that the revenue from the tariff will go to the funding of youth employment schemes.
This will be a contribution by all to meeting a primary social obligation.
(78) These derogations will of necessity have to be agreed by the European Community.

But, given that the aims of the three year plan are to cut inflation, current borrowing and the payments deficit, the Community will look more favourably on this course of action than might otherwise be the case.

(79) These proposals do not mean that Labour is advocating an abandonment of free trade and the spirit or letter of our obligations under the European Treaties, The protocol negotiated for Ireland, is an integral part of the Treaty and was won through pressure from Labour precisely to cover the type of critical situation which now prevails in the economy.

It is the duty of Government to make use of exceptional clauses at exceptional times, and it is in the ultimate interest of both Ireland and the Community that the Irish economic crisis is rectified in a planned, coherent and practical fashion.
(80) In summary, the Balance of Payments deficit is a serious constraint on all measures designed to salve the crisis.
If it is not reduced - and reduced dramatically - further devaluation will be imposed upon us, leading to inflation and more unemployment.
(81) At the same time, with unemployment surging upwards, Labour cannot countenance a deflationary policy as the remedy to the Balance of Payments crisis.
The unemployed cannot be made the victims of previous irresponsibility or a general refusal by all to face the facts of the present crisis.
(82) For these two reasons Labour will ask the European Community to permit the use of the protocol in imposing a tariff as suggested.
But, in addition, Labour will also seek substantial stand-by credit from other member states so as to sustain the value of the Irish pound during the adjustment period.
(83) The proceeds of the tariffs will be devoted in their entirety to the protection and creation of employment.
Employment: NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION

(84) The Labour Party has consistently argued that the private enterprise sector alone cannot create adequate employment to most the needs of an expanding population even in the most favourable economic climate.
Experience alone has shown this.
In these circumstances the state has a clear responsibility to engage directly in employment creation in the commercial sector to a considerably greater degree than at present.

(85) It is, therefore, proposed to create a National Development Corporation with the task of creating wealth and employment in potential growth sectors of the economy, either on its own or in joint ventures with other enterprises.
The National Development Corporation will have equity capital of £ 300 million to be taken up over a period of years.
Its upper borrowing limit will be £ 1,000 million.
(86) These proposals were activated prior to the 1977 General Election and had been worked at in considerable detail.
The principle has been Labour Party policy for many years.
(87) As a general rule the Corporation will invest in new projects and it will have power to invest in any organisation, public, co-operative or private.
It will also have the power to organise and develop new projects in its own right or through subsidiaries.
(88) It must be emphasised that the Corporation will not be a grant giving body.
That is the role of the IDA, which will remain unchanged.
(89) But it is incontestable that, against a drop of 10,000 in industrial employment over the last twelve months, a major innovation of this type is urgently needed.

Recent IDA criticism of lost opportunities, indicates that even in the middle of a depression a proper entre-preneurial approach by existing private enterprise could have created tens of thousands of additional jobs.
The Corporation will fill this gap in national enterprise.
Employment: Youth Employment Guarantee
(90) Labour realises that economic growth needed to substantially reduce unemployment will not occur overnight.
Interim and immediate measures are required to reduce the number out of work.
On the basis of current trends, unemployment could approach 200,000 within a relatively short period unless emergency measures are adopted.
The problem is particularly acute among the younger age group.

(91) The Labour Party believes that the whole community is prepared to make sacrifices for those, especially the young, who cannot find jobs, provided the sacrifices made are seen to lead directly to job creation and are not squandered for other purposes.
(92) Labour believes that the question of youth unemployment particularly requires decisive and direct action.
Our uniquely high population growth demands special measures.
These must revolve around an employment guarantee to our young.

(93) Labour will pledge to every person entering the Labour market that after three months if they have not found employment they will be guaranteed any one or a combination of the following for a period of three years:
(a) Training in AnCo;
(b) Participation in a Work Experience Programme;
(c) Employment in Environmental Improvement Schemes;
(d) Employment in Community and Youth Work;
(e) Employment by voluntary social and community organisations.
(94) The guarantee will also apply to any person under 25 years who has been continuously unemployed for more than twelve months.
(95) In all cases, training will be an integral part of the guarantee, with particular emphasis on the development of manual, managerial and entrepreneurial skills.

(96) In addition, Labour will introduce, as part of this guarantee scheme a system of grants to meet capital and labour costs for young people establishing co-operative enterprises on their own initiative.

(97) The cost of the Youth Employment Guarantee Scheme will be funded partly out of the tariff receipts (which will be devoted entirely to this project), partly by EEC grants from the Social Fund and partly from savings on welfare payments.
The balance will be met by a special levy on all incomes, excluding social welfare recipients, farmers under £ 40 PLV and others on low incomes.
The Youth Employment Levy will not exceed 1% of incomes and all of the revenue from it will be devoted to this purpose.
Unemployment is always an obscenity, but it is even more greviously so amongst those seeking a start in life.
(98) The guarantee scheme will be a component part of the three year plan.
Industrial Relations and Profit Sharing
(99) Major changes in psychological attitudes towards inflation, incomes moderation, innovation and growth, are essential to the success of the national plan.
(100) A fundamental reorganisation of company structures is demanded as an essential precondition of these changes.
In the public sector this will include the extension of the worker director principle.

It must also involve the implementation of the self management principle, particularly in the area of public administration where so much initiative and ability is currently frustrated by outmoded bureaucratic structures.
(101) In the private sector it must consist of giving employees a meaningful stake in the enterprise for which they work.
Labour will, therefore, extend to them the right to share in profits.
Consultation will take place with the trade unions and employer organisations on the most appropriate schemes.
(102) Linked to the concept of profit sharing, Labour will introduce legislation to give employees the right to information on the financial state of their firms.
Too often in the past employees have been shown the books as a prelude to being shown the door when it is too late to avoid a closure or redundancy.
(103) It is unfair and intolerable that workers should be unaware of the fortunes of the enterprise in which they work.
Workers have a moral right to this information in good times and bad.

(104) In addition, Labour will extend the concept of worker participation into the private sector by providing a legislative framework for the establishment, throughout industry and commerce, of representative Works Councils.
This is an essential prelude to the extension of the concept of Worker Directors into the private sector which Labour proposes.
(105) These major innovations will do much to contribute to a spirit of consensus rather than of confrontation which currently dominates the industrial relations scene.
They would also reflect the value of each individual worker and the contribution they make collectively to the common good.
Banking
(106) It is clearly essential that the investment and credit policies of the banking system should conform to the objectives of the National Plan.
New measures are needed to ensure that they do.
(107) The role of the Central Bank will be strengthened so that it can exercise greater control over credit policy within the context of the National Plan.
To avoid conflict of interest within the banking system, representatives of the private banking sector will not be eligible to be members of the Board of the Central Bank.

(108) A review of the functions of existing stats controlled financial institutions - notably the Agricultural Credit Corporation, the Industrial Credit Corporation and the Post Office Savings Banks - will be carried out with a view to developing their role in and share of the banking system.
(109) As an immediate measure of securing greater public control, Labour proposes that the Government should acquire a share-holding in the banks with provision for its enlargement.
This method for expanding public control is favoured because of the banks' long tradition of association with British banks.
The process of disengagement to greater public control must be carried through without any loss of public confidence.
The steps to be taken must be seen as responsible ones in the light of economic policy and the implementation of the principle of community control over capital resources.
Taxation and the Management of the Economy
(110) The Labour Party is committed to the introduction of an equitable and redistributive taxation system.
(111) Taxation policy, in addition, must be related to policies on jobs, prices, investment and the social services.
(112) Labour is opposed to any changes in the taxation code which could have the end effect of cutting essential public and social services.
These must be preserved and, where possible, enhanced.

Given the present crisis in the public finances and an expanding young population, there is limited potential in the short-term for any significant relief in the combined burden of direct and indirect taxes.
(113) The Labour Party's proposals on growth and job creation will lead to increased tax buoyancy and revenues over the period of the National Plan.

In the short-term, however, any scope for income tax relief will be directed mainly to those in the bottom one-third of taxable incomes, to ensuring that employees on low incomes are protected against any increase in the real burden of taxation and to protecting those who should not pay tax from entering the taxation net while their real income remains unchanged.
(114) Labour accepts the principles outlined in the White Paper "Capital Taxation" published by the Government in 1974.
(115) The partial implementation of these proposals in 1975 has been overturned by Fianna Fail, principally by the abolition of wealth tax and the dilution of capital gains tax.
(116) Labour will widen the base for capital taxation.
Since the early seventies, the erosion in the yield from capital taxes has been startling.
Inflation has increased two-fold and the yield from income tax almost six-fold.
The yield from capital taxes has only increased by 30%.
This is not equity.
(117) Labour will introduce, therefore, a comprehensive and properly structured system of capital taxation, including a wealth tax, capital gains tax and capital acquisitions tax.
The objective will be to ensure equity by an adequate yield from capital taxation, rising to at least £ 100 million in three years over the 1981 base.
The mechanics of a comprehensive capital taxation system will, in addition, serve to limit the evasion of income tax.
Special arrangements will apply in levying an annual wealth tax on productive assets.
(118) In addition, Labour will initiate the following taxation reforms:
(a) Loan interest on loans for a second private residence will not be deductible for tax purposes;
(b) The basic rate of Corporation Tax on financial institutions will be raised to 65%.
In the short-term a special surcharge will be levied on bank profits as a component of financing for the Youth Employment Guarantee Scheme.
(c) Labour will introduce differential rates of PRSI for employers with the object of improving competitiveness in exposed sections of the economy.
The rate for manufacturing, tourism and other activities subject to severe international competition will be lowered.
The rate on activities in the sheltered sections of the economy will be raised.
The new rates will be evaluated in Labour's national planning frame­work and the scheme will be self-financing.
Small Businesses
(119) Even in today's economy, small firms have a crucial part to play.
(120) Despite the growth of large-scale industrial companies, and the threat of the multinationals, small firms are crucial for the future development of our economy.
Small firms account for ninety percent of manufacturing establishments and employ about one-third of all those in the manufacturing sector.
National policy must have due regard to their importance.
(121) Labour will appoint a Minister of State for the Small Business and self-employed sector, within the Department of Industry, Commerce and Tourism.
The sector requires expansion, promotion and representation at this level and Government must provide for the sector's proper involvement in the planning system.
(122) Small scale enterprises must have the opportunity to expand without constraints which arise specifically from their size.

Schemes designed to help small firms to cope with necessary national legislation (for example, labour and social legislation) which may have a particular impact on them will be introduced in such a way as to protect all legitimate rights.
(123) Small firms often claim to suffer special disadvantages from the workings of the tax system and from the banking and credit system.
Assistance will be provided to small businesses to ensure that they can deal efficiently with the demands of the tax system.
The banking system, under public control, will provide schemes of appropriate financial support, e.g. for stock-funding.
(124) Labour believes that the self-employed and the small businessman must be afforded the full cover of the social welfare system.
A scheme for the social insurance of the self-employed will be introduced to provide adequate cover in the case of all relevant contingencies.

(125) Labour will further strengthen the present Small Industries programme of the IDA to create, in conjunction with the National Development Corporation a Small Business Section with general responsibility for the development of the entire small business sector and for co-ordination of programmes, aids, advice, etc.
Energy
(126) Tackling the energy crisis is basic to economic recovery.
(127) The economic problems of the past decade have been caused to a major extent by the growing world energy crisis.
For the eighties there must be a coherent national energy policy, to ensure our economic survival.
Such a policy must be based upon a massive and determined effort to lessen our dependence on imported oil as an energy source.
Nuclear power does not meet the requirements of a balanced energy policy.
(128) Energy management must be based upon coherent long range plans and rational structures for their implementation.
All aspects of the national energy-providing industry must be brought under the direct control of the Minister for Energy and operated within the ambit of the National Plan.
(129) The Irish National Petroleum Corporation and An Bord Gais will have responsibility for the implementation of national oil and gas development.
This will encompass control of exploration;
contracting with developers and the provision of appropriate state-controlled refinery and distribution capacity.
(130) The prospects for commercial oil and natural gas finds appear good.
This represents a challenge as well as an opportunity.
Labour will devise a comprehensive long-term plan for the utilisation of the resources arising from these national assets.
The benefit derived from them will be used in capital investment.
(131) Labour believes that nuclear power is not an acceptable element in the national energy programme.
The environmental hazards, the unacceptable risks of waste disposal and the overall economic uncertainties add up to a powerful case against this option.
(132) Special emphasis must be placed upon
Agriculture and Land Policy
(133) Agriculture has experienced a severe crisis.
Real incomes on farms have declined to 1972 levels.
Output is stagnant, while employment in food processing has fallen.
(134) There is no plan for agriculture.
Since EEC entry, agricultural policy has focussed almost exclusively an annual price negotiations in Brussels.
These are vitally important, but they must be accompanied by domestic measures to boost production and growth.
Brussels cannot ensure that Irish agriculture and related industries achieve their full potential.
We must do that here at home.
(135) The Labour Party has provided for representation of farmers' organisations on the National Planning Board.
This will be of crucial significance to the future of agricultural planning.
(136) The Labour Party's proposals to cut domestic inflation will mean that farm incomes will rise.
The fact that Irish inflation has consistently outstripped EEC price rises is the primary cause of the present crisis in agriculture.
(137) The Labour Party favours the retention of the recently announced subsidies on calves and fertiliser and aids for first time silage makers.
These are necessary given the absolute need to expand farm output again in the shortest possible time.
(138) Labour will seek to secure adjustments in the Common Agricultural Policy to achieve enhanced incomes through greater productivity and batter structural policies.

(139) In relation to Land Policy, the central objective must be to increase mobility in land ownership and, in particular, to increase the supply of land available to smaller, potentially development farmers.
The other side of the coin is that policy must seek to prevent the continuing accumulation of land by non-farmers and by those larger farmers whose need for it is no longer great.

(140) Given the substantial gap between the supply of land which becomes available on the market and the demand for it at reasonable prices, it is clearly necessary to control access to the agricultural land market.
Accordingly, the Labour Party proposes that access to land be limited to full-time farmers or to individuals who, within three years of purchase, intend to become full-time farmers.
Access to the land market should also be limited to those who have demonstrated that they are competent to farm efficiently and to meet minimum training and vocational requirements.
(141) The Land Commission must retain its land acquisition and distribution functions.

In addition to the retention of the Commission's land purchase role and the allocation to it of an adequate budget for this purpose, as far as possible the land purchased should be retained by the Commission and used as a land bank for long-lease arrangements.

While we do not rule out the value of transferring title to individual smallholders, as far as possible, the Commission should take on the role of arranging and overseeing long term leases from older, heirless farmers who are not themselves working the land to younger more commercially orientated farmers.
(142) Improved policies to secure earlier transfers of land from father to son or within the wider local kinship group are required.
The fact that 80% of all annual farm transfers occur through inheritance arrangements points to the merit of focussing special attention on ways in which such transfers can be speeded up.

Policy in this area should emphasise the positive rewards of retirement and land transfers and, of course, the security, welfare and protection of the older retirees should at all times be guaranteed.
(143) The Labour Party envisages the appointment of Special Socio-Economic advisers to facilitate the transfer of land from father to son, within the wider kinship or through the Land Commission.
In addition, these advisers could facilitate and encourage long-leasing arrangements by older, heirless farmers to younger developmental farmers.
(144) The Labour Party favours the integration of land transfer policies with income maintenance and development aid programmes.
These should be devised and implemented by a single state agency in a co-ordinated, coherent way.

In other words land transfer policy, Small Holders Assistance, rates remissions, Disadvantaged Area Schemes, welfare programmes and all other developmental aid schemes should form a range of policy instruments available to a new Rural Development Agency to promote effective development programmes.
